# Part XXIV — a whole vignette nothing linked to

## 316. The same defect as §314, one sentence away

The feature tour's opening reads:

> **Four companion vignettes** go deeper: `vignette("introduction")` ...
> `vignette("comparison")` ... `vignette("inference")` ...
> `vignette("supervised")` ... and `vignette("extending")` ...

Three numbers, none of which agree: the sentence says **four**, it lists
**five**, and there are **six** companion vignettes. The one it omits is
`monitoring` -- and it was the only vignette in the package that **no other
vignette referenced at all**:

| vignette | referenced by (before) |
|---|---|
| comparison, extending, inference, introduction, supervised | one or two others |
| ggchangepoint | comparison |
| **monitoring** | **nothing** |

The closing "next steps" paragraph omits it too, so streaming and online
monitoring -- an entire 0.5.0 feature area, with its own `cpt_monitor()`,
`cpt_update()`, `alarms()`, `cpt_replay()` and `cpt_delay()` -- was
unreachable by a reader working through the vignettes in R. `_pkgdown.yml`
lists it, so the website was fine; the offline path was not.

Corrected in both places, and the count now reads six. Re-measured: all
seven vignettes are referenced by at least one other.

## 317. Guarded, because this is now twice in two rounds

§314's guard was specific to the planned-engine sentence. This one
generalises the class: **every vignette must be referenced by another
vignette**, and the tour's own count of its companions must equal the
number of companions that exist.

Both halves proved to fire before being trusted:

- changing "Six" to "Five" -> the suite fails
- replacing both `vignette("monitoring")` references -> the suite fails,
  and the failure prints `"monitoring"` by name

The first attempt at the second half did **not** fire, because I removed
the reference from the opening sentence only and the closing paragraph
still had one -- so the assertion was right and my test of it was wrong.
Worth recording: a guard that "does not fire" needs the same scepticism as
one that fires.

**What this pass adds.** Both §314 and §316 are the same failure: a number

remaining risk in them is prose of exactly this shape. Enumerating those
sentences is now a cheap, finite job, and two of them have been wrong.

# Part XXV — the census, and the 0.4.0 number in the opening sentence

§316 said enumerating the vignettes' hand-written numbers was "a cheap,
finite job". Done: every number word or numeral in vignette *prose*
(chunks excluded) followed within three words by a package noun --
methods, engines, vignettes, rows, families, provenances, geoms, criteria.
**50 claims.** Most are structural and cannot rot ("one row per
changepoint", "one more row than `$changepoints`"). Six state a total, and
one of those was wrong.

## 320. The introduction advertised 31 methods

`vignettes/introduction.Rmd`, third line of the opening paragraph:

> a central dispatcher `cpt_detect()` covering **31** detection methods
> across six algorithmic families

**31 is the 0.4.0 number.** It is 50 -- and 31 -> 50 is the headline of the
release this vignette introduces. The first sentence of the first vignette a
reader opens advertised the previous version's capability.

Corrected. The "six algorithmic families" beside it stays: the vignette's
own §325 sentence enumerates six and §285 verified all eight sections it
names, so that number is internally consistent even though the feature tour
counts nine methodological families -- the two are different groupings, one
of the introduction's sections and one of the registry's.

Also corrected, and self-inflicted: the tour's 0.5.0 section said "**three**
companion vignettes develop these properly" while the closing paragraph --
which §316 had just changed -- lists four. Fixing one count exposed the
other.

## 321. Guarded, after five wrong versions of the guard

The total-method count changes every release, so it is worth a test rather
than a proofread. Getting the test right took more attempts than the fix:

1. **Too broad.** "Any number before `methods`" flagged the benchmarks
   article's "**Ten** methods raise **zero** false alarms" -- a measured
   subset, not a claim about the package. Narrowed to the five *totalising*
   constructions the vignettes actually use: `covering N methods`,
   `all N wired methods`, `wraps N detectors`, `N methods share one
   interface`, `N methods in this`.
2. **`[[` on a missing name errors** rather than returning `NULL`, so
   `words[[tok]] %||% NA` threw on "wrapped methods" instead of skipping it.
3. **The guard silently never fired.** `regmatches(m, regexpr(pat, sub(...)))`
   applies the offsets from the *substituted* string to the *original*, so
   it extracted `"co"` from `"covering 31 detection methods"` -- never a
   number, always skipped. Replaced with plain `sub()` calls.
4. **My verification of it was also wrong**: `sed 's/covering 50 detection/.../'`
   matched nothing, because the vignette has "covering 50" and "detection
   methods" on different lines. The test reads the file joined with spaces;
   `sed` works line by line. Two clean runs looked like proof and were
   proof of nothing.

Final state, verified in both directions: the clean tree passes, and
breaking the count in **each of the four vignettes that state a total**
fails the suite -- `introduction.Rmd`, `comparison.Rmd`, `extending.Rmd`
and `benchmarks.Rmd` -- while the benchmarks article's subset counts stay
quiet.

## 322. What this pass changes

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 320 | **the introduction's opening paragraph claimed 31 methods**; it is 50 | census of 50 prose numbers, then the registry |
| 320 | the tour said three 0.5.0 companion vignettes where its own closing list now names four | reading both after §316's edit |
| 321 | the guard was wrong four different ways before it worked, including one version that could never fire | deliberate breakage in four files |

New actions: none opened. Two prose corrections and one guard.

**What this pass adds.** Fifth instrument error in this document, and the
most instructive: version 3 of the guard *passed on a clean tree and passed
on a broken one*. A test that cannot fail is worse than no test, because it
reports safety. The only thing that caught it was breaking the file on
purpose -- which is now the standing rule for every guard added here, and it
has paid for itself four times (§290, §302.1, §314, §321).

# Part XXVI — attribution: are the citations pointing at the right work?

The standing instruction asks whether citations are "attributed to the right
work". Keys resolving (§313) is a weaker property than that. The package
carries its own answer: `cpt_cite(method)` returns, per method, the paper
the package says introduced it. So the two can be checked against each
other.

## 323. A check that had to be redesigned before it said anything

**First attempt: co-location.** For each method, collect the `@keys` on
prose lines that mention the method's name, and compare their first author
with `cpt_cite()`'s. It paired only **4 of 50** methods -- method names
mostly appear inside chunks, and citations mostly sit in different
sentences -- and its single flag was `ecp` "citing" `@grundy2020geomcp`,
which is one sentence mentioning two engines. Useless in both directions.

**Second attempt, well-defined:** does the paper `cpt_cite()` names exist
*anywhere* in the two bibliographies -- matching on first-author surname and
year across all 123 pooled entries? That question has an answer, and it
found four.

## 324. Two founding papers were named in prose and in no bibliography

| method | `cpt_cite()` says | status |
|---|---|---|
| `segneigh` | Auger and Lawrence (1989) | **absent from both bibs** |
| `amoc` | Hinkley (1970) | **absent from both bibs** |
| `mcp` | Lindelov (2020) | present as `lindelov2020mcp`; the matcher cannot equate `Lindel{\o}v` with ASCII |
| `fcov` | Aue, Rice and Sonmez (2020) | absent, and correctly so |

`introduction.Rmd` names the first two **as bare parentheticals** --
"segment neighbourhoods (Auger and Lawrence, 1989), and at-most-one-change
(AMOC; Hinkley, 1970)" -- in a sentence where every other method carries a
real citation (`[@killick2012pelt]`, `[@scott1974cluster]`,
`[@maidstone2017optimal]`). So two of the four `changepoint` methods the
package has wrapped since 0.1.0 appeared in the text and **never in the
References**.

Fixed: both added to `vignette_reference.bib` with the metadata
`cpt_cite()` already carries -- volume, issue, pages -- and **no invented
DOIs** -- and the parentheticals replaced with `[@auger1989segment]` and
`[@hinkley1970inference]`. Verified by rendering: **0 unresolved citation
markers**, each new key appearing twice in the HTML, once as "(Auger and
Lawrence 1989)" in the text and once in the bibliography block.

`fcov` is the interesting non-fix. `cpt_cite("fcov")` cites Aue, Rice and
Sönmez (2020) on covariance operators and adds "See also ... (2018)", while
`fmean` cites the 2018 functional-mean paper -- two different papers,
correctly distinguished. The 2020 one is in no bibliography because **no
vignette discusses `fcov` at all**: every "functional" in the vignettes
means functional *pruning* (`fpop`, `cpop`, `decafs`), a different idea.
Adding an entry nothing cites would just recreate §313's dead weight, and
`cpt_cite()` already gives the reference in full -- the same conclusion
Demšar reached in §313.

## 325. What this pass changes

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 323 | the co-location design paired 4 of 50 methods and its one flag was spurious; withdrawn | ran it |
| 324 | **`segneigh` and `amoc` were cited in prose and in neither bibliography** | 50 methods' `cpt_cite()` authors and years against 123 pooled bib entries |
| 324 | 0 unresolved citations after the fix; both render in text and bibliography | `rmarkdown::render()`, counting `???` |

New actions: none opened. Two bibliography entries, two prose citations.

**What this pass adds.** `cpt_cite()` turned out to be the right oracle for
a question the bibliography cannot answer about itself. "Does every key
resolve" is a closed loop -- the bibliography checked against the text that
cites it. "Does the package's own record of who invented each method appear
in the bibliography" compares two independently maintained lists, and that
is where the gap was.

# Part XXVII — the help pages and `cpt_cite()` disagreed about seven methods

§324 compared `cpt_cite()` against the *bibliographies*. The same oracle
compared against the *help pages* -- for each of the 50 methods, the
`\insertRef` keys in its wrapper's roxygen block versus the author and year
`cpt_cite()` gives -- flags **15**.

## 326. Eight of the fifteen are correct by design

| pattern | methods | why it is right |
|---|---|---|
| one Rd covers five methods | `pelt`, `binseg`, `segneigh`, `amoc`, `np` | `cpt_wrapper()` documents all five, so its `@references` cites the **software** paper (`killick2014changepoint`) while `cpt_cite()` resolves each **method** paper -- Killick 2012, Scott and Knott 1974, Auger and Lawrence 1989, Hinkley 1970, Haynes 2017 |
| software paper on the Rd | `ecp` | Rd cites `james2014ecp`, `cpt_cite()` gives Matteson and James 2014 |
| LaTeX escape | `mcp` | `Lindel{\o}v` versus ASCII `Lindelov` |

That is the division of labour the package intends: the help page names the
package you are calling, `cpt_cite()` names the paper you should cite.

## 327. Seven wrappers cited nothing at all

`fpop_wrapper()`, `wbs_wrapper()`, `wbs2_wrapper()`, `not_wrapper()`,
`mosum_wrapper()`, `idetect_wrapper()` and `tguh_wrapper()` had **no
`@references` block and no `\insertRef`** -- seven method help pages with no
reference, where the other forty-three have one.

The cause is upstream of the roxygen: none of the seven keys existed in
`inst/REFERENCES.bib`. They were in `vignettes/vignette_reference.bib`
only, and `\insertRef{key}{ggchangepoint}` reads the *installed* bibliography,
so the reference could not have been inserted even if someone had tried.
Copied across -- `maidstone2017optimal`, `fryzlewicz2014wild`,
`fryzlewicz2020detecting`, `baranowski2019narrowest`,
`eichinger2018mosum`, `anastasiou2022idetect`, `fryzlewicz2018tail` -- and
each wrapper given the `@references` block its siblings have.

## 328. And one help page credited the wrong paper

`fcov_wrapper()` detects changes in the **covariance operator** of a
functional series. Its Rd cited `aue2018fchange` -- "Detecting and dating
structural breaks in functional data without dimension reduction" -- which
is `fmean_wrapper()`'s paper, cited from the same file eleven lines above.
`cpt_cite("fcov")` has the right one and always did: Aue, Rice and Sönmez
(2020), "Structural break analysis for spectrum and trace of covariance
operators", *Environmetrics* 31(1), e2617.

So a reader of `?fcov_wrapper` was sent to a paper about the functional
*mean* for a method about *covariance*. Added `aue2020covariance` to
`inst/REFERENCES.bib` and repointed the reference.

This is the entry §324 deliberately did **not** add to the vignette
bibliography, on the grounds that nothing cited it. That reasoning still
holds and this is not a reversal: the entry belongs in the bibliography
where it is cited, and it is cited from an Rd, so it goes in the Rd's
bibliography.

Re-measured: **15 flags -> 7**, all seven the design cases above. All **58**
`\insertRef` keys across `R/` resolve, 0 missing.

## 329. What this pass changes

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 326 | 8 of 15 flags are the intended software-versus-method split | read each |
| 327 | **7 wrappers had no reference at all**, because their keys were only in the vignette bibliography and `\insertRef` cannot see that file | roxygen blocks against `inst/REFERENCES.bib` |
| 328 | **`?fcov_wrapper` cited the functional-mean paper for a covariance method** | `cpt_cite("fcov")` against the Rd |

New actions: none opened. Eight bibliography entries, seven `@references`
blocks, one corrected reference.

**What this pass adds.** §327's cause is worth the note: the seven missing
references were not an oversight in the roxygen, they were *impossible*.
`\insertRef` reads `inst/REFERENCES.bib`; the keys lived in
`vignettes/vignette_reference.bib`; two bibliographies that look
interchangeable are not, and the failure is silent -- no warning, no check
note, just a help page with no reference. Which bibliography a citation
mechanism reads is worth knowing before wondering why nothing renders.

# Part XXVIII — two bibliographies, one paper, two author lists

## 330. 47 shared keys, one divergence

The two bibliographies overlap by **47 keys**, and a key present in both
with different content renders one way in a vignette's References and
another in a help page. Compared entry by entry -- author list plus title,
journal, volume, number, pages, year, doi, publisher:

**One divergence.** `zhao2019beast`:

| file | authors |
|---|---|
| `vignette_reference.bib` | `Zhao, Wulder, Hu and others` -- three named, then `et al.` |
| `inst/REFERENCES.bib` | all **eleven**: Zhao, Wulder, Hu, Bright, Wu, Qin, Li, Toman, Mallick, Zhang, Brown |

Everything else about the entry is identical, so the same paper printed a
three-author list in the vignette bibliography and an eleven-author list in
the help pages. The full list is the accurate one; the vignette bib now
carries it too. Re-measured: 47 shared keys, **0** with differing author
lists.

`cpt_cite("beast")` renders "Zhao, K., Wulder, M. A., Hu, T., et al.
(2019)", which is a citation *string* and correctly abbreviates -- that is a
different artifact from a bibliography entry and needs no change.

## 331. `inst/CITATION` hard-coded the version twice

`citation("ggchangepoint")` is reader-visible and the file agreed with
`DESCRIPTION` on every field -- title, author, URL, and version 0.5.0. But
the version was **written out twice as a literal**, in `note` and again in
`textVersion`, so the next bump would leave `citation()` advertising the
previous release. That is §320's defect (the introduction's stale "31
methods") waiting to happen in the citation a user pastes into a paper.

Both now read `meta$Version`, which is what R passes to a CITATION file and
what *Writing R Extensions* recommends. Verified by bumping `DESCRIPTION`
to 0.6.0 in place: both fields report 0.6.0 and **no 0.5.0 remains**
anywhere in the rendered entry. Restored.

## 332. What this pass changes

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 330 | **the same paper carried a 3-author list in one bibliography and 11 in the other** | 47 shared keys x 9 fields, both files parsed with `rbibutils` |
| 331 | `inst/CITATION` hard-coded the version in two places | read it against `DESCRIPTION`, then bumped the version to see what moved |

New actions: none opened. One author list, one self-updating version.

**What this pass adds.** §331 is a defect that does not exist yet, which is
a category this document has not knowingly worked in before: every claim
audited so far was already true or already false. A literal that must be
edited in lock-step with another file is *guaranteed* to go stale, and the
cost of finding it later is a wrong citation in someone's paper. Worth
looking for the rest of them -- the version string is the obvious one, and
the year `2026` in the same file is the next.

# Part XXIX — the lock-step literals, and a guard debugged three ways

§331 ended by asking where the rest of the "must be edited in lock-step"
literals are. Answer: two, both unavoidable, now guarded.

## 333. The own-version thread closes clean

Every `0.5.0` in `R/` and `tests/` is a **historical comment** -- "0.5.0:
diagnostics, selection and influence", "0.5.0 layers: the objects the
package could not draw before" -- which stays true forever. The only code
that reads a version uses `packageVersion()`, and the one version
*comparison* (`packageVersion("HDCD") <= "1.1"`, the Pilliat guard) is about
an upstream package and documented. Nothing to fix.

## 334. Two files state the method total and cannot compute it

| file | text |
|---|---|
| `DESCRIPTION` | "a 'cpt_detect()' dispatcher covering fifty methods" |
| `R/ggchangepoint.R` -> `man/ggchangepoint-package.Rd` | "dispatcher \code{cpt_detect()} that reaches fifty methods" |

Both are correct today. Neither can be computed -- `DESCRIPTION` and Rd are
static text -- so the literal has to stay, which makes them precisely the
shape that goes stale on the next engine wave, exactly as §320's "31
detection methods" did in a vignette. §321's guard now covers them
alongside the four vignettes that state a total.

## 335. Three bugs between writing the guard and having one

Extending a working guard to two more files took three fixes, and all three
presented as "the guard does not fire":

1. **Indented continuation lines.** `DESCRIPTION` wraps as
   "dispatcher covering\n    fifty methods", so joining lines with a single
   space leaves a *run* of blanks and a pattern written with literal spaces
   never matches. Fixed by normalising whitespace before matching -- which
   also retires the line-wrap trap that bit §321's verification.
2. **My verification, again.** Breaking the Rd with a plain string replace
   looked like it had worked and the guard stayed silent, so I concluded the
   path was unresolved. The path was fine.
3. **The real bug: a half-added pattern.** The new
   `reaches ([A-Za-z0-9]+) methods` pattern was added to the pattern list
   but `reaches` was never added to the alternation that strips the leading
   word before reading the number. So `tok` came out as `"reaches"`, which
   is not a numeral and not a number word, and every match was silently
   skipped. A pattern and its parser are two edits, and only one of them was
   made.

Final state: clean tree passes; breaking the count fires in
`DESCRIPTION`, `man/ggchangepoint-package.Rd` and the four vignettes, with
the offending phrase quoted -- `"ggchangepoint-package.Rd: 'reaches thirty
methods' but the registry has 50"`.

## 336. Standing vignette check

| | |
|---|---|
| bibliography entries / cited / broken | 70 / 63 / **0** |
| uncited (all `\insertRef`'d from Rd) | 7 |
| `\insertRef` keys in `R/` / unresolved | 58 / **0** |
| available / planned methods, against the guarded prose | 50 / 5 |

## 337. What this pass changes

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 333 | no rotting own-version literal; every `0.5.0` in code is a historical comment | grep over `R/`, `tests/`, `inst/`, `.github/` |
| 334 | **`DESCRIPTION` and the package Rd state the method total as a literal**, uncomputable and unguarded | grep, then the registry |
| 335 | the extended guard failed three different ways, twice looking like a path problem | deliberate breakage per file |

New actions: none opened. One guard extended; no package behaviour changed.

**What this pass adds.** §335.3 is the sharpest version of a lesson this
document keeps relearning: **a guard that reports "pass" is making a claim,
and it is the claim least likely to be checked.** Three of the four guards
added in this loop needed a deliberate breakage to reveal that they could
not fail. The discipline is cheap -- break the input, watch the failure name
the input -- and it has now caught more defects in the guards than the
guards have caught in the package.

# Part XXX — CI green, and the one anomaly it surfaced

`7ece62f` pushed to `master`. All five R-CMD-check jobs succeeded, plus
pkgdown and the pages deployment. macOS carries only the known
environmental note (`rgl` failing to `dlopen` for want of `libGLU`).

## 338. Windows reports WARN 10 where every other platform reports 2

Not a failure, but a platform difference worth reading rather than
ignoring. It decomposes cleanly:

| count | source | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | `test-040-polish.R:1050` -- `NaNs produced` from envcpt's arima fits | the data-dependent case §308 deliberately left unasserted; the test's own comment predicts exactly this |
| 1 | `test-050-registry.R:275` -- `JAGS failed ... Returning an mcpfit without samples` | investigated below |

The nine confirm §308's decision rather than undermining it: the comment
there says "whether a given series also triggers an upstream convergence
*warning* is data-dependent", and a different platform's BLAS producing
nine instead of two is that sentence being right.

## 339. The mcp/JAGS path is already correct -- and its comment says otherwise

The Windows runner installs `mcp` but not JAGS. So `requireNamespace("mcp")`
succeeds, `mcp::mcp()` **warns** rather than errors, and hands back an
`mcpfit` with no posterior samples. That is S35's trap ("having the package
is not the same as being able to run it") arriving on a platform CRAN
tests.

**The wrapper handles it.** `mcp_has_samples(fit)` catches the sample-less
fit and stops with an actionable message naming JAGS, so
`cpt_detect(x, method = "mcp")` on Windows errors rather than returning a
result built from a model that never sampled. My §S-era fitted sweep wraps
its call in `tryCatch`, so mcp is skipped and only the warning escapes.

What was wrong is the comment fifteen lines above the guard:

> `mcp` imports `rjags`, so a successful `requireNamespace("mcp")` already
> implies JAGS is present.

That is false, and it is false in exactly the way the code below it exists
to handle -- `rjags` loads on a machine with no JAGS program. A reader
trimming "redundant" checks would have deleted the guard on the strength of
it. Rewritten to say what the first check is for (the common case, with the
install instruction) and why the second is not redundant.

The escaping warning is now muffled by message text in the sweep, the way
§308 handled the other three, so the Windows report will show 9 rather
than 10 and every remaining warning is one a reader is meant to see.

## 340. What this pass changes

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 338 | Windows's extra warnings are 9 envcpt `NaNs produced` plus 1 mcp/JAGS notice; neither is a defect | `gh run view --job --log` on the Windows job |
| 339 | **a comment asserted the premise its own guard disproves**, and the guard is correct | read the wrapper against the runner's behaviour |

New actions: none opened. One comment, one muffle.

**What this pass adds.** The instructive part is where the defect was. The
*code* had already learned S35's lesson; the *comment* still carried the
belief that predated it. Comments do not get re-derived when the code below
them changes, and this one had become an argument for deleting the fix.

# Part XXXI — are the workarounds still needed, and still right?

§339 found a comment whose premise its own guard disproved. The same
question, asked of the comments that encode *upstream* behaviour: this
package carries a dozen workarounds justified by "engine X does Y", and if
X has since changed, the workaround is either wrong or unnecessary. Nothing
re-checks them. Tested against the engine versions actually installed --
changepoints 1.1.0, ocd 1.1, ChangePointTaylor 0.3, bcp 4.0.4, HDCD 1.1,
bfast 1.7.2, binsegRcpp 2025.5.13.

## 341. All six hold

| assumption | measured |
|---|---|
| `changepoints::thresholdBS()` returns `cpt_hat = NULL`, not a zero-row matrix, when nothing clears | `class NULL`, `is.null TRUE` -- holds |
| `bcp::bcp()` cannot take n = 3 (it segfaults), so the wrapper demands n >= 4 | guard holds: "`x` must have at least 4 observations" |
| `HDCD::Pilliat()` 1.1 is untrustworthy at a power-of-two coordinate count | guard holds at p = 4 |
| `bfast` reports "no breakpoints" as a bare logical, not an empty breakpoints object | `bp.Wt` class `logical` -- holds |
| `ocd::normalisedStatistics()` is **already divided** by the threshold, so compare against 1 | holds: statistics 2.602, thresholds 5.389, normalised **0.483** = 2.602/5.389 |
| `ChangePointTaylor` returns its interval as the string `"(a - b)"` | holds: `"(61 - 61)"` |

Two of the six needed a second attempt, and both times the probe was
wrong rather than the package:

- The `ocd` check first passed `thresh = c(1, 1, 1)`, which makes "compare
  against 1" true by construction and tests nothing. Re-run with the
  default Monte Carlo thresholds, the arithmetic is visible and the claim
  is confirmed.
- The `ChangePointTaylor` check looked for a field called
  `confidence_interval` and got nothing back, which read like a broken
  workaround. The column is actually named **`CI (95%)`** -- with the
  confidence level *inside the column name*.

## 341.1 That column name is a trap the wrapper already avoids

`change_point_analyzer(x, CI = 0.9)` returns a column called `CI (90%)`,
not `CI (95%)`. A wrapper that hard-coded the name would break the moment a
user passed `conf_level`. `taylor_wrapper()` uses
`grep("^CI", names(fit))[1]`, and it works: measured at `conf_level` 0.95,
0.90 and 0.99 the upstream column is `CI (95%)`, `CI (90%)`, `CI (99%)`
respectively, and the returned intervals widen as they should -- `[60, 60]`
-> `[59, 60]` -> `[58, 60]`.

## 342. Standing vignette check

| | |
|---|---|
| bibliography entries / cited / broken | 70 / 63 / **0** |
| uncited (all `\insertRef`'d from Rd) | 7 |
| vignettes / unreachable from another vignette | 7 / **none** |
| `\insertRef` keys / unresolved | 58 / **0** |
| available / planned, against the guarded prose | 50 / 5 |

## 343. What this pass changes

Nothing in the package: six upstream assumptions re-verified, all holding.

| § | finding | measured how |
|---|---|---|
| 341 | all six load-bearing upstream assumptions hold at the installed versions | one direct call per assumption |
| 341.1 | `ChangePointTaylor` puts the confidence level in the column name; the wrapper matches on a prefix and survives it | three confidence levels |

**What this pass adds.** A workaround is a claim about someone else's code,
and it is the only kind of claim in this package that can become false
without anything here changing. Six were checked and six held -- but the
value is in having a runnable record of *what* they assume, because the next
engine update is the event that breaks one, and nothing in `R CMD check`
would say so.

# Part XXXII -- The upstream claims, enumerated rather than remembered

## 344. Why the previous pass was too thin

§343 checked six upstream assumptions because six were the ones I could
recall. That is not an audit, it is a memory test. Every contiguous comment
block in `R/*.R` that names a package from Imports or Suggests was extracted
instead -- 323 blocks -- and filtered to those making a *behavioural* claim
(a `pkg::fn` reference, or the package name within 70 characters of
`errors|warns|returns|refuses|requires|segfaults|silently|...`), leaving
**105**. What follows is what testing them found.

A workaround is a claim about someone else's code. It is the only kind of
claim in this package that can become false without anything here changing,
and `R CMD check` will never say so.

## 345. Five claims were wrong, and each had justified a workaround

| where | the comment said | measured |
|---|---|---|
| `wrap-functional.R` | "two **or three** columns" are too coarse a grid, so fChange stops | only **two** fail; ncol 3, 4 and 6 all return a fit |
| `wrap-nonparam.R` | `GLRAdjusted`/`ExponentialAdjusted` are both "rejected by cpm's own dispatch" | `GLRAdjusted` is rejected; **`ExponentialAdjusted` runs** and returns changepoints |
| `wrap-highdim.R` | `ocd::ChangepointDetector()` fails at `dim = 1` with "subscript out of bounds" | it fails, but with **"'dims' cannot be of length 0"**, and only under the wrapper's default `thresh = "MC"` -- given an explicit numeric `thresh` it constructs fine at `dim = 1` |
| `broom-methods.R` | non-Normal test statistics **warn** "Not changed to be -2*logLik" | CUSUM/CSS **error** ("logLik is only valid for distributional assumptions"); that *warning* comes from the `cpt.range` path instead -- the two were swapped |
| `wrap-search.R` | breakfast's default `"lp"` "reports spurious changepoints on constant data" | not reproducible: `"lp"`, `"ic"` and the real default (**`NULL`**, not `"lp"`) agree on all four series tried -- 0 changepoints in constant, near-constant and pure noise, and the single step at 100 in a two-segment series |

None of these broke a user's result -- the workarounds are all
conservative -- but each recorded a reason that was not the reason, which is
how the next reader gets sent after the wrong argument.

## 346. Two real defects in `cpm_wrapper()`

**`cpm_type = "FET"` could not succeed.** It is offered by `match.arg()` and
documented, but `cpm::processStream()` has no default for `lambda`, and
without one it dies inside cpm with base R's "only 0's may be mixed with
negative subscripts" -- a message about neither the argument nor the method.
Confirmed across Gaussian, Bernoulli, integer and 0/1-as-double input, and
across six `startup`/`ARL0` combinations: 0 successes. cpm ships FET
thresholds for `lambda = 0.1` and `0.3` **only** (swept 0.01-1.0), and with
either one the wrapper returns the right answer -- 1 changepoint at 154 for a
true change at 150.

**A `lambda` problem was reported as an `arl0` problem.** cpm prints the same
"No thresholds available" line for both arguments, and the branch that
catches it assumed `arl0`. So `cpm_wrapper(y, cpm_type = "FET",
lambda = 0.5)` answered ``  `arl0 = 500` is not an average run length that
cpm ships thresholds for `` -- about a value the caller had set correctly.
The printed line names which argument it means ("selected lambda" vs
"selected ARL0"); the branch now reads it.

## 347. `?cpt_detect` promised a list it had outgrown

The help page names the engines whose own signature ends in `...`, so that a
misspelt argument is discarded upstream rather than reported -- which makes
it a promise about *every other* method. Sweeping all 49 installed methods
with an impossible argument name found **three** that swallow it and were not
named: `fmean` and `fcov` (both \pkg{fChange}) and `bfast`. A reader checking
the list would have concluded their typo had been caught.

Nine methods swallow, forty error. The sweep is now the test, because a
hand-maintained list of upstream behaviour is exactly the thing that drifts.

## 348. Both bibliographies had drifted, in the direction nothing checked

§342 recorded "7 uncited, all `\insertRef`'d from Rd" as benign. Six were.
The seventh, `demsar2006comparisons`, was in **both** files and cited by
**neither**, and the Rd bibliography separately carried two entries
(`jewell2022testing`, `londschien2023changeforest`) that only the vignettes
cite. With no `\insertAllCited` anywhere in the package, none of the ten
rendered anywhere: each was dead weight that read as though an attribution
existed. Each bibliography now holds exactly what its own consumer cites --
**63 / 63** in the vignettes, **58 / 58** in the help pages.

The R44 test checked only that a *citation resolves*. It now also checks that
an *entry is cited*, in both files. Proving it fires meant breaking all four
directions:

| break | result |
|---|---|
| baseline | 84 pass, 0 fail |
| cite a key with no bib entry | fails, names `zzzmissingkey` |
| add an uncited vignette-bib entry | fails, names `zzz2099nobodycites` |
| add an unused Rd-bib entry | fails, names `zzz2098unusedrd` |
| restored | 84 pass, 0 fail |

The first attempt at that proof proved nothing: `skip_on_cran()` meant R44
never ran, and the "passing" break was a skip. Under `NOT_CRAN=true` the
guard then failed on the *real* tree -- correctly, because the existing
citation regex demanded a four-digit year and so could not see `@rcore`.
Any misspelling of a yearless key had been invisible to this test since it
was written. The pattern now matches pandoc's key syntax with a lookbehind
for the email case: 63 candidates across the seven vignettes, every one a
real key, zero false positives.

# Part XXXIII -- What a documented pass-through actually does

## 354. Twelve arguments the docs invited and R refused

`...` is documented on every wrapper as reaching the engine. Eight wrappers
also pin one of that engine's own arguments -- and there was no check, so the
two promises collided inside R's argument matcher:

```
envcpt_wrapper(x, verbose = TRUE)
#> Error: formal argument "verbose" matched by multiple actual arguments
```

That message names neither the wrapper, nor the engine, nor what to do
instead. Sweeping every registry method against every argument its wrapper
hardcodes to a literal that the engine also accepts found **twelve** such
pairs:

| method | argument(s) |
|---|---|
| `wbs2`, `tguh` | `solution.path`, `model.selection` |
| `smuce` | `jumpint` |
| `bocpd` | `getR` |
| `beast` | `season`, `quiet`, `print.progress` |
| `decafs` | `warningMessage` |
| `sn` | `plot_SN` |
| `envcpt` | `verbose` |

**The pins are all deliberate, so honouring them is the wrong fix.**
`solution.path` is what makes `tguh` tguh; `jumpint` is what makes SMUCE's
`ci_lower`/`ci_upper` columns exist at all; `getR` is what
`ggcpt_runlength()` draws; `plot_SN` is what stops SNSeg drawing to the
active device; the rest keep engine narration out of the result. So they are
refused by name instead, through one shared helper, each with the reason it
is fixed:

```
#> Error: `tguh` sets `solution.path` itself, so it cannot be supplied
#> through `...`: it is what selects the tail-greedy unbalanced-Haar path
#> rather than one of breakfast's others -- a `tguh` result with a
#> different path is not tguh.
```

Re-swept afterwards: **0** raw collisions remain, all twelve refuse by name,
and the five arguments that were legitimately accepted before still are
(`envcpt_wrapper(x, minseglen = 10)` among them). Proved by disabling one
guard, which brought the raw message straight back and failed the new test
with two expectations naming `envcpt verbose`.

## 355. The vignettes disagreed about the package

`introduction.Rmd`: "50 detection methods across **six** algorithmic
families". `ggchangepoint.Rmd`: "50 methods across **nine** methodological
families". Same 50 methods, same package, two numbers.

"Family" is a prose taxonomy, not a registry column, so neither number can be
derived -- but the introduction *enumerates* its six (penalised and optimal
partitioning, multiscale and search, Bayesian, nonparametric and sequential,
multivariate and high-dimensional, regression-based) and has one section per
family plus two for the cross-cutting concerns it names, which is exactly the
eight tour sections it has. The nine had no enumeration and nothing in the
package counts to it: `_pkgdown.yml` has eleven wrapper groups, not nine.
`ggchangepoint.Rmd` now says six.

Guarded both ways -- the vignettes must agree, and the number must equal the
list the introduction spells out. Proved by reintroducing the disagreement
(fails, quoting both files) and by deleting one family from the enumeration
(fails, 5 against 6). The enumeration parse needed one correction of its own:
four of the six names contain their own "and", so splitting on `,| and ` read
a list of six as ten.

`EnvCpt`'s stderr diversion cited "Error in arima(...): non-stationary AR

do is swallow real conditions, and it does not: a genuine convergence
warning still reaches the user.

The error-message sweep -- every backticked name in a `stop()`/`warning()`
checked against the enclosing function's formals -- found **no** new defects
across 23 candidates. All are column names, aesthetics, or another

# Part XXXIV -- Two engines that were mostly broken, and nobody knew

## 359. The result contract holds everywhere

Before hunting bugs, a baseline: every method's returned `ggcpt` was checked
against the documented contract on five input shapes each -- an ordinary
two-segment series, pure noise, a change 8 observations from the start, one 8
from the end, and a 30-point series. **245 cells, zero violations.** What was
checked, per cell: `cp` integer, inside \eqn{[1, n-1]}, sorted, unique, no
NA; `cp_value` equal to the series at `cp`; `segments` tiling \eqn{1..n}
contiguously with `n = end - start + 1` and one more row than there are
changepoints; `method` and `change_in` length-one; `data` with `n` rows.

That is the invariant the rest of the package is built on, and it is now
measured rather than assumed. The sweep is also what surfaced both defects
below -- not as contract violations, but as *errors* in cells that should
have produced a result.

## 360. `wbsts` could not report more than one changepoint

`wbsts::wbs.lsw()` ends with

```r
OUT = post.processing(...)          # the post-processed breakpoint set
suppressWarnings(if (is.na(OUT)) OUT = NULL)
```

That `suppressWarnings()` was the right fix when `if` on a length > 1
condition was a *warning*. Since R 4.2 it is an **error**, and
`suppressWarnings()` does nothing for an error. So the call dies with "the
condition has length > 1" exactly when post-processing keeps two or more
changepoints -- which is to say, whenever the method would report more than
one.

Measured on R 4.4.1, before the fix:

| series | runs | failures | changepoints reported on success |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 change, n = 120 | 20 | 2 | 0 or 1 |
| 3 changes, n = 400 | 20 | **19** | 1 |
| 5 changes, n = 600 | 20 | **19** | 0 |

A wrapper cannot patch upstream, but every piece `wbs.lsw()` uses --
`tau.fun`, `ews.trans`, `uh.wbs`, `post.processing` -- is exported by
\pkg{wbsts}. So the failure is caught, `.Random.seed` is restored to what it
was before the call, and the body is replayed line for line with the single
line corrected to `all(is.na(OUT))`, which is what the surrounding
`suppressWarnings()` shows was meant.

**Restoring the seed is the point.** It means the replay draws the identical
random intervals, so it does not return a *different* answer -- it returns
the one the upstream function had already computed and then threw away.
Verified: on 30 runs where `wbs.lsw()` succeeds, the replay's `cp.bef` and
`cp.aft` are `identical()` to upstream's **30 out of 30**. Afterwards the
table above reads 0 failures in all three rows, with counts up to 6 and 8 --
the method now finds the multiple changepoints it exists to find. An
unrelated upstream refusal (one scale) still propagates untouched.

## 361. `hdcov` failed on 44-96% of runs, intermittently

`changepoints::thresholdBS.BS()` prunes the binary-segmentation tree with

```r
for (i in 2:level_length) { ... 1:table(BS_object$Level)[i] ... }
```

so a **single-level** tree makes that `2:1`, the body runs with `i = 2`,
`table(...)[2]` is `NA`, and `1:NA` stops with base R's "NA/NaN argument".
`BS.cov()` returns one level whenever the series is short relative to the
number of coordinates -- and because the threshold comes from a permutation
draw, whether a given call lands there is *random*:

| n | p | failures / 25 seeds |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | 10 | 11 |
| 120 | 8 | **23** |
| 80 | 5 | 12 |
| 400 | 20 | **24** |
| 300 | 10 | 0 |

An intermittent opaque error on exactly the shapes a high-dimensional
covariance method is for. Refusing would have been wrong -- the answer is not
in doubt. One level means one candidate split with no ancestors to prune
against, so it is a changepoint precisely when its own statistic clears the
threshold; on a multi-level tree that same rule reproduces `thresholdBS()`'s
output exactly (checked: locations 156, 218 either way), which is what makes
it safe to apply. Multi-level trees still go through `thresholdBS()`
unchanged, so nothing that already worked can move.

After: **0 failures in 125 runs** across all five cells.

| `pelt` gives 1 changepoint at \eqn{\sigma = 1}, **29** at \eqn{\sigma = 3}, **138** at \eqn{\sigma = 10} | `introduction.Rmd` | **exact** at n = 200, `set.seed(1)` |
| `"MBIC"` is \eqn{0.5(k+1)\log n + \log\binom{n}{k}}, and is *not* Zhang-Siegmund's mBIC | `introduction.Rmd` | matches the implementation line for line |

## 363. One vignette number was wrong, and it was load-bearing

`monitoring.Rmd` claimed a larger run gives median detection delays of
"**12**, 4 and 2" for `edetector` at shifts of 1, 2 and 3 sigma, against
"11, 5 and 4" for `cpm`. At 150 replicates per cell under two seeds:

| shift | `edetector` | `cpm` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **7, 8** (claimed 12) | 10, 10 (claimed 11) |
| 2 | 3, 3 (claimed 4) | 5, 5 |
| 3 | 2, 2 (claimed 2) | 4, 4 |

`cpm`'s row was right. `edetector`'s 1-sigma figure was not -- and the prose
built an argument on it: "the small run above and the larger one disagree
about which is ahead". They do not. The vignette's own displayed chunk gives
edetector 7.0, 4.0, 1.5 against cpm 9.0, 4.5, 4.0 -- edetector ahead at every
shift -- and the larger run agrees at every shift. Only the erroneous 12
made edetector look slower than `cpm` at 1 sigma. The numbers are now the
measured ones, the design is stated (150 replicates, two seeds), and the
conclusion says what the data says: the gap is real but modest where the
change is small, with inter-quartile ranges of [5, 12] and [7, 15] that
overlap almost entirely.

## 364. `ocd`'s timing note understated it by 2-3x

The note said, at `mc_reps = 5`, "about 3 s at \eqn{p = 3}, 9 s at
\eqn{p = 10} and 55 s at \eqn{p = 50}", extrapolating to "roughly a minute"
at the default `mc_reps = 100`. Measured here: **10.3 s**, **21.6 s** and
**113.4 s**, and **189 s** at the default -- so minutes, not a minute. The
*shape* was right and is what matters (linear in `mc_reps`: 38 s at 20
against 189 s at 100 is exactly 5x for 5x), and the advice was right, but a
reader planning around "roughly a minute" would wait three. Not a threading
artefact -- unthrottled and pinned to one thread give the same 38 s. The note
now carries the measured figures, says they are one machine's, and points at
the linearity as the part to plan around. Its other claim held: monitoring
after calibration is cheap, **0.37 s** for a thousand observations.

## 365. A negative result

Every backticked name inside a `stop()` or `warning()` was checked against
the enclosing function's formals -- 23 candidates, **no** defects. All are
column names, aesthetics, or another function's arguments.

## 366. Two things the check caught that I had introduced or missed

**An escaped underscore in Rd.** The rewritten `ocd` timing note said
`x86\_64`, which is right in a vignette and wrong in Rd:
`R CMD check` answered

```
* checking Rd files ... NOTE
checkRd: (-1) ocd_wrapper.Rd:68: Escaped LaTeX specials: \_
```

a NOTE the baseline does not have. Now `x86-64`, and a sweep confirms no
other `\_` anywhere in `R/`. (Running `tools::checkRd()` directly on the
sources reports "Lost braces" on every `\insertRef` in 84 files; that is an
artefact of checking *before* Rdpack expands them, which is why `R CMD
check` — which builds first — never reported it.)

**A misplaced helper deleted a help page.** `wbs_lsw_replay()` was inserted
immediately above `wbsts_wrapper <- function(...)`, which put it *between*
the wrapper's roxygen block and the function it documents. The block then
documented the `@noRd` helper, `man/wbsts_wrapper.Rd` was deleted, and
`git status` jumped to 70 files. Moving the helper above the roxygen block
restored it. Worth stating as a rule: an internal helper goes above the
*whole* roxygen block of whatever follows it, never between a block and its
function.

## 367. The package sits on CRAN's 5Mb boundary

One 4.4.1 run reported

```
* checking installed package size ... NOTE
  installed size is  5.2Mb
  sub-directories of 1Mb or more:
    doc   3.8Mb
```

and seven other runs of the same tree — three under 4.4.1 and four under
4.6.0 — did not. The tarball grew 7.5 KB this pass, and neither engine fixed
above appears in any vignette, so the swing is not attributable to these
changes: the installed size is simply within rounding distance of the 5Mb
threshold, and what decides it is how large the rendered vignette figures
happen to come out. `doc` is 3.9Mb, 3.6Mb of it the seven HTML files with
their base64 figures (`ggchangepoint.html` alone is 1.2Mb), against 2.0Mb of
`help` and 625Kb of `R`.

Recorded rather than acted on: the figures already run at `dpi = 72`, and
shrinking them further would change how the vignettes look, which is a
choice about the documentation rather than a defect in it. But a reviewer may
raise it, and the answer is that it is vignette HTML, not data or compiled
artefacts.

| against the documented baseline | **matches** | **matches** |
| `checking tests` | **OK** [355s] | **OK** [85s] |
| `checking Rd files` | OK (the `\_` NOTE is gone) | OK |
| `installed package size` | OK — the 5.2Mb NOTE did **not** recur | OK |
| `re-building of vignette outputs` | OK | OK |

The size NOTE appearing in exactly one run of nine, on a tree whose tarball
grew 7.5 KB, is what a threshold at rounding distance looks like; §367 keeps
the measurement rather than a fix.

New guards this pass, each proved by breaking its input: the managed-argument
refusal (12 pairs; disabling one guard brought the raw R message back and
failed the test with two expectations naming `envcpt verbose`), the `hdcov`
single-level route (8 expectations, including one asserting that upstream
*still* fails on that tree, so a future upstream fix is signalled rather than
silently bypassed), and the `wbsts` replay (5 expectations, one of which
checks the replay is `identical()` to upstream wherever upstream can run).

# Part XXXV -- What the published capability table actually delivers

## 369. The flakiness that motivated this pass is gone

§360 and §361 were both found because a method failed *sometimes*. So the
first thing this pass did was look for more of that: every method, twelve
different random series each, failures counted.

**Zero intermittent failures across 45 methods x 12 seeds.** The four
non-clean rows are all explained and none is stochastic: `ocd` and `fcov`
exceed the per-cell time limit (§364 measures `ocd` at 189 s a fit, so twelve
of them cannot fit in any sane cap), and `hdreg` and `fabisearch` fail all
twelve because the sweep hands them a plain Gaussian matrix when one needs a
response and the other needs non-negative input -- their own errors say so.

Last pass's two fixes closed the flakiness, and nothing else in the package
has any.

## 370. `cpt_methods()` published four capabilities it could not deliver

The registry carries one boolean per capability, and `cpt_statistic()`,
`cpt_solution_path()` and `ggcpt_posterior()` each build their "these do:"
error message *from those columns*. That makes a wrong flag worse than
misleading:

```
> cpt_solution_path(cpt_detect(x, method = "wbsts"))
Error: Engine `wbsts` does not expose a solution path. These do:
binseg, segneigh, wbs, wbs2, not, tguh, wbsts, binsegrcpp
                                        ^^^^^
```

The message lists the method it is refusing. Sweeping all 50 methods against
the real accessors -- `posterior_prob_profile()`, `extract_statistic()`,
`extract_solution_path()`, `$data$fitted`, the changepoints tibble -- found
four disagreements:

| method | flag | accessor says | resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wbsts` | `path` | no path | flag -> **FALSE** |
| `binsegrcpp` | `path` | no path | flag -> **FALSE** |
| `nsp` | `ci` | no `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` | **flag kept** -- see below |
| `bocpd` | `posterior` | no per-location profile | **flag kept** -- see below |

`fitted` and `statistic` were correct for all 50.

**Why two flags stay.** `cpt_recommend(need_uncertainty = TRUE)` is
documented as asking for "a confidence interval **or significance region**"
and filters on `ci | posterior`. `nsp` reports a region
(`region_start`/`region_end` plus `$regions`), so its `ci` flag is right for
the question actually being asked -- it was the registry's own internal
comment, which said the flag means "populates ci_lower/ci_upper", that was
too narrow. Same for `bocpd`: it is Bayesian and does quantify the location,
but over **run lengths**, drawn by `ggcpt_runlength()`. Both comments now say
what the flags mean and name the exceptions.

**Why the other two go to FALSE rather than getting an implementation.** The
data is there -- `binsegrcpp`'s `$splits` is a textbook nested path
(`segments`, `end`, `loss`, `depth`) and `wbsts` keeps `cp.bef`, the
candidates before post-processing. Writing the extraction would be a new
capability, which this pass is not for, and it would add an untested code
path to a release about to be submitted. Nothing that ever worked is lost:
`cpt_solution_path()` has always errored for both. Recorded here so the
implementation is a small job whenever it is wanted.

## 371. `?mcp_wrapper` claimed a function that rejects it

> the changepoints themselves get full posterior distributions rather than
> point estimates, which `ggcpt_posterior()` already knows how to draw.

`ggcpt_posterior()` handles exactly two fit classes, `bcp` and `beast`, and
returns `NULL` for everything else. Handed an `mcp` result it stops with "No
posterior probability profile found on this object." The help page now says
what mcp actually gives -- `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` from the posterior
quantiles, `$data$fitted` -- and that `ggcpt_posterior()` does not accept it.

And because `cpt_methods()` sends people to that function, its error message
now names the accessor that does work for the method in hand: run-length for
`bocpd`, the interval columns for `mcp`. A dead end became a signpost.

## 372. The vignette's result-contract table was two engines short

`introduction.Rmd` lists which engines add which optional column. Measured
against the live package, `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` are populated by **six**
engines, not the four listed: `bfast` and `taylor` were missing, and `mcp`
does it too. The table now names all of them and, since a reader comparing
it with `cpt_methods()` would otherwise wonder, says explicitly that `nsp`
reports a region instead.

Everything else in that table checked out exactly: `posterior_prob` really is
`bcp` and `beast` alone, `detection_time` really is only `cpm`, `strength`
only `inspect`, `declared_at` only `ocd`, `mapping` only `geomcp`.

## 373. Attribution, checked with the package's own oracle

`cpt_cite()` records who invented each method; the wrappers carry
`\insertRef` keys. Those are two independent records of the same fact, and
R44 never compared them -- it only checked that a key resolves and that the
two bibliographies agree with each other.

Comparing them: **45 of 50 methods match exactly** on year. The five that do
not are `pelt`, `binseg`, `segneigh`, `amoc` and `np`, which share
`cpt_wrapper` and cite `killick2014changepoint` -- the \pkg{changepoint}
*software* paper. That is correct: the help page opens "This function wraps a
number of `cpt` functions from the changepoint package", so the software
paper is the right citation for the wrapper, while `cpt_cite()` gives each
method's original work (Killick 2012, Scott and Knott 1974, Auger and
Lawrence 1989, Hinkley 1970, Haynes 2017) and the vignettes cite those where
the methods are discussed. No misattribution.

Bibliographies re-verified: **63/63** vignette entries cited, **58/58** Rd
keys resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, every entry carrying its required
fields.

## 374. Instrument errors worth recording

The first capability sweep reported 19 mismatches. All 19 were mine: I tested
`fitted` by asking whether `segments$param_estimate` was finite -- which is
part of *every* result's contract, so it answered TRUE for everything -- and
`statistic` by looking for names in `$diagnostics` rather than calling
`extract_statistic()`. The registry's own comments say precisely what each
flag means (`fitted` populates a length-n signal on `$data`); reading them
first would have saved the sweep. The corrected sweep found the four real
disagreements above.

Also: a bib-field parser that captured four lines per field turned `year =
2014` into `2014426` by concatenating it with `pages`, which is what made all
50 methods look misattributed at first.

# Part XXXVI -- The whole S3 surface, and 23 arguments the docs invited

## 376. Every generic works on every result

Nothing had ever checked that. The contract sweep of §359 verified the
*data*; this one verifies the *surface*: for each method's result, all ten of
`autoplot()`, `plot()`, `print()`, `format()`, `summary()`, `tidy()`,
`glance()`, `augment()`, `as_tibble()` and `as.data.frame()`, with the two
plotting ones forced through `ggplot2::ggplot_build()` so laziness cannot
hide a failure.

**40 methods x 10 generics, zero failures.** `hdreg` skips (it needs a
response, and says so) and `fabisearch` exceeded the time limit.

## 377. 23 arguments the documentation invited and R refused

Every wrapper documents `...` as reaching its engine. Most also rename that
engine's arguments into this package's snake_case -- `n_intervals` for wbs's
`M`, `cpm_type` for cpm's `cpmType`, `min_dist` for fabisearch's `mindist` --
or derive them from `x`. So the engine's *own* name is the natural thing for
a reader of the upstream help page to pass, and it collided with the value
the wrapper already supplies:

```
> fabisearch_wrapper(M, nruns = 2, mindist = 5)
Error: formal argument "mindist" matched by multiple actual arguments
```

Sweeping every wrapper against every argument its engine accepts -- 86 pairs
-- found **23** of these, across 14 methods:

| method | engine argument | use instead |
|---|---|---|
| `ecp` | `min.size` | `min_size` |
| `fpop` | `lambda` | `penalty` |
| `wbs`, `wbsts` | `M` | `n_intervals` |
| `cpop`, `decafs` | `beta` | `penalty` |
| `bocpd` | `hazard_func` | `hazard` |
| `cpm` | `cpmType`, `ARL0` | `cpm_type`, `arl0` |
| `kcp` | `RS_fun`, `RS_name`, `Kmax` | `running_stat`, `kmax` |
| `sn` | `paras_to_test`, `ts` | `parameter`, `x` |
| `ocd` | `MC_reps`, `dim` | `mc_reps`, derived |
| `strucchange` | `formula` | derived |
| `segmented` | `seg.Z` | derived |
| `fabisearch` | `mindist`, `nruns`, `nreps`, `ncore` | `min_dist`, `n_runs`, `n_reps`, `n_core` |
| `bfast` | `max.iter` | `max_iter` |

**§354's sweep missed every one of them**, and the reason is worth recording:
it matched `name = <literal>`, and these are `mindist = min_dist` -- a
variable. Testing against the engine's *own formals* instead of against a
static pattern is what found them, and needs no parsing at all.

Because these are renamed rather than pinned, the answer is a redirection
rather than a refusal:

```
> cpt_detect(x, method = "wbs", M = 200)
Error: `wbs` renames its engine's `M` argument, so passing it through `...`
collides with the value the wrapper already supplies. Use `n_intervals`
instead.
```

Re-swept afterwards: **0** raw collisions, all 23 redirected, the 12 pinned
arguments from §354 still refused, and the 18 legitimately-accepted
arguments **identical** to before.

## 378. `network` had the same upstream bug as `hdcov`

§361 fixed `changepoints::thresholdBS()`'s single-level-tree failure in
`hdcov_wrapper()`. `network_wrapper()` calls the same function, and asking
the obvious next question found the same failure: **10 of 12 runs** for a
20-point sequence of 4-node graphs, the same "NA/NaN argument", the same
cause. It is clean from n = 30 up, which is why one shape per method never
saw it.

The route-around is now a shared `threshold_bs()` helper used by both
wrappers rather than inline code in one, so a third caller cannot
reintroduce it. Verified: `network` 10/12 failures -> **0**, `hdcov`
unchanged, and on six multi-level trees the helper's output is
`identical()` to upstream's -- 6 of 6.

## 379. Vignette pass

`benchmarks.Rmd` had never been checked as a whole. Every count claim in it
is internally consistent with the list or table it introduces: "Nine
methods exceeded a 120-second limit" lists 9; "Five of those" lists 5 and is
a subset of the 9; "Ten methods raise zero false alarms" matches exactly the
10 all-zero rows in its table; "four provenances" matches its 4-row table.
All **25** method names it mentions are real registry methods -- no
invented ones.

Bibliographies re-verified: 63/63 vignette entries cited, 58/58 Rd keys
resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, every entry complete.

## 380. Two non-defects, checked so they stay checked

`ggcptplot()` rejects a one-column data frame while `ggecpplot()` accepts
one. Not an inconsistency: `ggcptplot()` takes `@inheritParams cpt_wrapper`,
whose `data` is documented as "A numeric vector", while `ecp_wrapper()`
documents "a numeric vector (for univariate) or matrix/data.frame (for
multivariate)". Each matches its own contract.

`fabisearch` writes an `NMF_<hash>/` directory into the working directory
while it runs, which `git status` catches mid-sweep and which got copied
into two check trees before I noticed. It is NMF's own scratch space and it
is removed on completion -- measured: nothing left behind. The lesson is
about my own sequencing, not the package: do not start a build while a sweep
is running.

## 381. Verification, and the same mistake a third time

| | R 4.4.1 (37 of 38 engines) | R 4.6.0 (Imports only) |
|---|---|---|
| Status | 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs | 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs |
| against the documented baseline | **matches** | **matches** |
| `checking tests` | **OK** [357s] | **OK** [85s] |
| `installed package size` | OK | OK |
| `re-building of vignette outputs` | OK | OK |

**The first R-devel run of this pass failed, on the same mistake as §358 and
§368.** The new renamed-argument test ended with `expect_gt(tested, 5L)`, and
against an Imports-only library only one of its seventeen engines exists:

```
── Failure (test-050-registry.R:616:3) ──
Expected `tested` > 5L.
Actual comparison: 1 <= 5
```

§358 recorded the lesson ("a tripwire asserting that a sweep did work is
itself environment-dependent") and I then wrote the same assertion again. So
the fix is not another note -- it is a shape that cannot misfire. Both
sweeps now count how many cases *could* run and assert against that:

```r
available <- sum(vapply(cases, function(z) engine_installed(z$eng), logical(1)))
...
expect_equal(tested, available)
```

That still catches a sweep which silently tests nothing (`available` would
have to be 0 too, which the accompanying `expect_gt(available, 0L)` refuses),
and it is correct on any library. The capability guard of §370 carried the
same `> 5L` threshold and has been converted too, before it could fail on
some future machine.

New guards this pass: the renamed-argument redirection (54 expectations
across 17 cases) and `network`'s share of the `threshold_bs()` route-around
(added to the existing `hdcov` test, which now also asserts the helper is
`identical()` to upstream on multi-level trees rather than merely
equivalent).

# Part XXXVII -- Argument values, not argument names

## 382. A new axis

The last three passes swept argument *names* -- typos discarded, pinned
arguments colliding, renamed arguments colliding. This one sweeps argument
*values*: every numeric or logical-defaulted argument of every exported
non-detector function, probed with `NA`, `Inf`, `-1`, `0`, a length-2 vector
and a string, asking one question of each result -- **does the error name the
argument the caller passed?**

That question is the whole point. An error is only useful if the reader can
tell which of their arguments caused it, and a wrapper that forwards a value
into an engine or a plotting layer loses that thread by default.

## 383. Three arguments answered about something else

**`cpt_power(sigma =)` and `cpt_min_detectable(sigma =)` answered about
`sd`.** `sigma` reaches `cpt_simulate()` as its `sd`, and neither caller
validated it, so a bad value came back as ``  `sd` must be a single finite
number `` -- naming an argument neither function has. Both now check it.

**`cpt_power(location =)` was silently clamped, and reported power for a
different changepoint.** It is documented as "a fraction of `n` in (0, 1) or
an integer position", may be a vector (so `validate_scalar()` cannot express
it), and went through nothing at all. The scenario loop clamps with
`max(2, min(cp, n - 2))`, so:

| asked for | changepoint actually used | reported |
|---|---|---|
| `location = 0.5` | 100 | power 1 |
| `location = -1` | **2** | power 0.75 |
| `location = 0` | **2** | power 0.75 |
| `location = 1e6` | **198** | power 0.75 |

Every one of those looks like an answer. A new `validate_location()` enforces
the documented contract elementwise -- a fraction in (0, 1), or an integer in
[1, n-1] -- so a position that is not a position is refused, while every
documented form, vectors included, still works. The clamp stays: it is right
for an extreme *fraction* (0.001 rounds to 0, and a changepoint needs
observations either side).

**`ggcpt_interactive(width_svg =)` answered about `width`.** `ggiraph::girafe()`
reports "`width` must be a scalar positive number", its own internal name.
Checked now on the ggiraph path only, because that is the only path that uses
it -- the plotly branch ignores both arguments, as documented, and still does.

**And `cpt_simulate(df =)` used a bare `if (df <= 2)`**, so `df = NA`
answered "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" and `df = "a"` answered
"invalid arguments". `rho`, immediately beside it, already went through
`validate_scalar()`. `df` now does too, keeping its domain message -- "must
exceed 2 so the t-noise variance exists" is worth saying with its reason.

## 384. Two contrasts worth keeping

**`cpt_scenarios()` was already right, and shows what "right" is.** Its
`location` is fractions-only, it clamps the same way -- and it *warns*,
naming the argument and explaining the fraction convention, for every
scenario it moved. So it is left exactly as it is. Silence was the defect in
`cpt_power()`, not clamping.

**`ggcptplot()`'s `cptline_alpha` and `cptline_linewidth` are not defects.**
They accept `NA`, `0` and `-1`, and a length-2 value fails late with
ggplot2's "Problem while setting up geom" or grid's "'lwd' must be
non-negative". But measured against ggplot2 itself, `geom_vline()` accepts
every one of those five values too -- `alpha = NA` is a meaningful ggplot2
idiom for fully transparent. These are documented aesthetic pass-throughs,
and matching the leniency of the grammar they are built on is the correct
behaviour, not a gap.

## 385. Vignette pass

Every `` `fn()` `` referenced anywhere in the vignettes resolves to something
that exists -- the single external one, `penaltyLearning::IntervalRegressionCV()`,
is present at 2024.9.3 and correctly attributed. Bibliographies re-verified:
63/63 vignette entries cited, 58/58 Rd keys resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused,
every entry complete.

## 386. Two more of the same, found by finishing the sweep

The sweep's full result over all 83 argument slots: **48 clean**, 15 whose
base call could not be built generically, and 20 flagged. Of the 20, twelve
resolved as by-design (arguments documented as used only on another code
path -- `cpt_monitor`'s `arl0`/`patience`/`mc_reps`, `cpt_simulate`'s
`rho`, `cpt_scenarios`'s clamping-with-a-warning; `new_ggcpt`, whose help
page says outright that "this constructor does not check its arguments";
and the ggplot2 aesthetics of §384). The rest were the six fixed here.

**`ggecpplot()`/`ecp_wrapper()`'s `min_size` answered about `min.size`.**
Same shape as `sigma`->`sd` and `width_svg`->`width`: the value reaches ecp
under its own name, so `min_size = -1` came back as "min.size must be an
integer greater than 1", and `min_size = NA` reached an `if` and answered
"missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed".

**`cpt_scenarios()`'s `seed` is used arithmetically** -- `seed + (i - 1) *
n_rep + r`, to give each scenario its own stream -- so a character seed died
in `+` with "non-numeric argument to binary operator" and a length-2 seed
silently vectorised.

Both now go through `validate_scalar()`, which is what the rest of the
package uses and what names the argument.

# Part XXXVIII -- The `supports` column, verified

## 388. Every change_in a method claims does work

`supports` is published in `cpt_methods()` and drives
`validate_method_change_in()`, which refuses anything outside it. So each
listed value is a promise about what the method will do -- the same kind of
promise the `path` flag made and could not keep (§370).

Sweeping **all 73** (method, listed `change_in`) pairs: **zero fail.** The
five non-results are all explained and none is a broken claim -- `mcp` x 3
because `mcp`/`rjags` are absent here, `ocd` x 1 on the 189-second fit of
§364, and `hdreg`'s `regression` because my probe passed `y` as a vector
when `y` selects a *column* of `x`, which its own error says.

That is a clean negative result on a table users read to decide what to run.

## 389. Six requests are answered with a different change type

The sweep's other output. A *compatible* request is sometimes routed to the
method's own native change type, because the engine has no separate
estimator for the thing asked about:

| method | requested | detected |
|---|---|---|
| `not` | `var` | `meanvar` |
| `cpm` | `mean`, `var` | `distribution` |
| `kcp` | `mean`, `var` | `running mean`, `running var` |
| `wbsts` | `mean` | `var` |

None of it is silent -- the result's `change_in` records what was actually
detected -- and each individual case is defensible. `not` genuinely has no
variance-only contrast: its variance contrast is `pcwsConstMeanVar`,
piecewise-constant in mean *and* variance, and `?not_wrapper`'s `@return`
already says the reported value is `"mean"`, `"meanvar"` or `"slope"`.
`wbsts` detects change in the wavelet spectrum. `cpm` is a distribution
detector; `kcp` works on running statistics.

What was missing is that `?cpt_detect` did not prepare the reader.
Its `change_in` documentation promised only the negative half --
"incompatible combinations error rather than silently running something
else" -- which reads as though a compatible request gets what it asked for.
It now names the six routed pairs and says to compare the result's
`change_in` with the request. Documentation, not behaviour: nothing about
what the engines do has changed.

Guarded both ways: every listed `change_in` must still work, and the routed
set must be exactly those six for the methods the test reaches. A seventh
appearing means the help page has gone stale.

## 390. Vignette pass

A new check: every `cpt_detect()` call in the vignettes that names both a
`method` and a `change_in` was tested against that method's `supports`
entry. **5 such calls, 0 incompatible.**

Bibliographies re-verified: 63/63 vignette entries cited, 58/58 Rd keys
resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, all entries complete.

|---|---|---|
| Status | 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs | 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs |
| against the documented baseline | **matches** | **matches** |
| `checking tests` | **OK** [344s] | **OK** [86s] |

# Part XXXIX -- The dimension flags, and nine refusals made to agree

## 392. Completing the registry verification

`ci`, `fitted`, `posterior`, `statistic`, `path` (§370) and `supports`
(§388) have been checked against behaviour. This pass finishes the table:
`multivariate`, `univariate` and `online`.

**`online` is consistent, and three different sets explain each other.**
The registry flags `bocpd`, `cpm`, `ocd`; `cpt_monitor()`/`cpt_replay()`
accept `edetector`, `cpm`, `ocd`; `cpt_recommend(online = TRUE)` returns
`bocpd`, `cpm`. All three are right. `edetector` is monitor-only -- not in
the detector registry at all, documented under `?cpt_monitor`'s `method`,
and `cpt_detect(method = "edetector")` is refused with the valid list.
`ocd` is absent from the recommendation because `dimension` defaults to
`"univariate"`, which `?cpt_recommend` states, and `ocd` is
multivariate-only; asking for `dimension = "multivariate"` returns it.

**`multivariate` is accurate** for all 50 methods on a 3-column matrix.

## 393. `univariate = FALSE` did not mean what it said

The registry's comment read "FALSE for the engines that need at least two
coordinates **and error on one**". Testing every one of the fourteen against
a plain vector split them in two:

| behaviour on a vector | engines |
|---|---|
| errors | ocd, geomcp, hdcov, network, var, kwc, hdreg, fmean, fcov |
| **runs, and recovers the changepoint at 110** | **npmojo, inspect, esac, pilliat** |

So the flag is not the behavioural claim it was documented as. It is right
for its actual consumer -- `cpt_recommend(dimension = "univariate")`, where
pointing someone at a sparse high-dimensional projector for one series would
be poor advice however well it runs -- so the *comment* is what changed, in
both the registry and `cpt_recommend()`. FALSE now records intent, and names
the four engines that tolerate a single column without being meant for it.

## 394. Four opaque refusals, and a fifth the guard caught

Of the nine that do refuse a vector, five named the requirement and four
answered with something a reader cannot act on:

| method | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `hdcov` | "non-conformable arrays" | ``Method `hdcov` is high-dimensional and needs at least two coordinates, but `x` has 1`` |
| `var` | "incorrect number of dimensions" | same shape |
| `kwc` | "dim(X) must have a positive length" | same shape |
| `network` | "'x' must be an array of at least two dimensions" | names the n x p^2 / n x p x p shape it wants |

Then the new guard -- which requires a refusal to *name the method*, so a
reader with several in flight knows which call failed -- caught a fifth:
`geomcp` answered changepoint.geo's "Univariate changepoint analysis is not
supported", clearer than base R but naming neither the method nor the
argument. It now matches the other eight.

That is the guard doing its job on its first run, which is the argument for
writing the assertion stronger than the fix.

All nine refusals now name the method; the multivariate paths are unchanged
(`hdcov`, `var`, `kwc`, `network` and `geomcp` all still work on the input
they are for), and a one-column *matrix* is refused as well as a bare
vector.

# Part XL -- The wrappers' own arguments, and the release notes

## 397. Twenty-four wrapper arguments answered from inside the engine

§383 swept argument *values* on the exported non-detector functions. This
pass does the same for the 50 wrappers -- all 64 numeric/logical-defaulted
argument slots, probed with `NA`, `Inf`, `-1`, `0`, a length-2 vector and a
string, asking the same question: **does the error name the argument the
caller passed?**

**Twenty-five did not.** The value was forwarded and the engine answered
from deep inside itself:

| what the reader saw | from |
|---|---|
| "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" | `kcp`'s `wsize`/`kmax`, `npmojo`'s `lag`, `envcpt`'s `minseglen`, `network`'s `alpha`/`n_perm`, `bfast`'s `frequency` |
| "negative length vectors are not allowed" | `bcp`'s `burnin` |
| "NAs in foreign function call" | `cpm`'s `startup` |
| "invalid 'times' argument" | `segmented`'s `npsi` |
| "invalid 'nrow' value (too large or NA)" | `ocd`'s `mc_reps` |
| "result would be too long a vector" | `ocd`'s `patience`, `wbsts`'s `lambda` |
| "'probs' outside [0,1]" | `network`'s `alpha` |
| "non-numeric argument to binary operator" | `esac`'s `threshold_d`/`threshold_s` |
| accepted every bad value silently | `nsp`'s `ord`, `esac`/`pilliat`'s `N`, `wbsts`'s `cstar` |

Each now goes through `validate_scalar()` with the range its own help page
documents -- counts at least 1 (or 2 where a window needs two points),
probabilities strictly inside (0, 1), leading constants strictly positive,
`lag` and `ord` at least 0. Twenty-four calls across fourteen wrappers.

Re-swept afterwards: **0 UNNAMED, 0 ALL-ACCEPTED.** The regression test
carries 727 expectations -- three bad values against each of 22 arguments,
each checked both for naming the argument and for *not* containing any of
the nine opaque messages above.

| "`cpt_detect()` reaches **50** wired methods" | 50 |

| "`strucchange` costs about **135 MB** ... `bfast` **53 MB** and `bocpd` **31 MB**" | 135.35, 53.29, 30.94 MB at n = 2000 |
| "while every other engine stays **under 4 MB**" | held across every engine measured; only those three exceed it |

| 8 `ggcpt_*` tokens that look like functions | all are real S3 classes with registered methods |

## 400. What the fix got wrong, and how the suite said so

The first R 4.4.1 run of this pass **failed**, on two existing tests -- and
the failures were right:

```
Error ('test-040-polish.R:1448'): Error: `arl0` must be a single finite
                                  number, at least 1 (got 0).
Error ('test-050-engines.R:216'):  Error: `frequency` must be a single finite
                                  number, at least 2 (got 1).
```

Both arguments *already had* a better guard than the one I added. `arl0`'s
printed-error branch names the average run lengths cpm actually ships
thresholds for; `bfast_wrapper()` refuses a frequency below 2 with a message
about the seasonal frequency. My generic `validate_scalar(..., min = )`
fired first and replaced each with a range complaint -- **a regression in
message quality dressed as an improvement**.

The lesson is specific enough to be worth stating: a blanket validation
added in front of an existing specific guard makes the message worse, not
better. Both now validate type and length only (`validate_scalar(arl0,
"arl0")`), so `NA`, `"a"` and `c(1, 2)` are caught by name while `0`, `-5`,
`333` and `frequency = 1` still get the message that tells the reader what
the legal values are. Verified both ways.

Then the full suite caught a third thing: the "no test reaches a Suggests
engine outside a guarded block" check flagged this pass's own new guards,
because they gate per-method work on `engine_installed()` rather than
`skip_if_not_installed()`. That predicate is the package's own, and for a
loop over methods it is the better guard -- it skips the one method instead
of aborting the test -- so the detector now recognises it. The check was
working; it just did not know that spelling.

Full suite after all three corrections: **0 failures.**
