**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 163 | PASS 1853`.

Statuses are the documented baselines: qpdf, pdflatex and tidy absent, plus
the `rjags`/`mcp` dependency NOTE. `checking installed package size` reports
**OK** for the third round running, which is now settled rather than
watched.

## 465. What four rounds of sweeping have actually produced

| part | class swept | code defects | documentation defects |
|---|---|---|---|
| XLV | factor / multi-column input | 9 | 0 |
| XLVI | non-finite input | 3 | 0 |
| XLVII | degenerate input (constant, too short) | 7 | 0 |
| XLVIII | result contract and accessors | 0 | 3 |
| XLIX | documentation against behaviour | 0 | 7 |

The crossover is the point. The first three parts found code that quietly
did the wrong thing; the last two found none, because those sweeps had
already been run. What they found instead was text that no longer described
the code -- and the two rounds of it produced ten corrections, every one of
which a reader would have believed.

Both halves needed the same method, and it is the only method that has
worked in this loop: **enumerate the routes and check each one, rather than
inspecting the thing you suspect.** The `augment()` list was found by
accident in XLVIII and fixed in one place; the deliberate sweep in XLIX
found the same list next door, two more like it, and three copies in the
vignettes. Fixing an instance is not fixing a class -- which is exactly what
§422 said about a guard in one branch of a `switch()`, in a part that was
about code.

The guards now reflect that. Three of this round's four defects are covered
by one test that scans every Rd page and every vignette for a shared
convention and checks it against the registry in both directions, so the
class is closed rather than the instances.

# Part L -- NEWS.md, and the accepted values nobody had counted

Part XLIX closed the stale-enumeration class for capability lists. The
obvious next question is whether the release's own front matter is accurate,
because `NEWS.md` is what a CRAN reviewer reads before anything else and it
had not been checked once in this loop.

## 466. NEWS.md holds up

Every checkable claim in the 0.5.0 section was verified against the live
package:

- **"Engine wave #2 -- 19 new methods."** Counted from the section's own
  bullets: `nsp`, `mcp`, `esac`, `pilliat`, `hdcov`, `network`, `var`,
  `hdreg`, `fmean`, `fcov`, `kwc`, `fabisearch`, `pettitt`, `buishand`,
  `snht`, `taylor`, `bfast`, `wbsts`, `binsegrcpp`. Nineteen exactly.
- **"`cpt_detect()` reaches 50 wired methods."** The registry has 50
  available.
- **"New `change_in` levels `"covariance"`, `"network"`, `"regression"` and
  `"seasonality"`."** All four route. The last one took a second look:
  `bfast_wrapper(x)` on its own reports `change_in = "mean"`, which looked
  like the level did not exist -- but `change_in` is a documented argument
  of that wrapper with `"mean"` as its default, and
  `cpt_detect(x, method = "bfast", change_in = "seasonality")` puts
  `"seasonality"` in the slot. Both routes honour the same argument; there
  was nothing wrong.
- **161 function names** appear in backticks across the file. The 43 that
  are not package exports are base R, other packages, S3 method names
  written out, and this package's own internals (`need_pkg`,
  `validate_data`, `build_segments`) -- all legitimate in a file that
  describes internal fixes.

## 467. Two more clean sweeps, and one worth keeping

**Every documented default against its formal** and **every `@return`
`change_in` claim against the live object** both came back clean (§458 in
the previous part covers the method; the counts were 166 and 9).

**`@family changepoint engines`:** 43 of 43 engine wrapper pages carry it,
so the "See also" list on every engine page is complete.

**Reproducibility.** Each of the 50 methods was run twice in the same
session, without a seed, and the changepoints compared -- a stochastic
method consumes RNG state and so answers differently on the second call,
which is what makes this a real test rather than a tautology.

44 of 50 are stable (28 of them deterministic with no `seed` argument at
all, 16 stable and offering one anyway); 5 could not be called with the
probe's input shape. Exactly one varies: **`taylor`**, a bootstrap method,
which is *supposed* to. Its contract holds where it matters:

```
no seed:      70,94,140  |  70,140  |  70,140
seed = 1:     70,94,140  |  70,94,140  |  70,94,140
seed = 2:     70,140
cpt_detect(seed = 1):  70,94,140  |  70,94,140
```

so the seed controls the answer, gives a different answer for a different
value, and works through the dispatcher as well as the wrapper. **Every
method in the package is either deterministic or has a working seed.**

## 468. The four accepted values the vignettes never mentioned

The defect of the round, and it is user-facing rather than cosmetic. Both
vignettes told the reader what `change_in` accepts:

> the `change_in` argument accepts `"mean"`, `"var"`, `"meanvar"`,
> `"slope"`, and `"distribution"`.

Five values. The registry's `supports` column routes **nine**:

| value | methods |
|---|---|
| `mean` | 37 |
| `var` | 10 |
| `distribution` | 6 |
| `meanvar` | 6 |
| `slope` | 6 |
| `covariance` | 3 (`hdcov`, `fcov`, `kwc`) |
| `network` | 2 (`network`, `fabisearch`) |
| `regression` | 2 (`var`, `hdreg`) |
| `seasonality` | 1 (`bfast`) |

The four missing are precisely the ones NEWS credits to wave 2 -- so the
release notes announced them, `cpt_detect()`'s own `@param` listed all nine
correctly, and both vignettes still described the pre-wave-2 package. A
reader of either would not have known they could ask for a covariance or a
network change at all.

That is the same split Part XLIX found twice: the function documentation
right, the vignette stale. Nineteen new engines were added and the
vignettes' sentence about what the argument accepts was not revisited.

Both now list all nine and point at `cpt_methods()`'s `supports` column, and
a guard checks every enumeration of four or more quoted `change_in` values
-- in any vignette or in `cpt_detect.Rd` -- against
`unique(unlist(reg$supports))`, in both directions. It requires at least
three such enumerations to exist, so it cannot pass by matching nothing.

## 470. Six rounds of sweeping, and what is left

| part | class swept | code | docs |
|---|---|---|---|
| XLV | factor / multi-column input | 9 | 0 |
| XLVI | non-finite input | 3 | 0 |
| XLVII | degenerate input | 7 | 0 |
| XLVIII | result contract and accessors | 0 | 3 |
| XLIX | capability enumerations | 0 | 7 |
| L | NEWS.md, defaults, families, reproducibility | 0 | 2 |

The code classes are closed and staying closed: three consecutive rounds
have swept behaviour and found nothing. The documentation classes are
closing too -- this round needed four sweeps to find one defect, where Part
XLIX found four in one.

What the last three rounds have in common is worth recording as the thing to
keep doing rather than as a result: **the registry is the only source of
truth this package has, and every list in the documentation is a copy of
part of it.** Copies drift. So each round the copies get compared to the
original and then replaced with a pointer to it -- `cpt_methods()`'s
`fitted` column, its `ci` column, its `supports` column -- and a guard is
left behind that checks the pointer's claim in both directions.

Three such guards now exist, covering capability lists in every Rd page and
vignette, and `change_in` enumerations wherever they appear. The next copy
to go stale should fail a test rather than wait to be noticed.

# Part LI -- The one capability flag nobody defined

Part L's closing note said the registry is the package's only source of
truth and every documentation list is a copy of part of it. This part asks
the same question one level down: not whether the copies match, but whether
the registry's own columns are *defined* anywhere -- and finds the one that
is not.

## 471. The packaging metadata is consistent

Two mechanical checks first, both clean, both worth having run before a
submission.

**Registry engines against DESCRIPTION.** The registry names 38 distinct
upstream engine packages; every one is declared in `Imports` (12) or
`Suggests` (56). Nothing is referenced that is not declared.

**Every declared Suggests actually used.** All 56 appear in `R/`, `tests/`,
`vignettes/` or `man/` -- as a namespace call, a `need_pkg()`, a
`requireNamespace()`, a `skip_if_not_installed()`, or a `\pkg{}` reference.
No dead dependencies. The 21 Suggests that are not engines are all doing
something: build tools (`knitr`, `rmarkdown`, `testthat`, `withr`,
`vdiffr`), a system dependency (`rjags`, for `mcp`), a transitive engine
dependency (`NMF`, for `fabisearch`), feature packages
(`crossvalidationCP`, `changepoint.influence`, `penaltyLearning`),
time-index readers (`zoo`, `xts`, `tsibble`), output formats (`jsonlite`,
`gt`, `ggrepel`, `plotly`, `ggiraph`) and the parallel stack (`progressr`,
`future`, `future.apply`).

`Rdpack` is the one Imports entry with no `::` call anywhere, which is
correct rather than dead: it works through the 63 `\insertRef{}` macros
across 52 Rd pages, and `DESCRIPTION` carries the `RdMacros: Rdpack` field
they need.

## 472. `online` is not what a reader will take it for

`cpt_methods()` returns nine capability flags and its help defines six of
them -- `ci`, `fitted`, `posterior`, `statistic`, `path`, `scale_space`.
`multivariate` and `univariate` need no gloss. `online` was left undefined,
and it is the only one whose meaning is not guessable, because the obvious
guess is wrong:

```
registry `online` = TRUE:   bocpd, cpm, ocd
cpt_monitor() methods:      edetector, cpm, ocd
```

The sets overlap without coinciding, in both directions:

- **`bocpd` is marked `online` and the monitor will not take it.** A reader
  who tries gets base R's bare `match.arg` error -- *'arg' should be one of
  "edetector", "cpm", "ocd"* -- which names three methods without saying why
  the one they picked, from a column called `online`, is not among them.
- **`edetector` is one of the monitor's three and has no row in
  `cpt_methods()` at all**, because it is implemented natively in this
  package rather than wrapped from CRAN. So the table a user browses to find
  streaming methods cannot show them the default one.

What `online` actually means is a property of the algorithm -- it consumes
observations one at a time -- and the registry reports it because it governs
batch behaviour: an online detector's threshold is a rate per observation,
so run over a whole series it reports roughly \eqn{n / \mathrm{arl0}}
changepoints by construction. That is the same arithmetic
`vignette("benchmarks")` measures for `cpm` and this loop verified in Part
XLIII, and it is a genuinely useful thing to know from the table. It is just
not permission to call `cpt_monitor()`.

The help now says all of that, including both asymmetries by name. No
behaviour changed: `bocpd` in batch through `cpt_detect()` was always
right, and the monitor's three were always its three.

A guard pins both sets and both asymmetries, and checks they are really
unreachable the other way rather than merely absent from a default -- so if
a later round wires `bocpd` into the monitor, or gives `edetector` a
registry row, the text has to be revisited before the test passes.

## 473. Verification

Both check copies held the round's two edits, and the gate ran clean.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 45 | PASS 3303`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 165 | PASS 1860`.

Statuses are the documented baselines. `checking installed package size`
reports **OK** for the fifth round running.

The new guard raised `PASS` on both runs (3295 to 3303, 1853 to 1860)
rather than `SKIP`, which is the intended difference from the engine sweeps
of Parts XLVI-XLVIII: it reads formals and registry columns and makes two
`expect_error()` calls, so it costs nothing and there is no reason for a
CRAN reviewer's run to skip it.

# Part LII -- Formulas, and a number returned when nothing ran

Part LI's sweeps ran up against a wall worth noting: the check "every
registry engine is declared in Imports or Suggests" was re-derived by hand
this round before I noticed `test-doc-coverage.R` has held exactly that
test since an earlier part. That is Part L's bibliography lesson twice over
-- **look for the shipped test before writing the sweep** -- and it redirected
this part to something the eighteen existing guards do not cover:
whether the *formulas* the vignettes state are the formulas the code
computes.

## 474. Every metric formula matches its definition

`vignette("comparison")` defines the evaluation metrics precisely, which
makes them checkable rather than merely plausible.

**The covering metric.** The vignette gives, following van den Burg and
Williams (2020),
\deqn{\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{S}') = \frac{1}{n}
      \sum_{A \in \mathcal{S}} |A| \max_{A' \in \mathcal{S}'} J(A, A')}
with \eqn{J} the Jaccard index and \eqn{\mathcal{S}} the partition induced
by the **truth**. `calc_covering()` implements it with two `findInterval()`
lookups rather than scanning every prediction segment against every truth
segment -- an optimisation its own comment measures at 7.5 s down to
hundredths of a second for 3000 changepoints. That is exactly the kind of
rewrite that can be wrong at a boundary and still look right, so it was
compared against a naive reference written straight from the formula:
**408 cases, zero mismatches, maximum difference 2.2e-16.** The cases
included every boundary worth worrying about -- empty prediction, empty
truth, changepoints at the first and last legal index, duplicates, two
disjoint clusters -- and 400 random ones.

**The rest.** Hausdorff distance against the stated
\eqn{\max\{\max_p \min_t |p - t|, \max_t \min_p |p - t|\}}: 300 of 300
agree. Annotation error against \eqn{||\mathcal{P}| - |\mathcal{T}||}: 300
of 300. And every NA convention the vignette justifies in prose holds --
Hausdorff `NA` when either set is empty, MAE and RMSE `NA` when nothing
matched, precision/recall/F1 all 1 when both sets are empty.

Nothing was wrong. Both checks are now shipped tests, because a
hand-optimised numeric routine and a set of documented edge-case
conventions are worth pinning even when they pass.

## 475. `power = NaN` was a number, not an error

The defect of the round, found by asking whether `cpt_power()`'s reported
Monte Carlo standard error is the binomial one. It is --
\eqn{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n_{\mathrm{sim}}}} at intermediate powers, and 0 rather
than NaN at power 1 -- but getting there meant passing a wrong argument
name, and that is where the real problem was.

`cpt_power()` forwards `...` to `cpt_detect()` inside a per-replicate
`tryCatch`. That guard is right: an engine can fail on one unlucky draw and
one bad draw must not abort a 500-replicate run. But nothing distinguished
"a few replicates failed" from "every replicate failed", and in the second
case `mean(hits, na.rm = TRUE)` on an all-`NA` vector is `NaN`:

```r
cpt_power(n = 120, jump = 1, n_sim = 10, bogus = 1)
#>   power = NaN, mc_se = NA        <- silently, with no warning
```

The engine had already produced a perfectly clear diagnosis -- *unused
argument (bogus = 1)* -- and the `tryCatch` threw it away. What reached the
caller was a **number**: something they could put in a table, plot against
jump size, or read as "this design has no power".

`cpt_min_detectable()` then made it worse. Its bisection does
`if (trace[[2]]["power"] < power)`, so the NaN surfaced as base R's

> Error: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

which names neither the argument nor the function at fault.

Two fixes, one at each level. `cpt_power()` keeps the first swallowed error
and warns when a scenario completed no replicates, naming the count and
quoting the engine's message; it still returns the row, because one dead
scenario in a grid must not destroy the others. `cpt_min_detectable()`
refuses a non-finite power outright, saying that the search has nothing to
bracket and pointing at `...` as the usual cause.

Correct usage is untouched: `power = 0.8` with `mc_se = 0.0894`, which is
\eqn{\sqrt{0.8 \times 0.2 / 20}}, and a minimum detectable jump of 1.0188
achieving power 0.875 against a target of 0.8.

## 476. The new warning immediately found a degenerate test fixture

The warning added in §475 did what a good warning does: it fired somewhere
nobody was looking. The 4.6.0 run's warning count went from 0 to 2, and
tracing it led to `test-050-tools.R`, in the fixture list of the test that
checks `tidy()` works on every result class:

```r
ggcpt_power = cpt_power(n = 60, jump = c(1, 3), n_sim = 4, seed = 1,
                        progress = FALSE),
```

`cpt_power()` has no `progress` argument. It went into `...`, reached
`cpt_detect()`, the wrapper refused it, and **every replicate of both
scenarios failed** -- so this fixture has been a power object whose `power`
and `mc_se` were `NaN` for as long as the test has existed. The test passed
regardless, because it only asked whether `tidy()` returns a data frame, and
`tidy()` is perfectly happy to tidy a degenerate object.

Two edits. The stray argument is gone, so the fixture is a real power
result. And the test now asserts what it never checked:

```r
expect_true(all(is.finite(objs$ggcpt_power$power)))
expect_true(all(is.finite(objs$ggcpt_power$mc_se)))
```

which is the assertion that would have caught this in the first place. The
`progress = FALSE` was almost certainly copied from the `cpt_benchmark()`
call three lines above it, which does take one.

This is the second time in this loop that adding a guard has exposed a
silently-wrong *test* rather than a silently-wrong function -- Part XLIX's
Suggests-engine guard caught the multivariate contract test conflating an
absent engine with a failed call. A test suite is code, and it goes wrong in
the same ways.

## 477. Verification

The gate ran clean and both check copies held the round's edits.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 45 | PASS 3476`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 165 | PASS 2033`.

Statuses are the documented baselines, and `checking installed package
size` reports **OK** for the sixth round running.

Two numbers here are the round's result rather than bookkeeping.

`PASS` rose sharply -- 3303 to 3476 on 4.4.1, 1860 to 2033 on 4.6.0 --
because the metric-formula tests compare a few hundred cases against
independent references and every comparison is an expectation. They cost
about a second, so there is no reason to skip them on CRAN.

And **`WARN` on 4.6.0 is back to 0**, having gone to 2 when the new warning
first fired. The two warnings were the degenerate fixture of §476, and their
disappearance is the confirmation that it was the only `cpt_power()` call in
the suite with a stray argument. The 4.4.1 run keeps its long-standing pair,
which is upstream `envcpt` reporting "essentially perfect fit: summary may
be unreliable" -- understood, and nothing to do with this round.

# Part LIII -- Sweeping the test suite as code

Part LII ended on the observation that adding a guard had twice exposed a
silently-wrong *test* rather than a silently-wrong function, and that a test
suite is code which goes wrong in the same ways. This part takes that
literally: the defect it fixed last round -- a named argument that does not
exist, absorbed by `...`, producing a degenerate object that still passed --
is a class, so the class gets swept.

## 478. Every stray named argument in the package's own call sites

A parser walk over every `.R` file in `R/` and `tests/testthat/`, resolving
each call to a ggchangepoint function and comparing the names it passes
against that function's formals. A name that is not a formal is absorbed by
`...`, which is how `progress = FALSE` reached `cpt_detect()` and killed
every replicate in §476.

41 call sites pass a name the callee has no formal for. **All 41 are
legitimate**, which is worth stating precisely because the sweep looked
alarming at first glance:

- The large majority are engine arguments flowing through `cpt_detect()`'s
  documented `...` -- `seed`, `arl0`, `minseglen`, `n_intervals`, `thresh`,
  `mc_reps`, `contrast`, `cpm_type`, `frequency`, `h`, `alpha`, `family`,
  `nperm`, `n_bootstraps`, `response`, `gamma_set`, `lambda_set`. That is
  the dispatcher working as designed.
- `geom_cpt_ci(inherit.aes = )` and `scale_fill_cpt_label(name = )` are
  ggplot2 layer and scale arguments, absorbed the way every ggplot2 layer
  absorbs them.
- `rcpt(changepoints =, change_in =, params =)` looked wrong until I read
  the signature: `rcpt`'s *only* formal is `...`, so nothing else is
  possible.
- `cpt_benchmark(truth = )` was the parser seeing a key inside a nested
  list, `list(s = list(series = x, truth = list(78L, 82L)))`, not an
  argument at all.
- `cpt_power(bogus =)` and `cpt_min_detectable(bogus =)` are last round's
  deliberate probes, and `cpt_detect(zzz_not_an_argument =)` is the
  doc-coverage test's.

One was worth checking rather than assuming: `cpt_stability(x, method =
"pelt", B = 10, seed = 1, index = d)` in `test-050-index.R`, a file whose
whole subject is index propagation. `index` is not a formal of
`cpt_stability()`, so if `...` went anywhere but `cpt_detect()` the test
would have been asserting nothing. It does go there, and the index survives
into the embedded result -- `all.equal()` on runs with and without it
reports "Component `changepoints`: Component 2: target is numeric, current
is Date". Real propagation, real test.

## 479. Two tests were reporting "empty test" instead of a reason

The suite's own report says so, and had been saying so for as long as the
4.6.0 run has existed:

```
• empty test (2): 'test-040-bugfixes.R:461:1', 'test-050-registry.R:267:1'
```

Both are loops over engines, and every engine in both is a `Suggests`:

- **R23**, "a constant series returns an empty result instead of an opaque
  engine error or a spurious changepoint", loops over `segmented`, `SNSeg`,
  `kcpRS` and `CptNonPar`, `next`-ing each absent one.
- **"every engine that declares a fitted signal delivers a full one"** loops
  over `reg$method[reg$fitted]`, and none of those nine engines is in
  `Imports`.

On a library without them the loop body never runs and the test registers
no expectations at all.

One correction to how I first described this, because the check output
settles it: testthat classifies a test with no expectations as a **skip**,
not a pass -- `PASS` and `SKIP` are unchanged at 2033 and 165 after the fix,
which is only possible if these two were already counted as skips. So they
were not masquerading as verification in the totals. What they were doing is
reporting the *symptom* as the reason: "empty test" tells you nothing about
why, and a reader of the summary cannot tell an untestable engine from a
loop that stopped iterating.

Both now count what they exercised and `skip_if(tested == 0L, ...)` with a
reason that names the cause, so the Imports-only run reads

```
• no engine declaring a fitted signal is installed (1)
• none of the engines in this test is installed (1)
```

instead of `• empty test (2)`. The counter earns its place beyond the
message: if either loop ever stops exercising engines on a *full* library --
a renamed method, a registry column changing meaning -- the skip appears
there too, where it is obviously wrong, rather than the test continuing to
pass silently. Behaviour on a full library is otherwise unchanged.

## 480. Vignette pass

Bibliographies via the shipped R44, which the gate runs: 63 of 63 citations
resolve, 58 of 58 `\insertRef` keys resolve, cross-file agreement holds,
nothing dangling or unused.

The new check this round follows the same theme, because the vignettes have
their own version of the vacuous-pass problem. They lean heavily on
conditional evaluation so they build on a machine without the Suggests --
35 of 83 chunks in `ggchangepoint.Rmd`, 17 of 30 in `introduction.Rmd`, 14
of 27 in `inference.Rmd`, gated on 29 `has_*` flags. A flag used in `eval =`
but never defined would abort the build; a flag defined but never consulted
is cruft.

**Every flag used is defined in the same vignette, and none is dead.** (The
first pass reported three undefined, which was my own pattern: `has_[a-z_]+`
stops at the capital R in `has_stepR`.)

The gate ran clean and both check copies held the round's edits.

The confirmation that mattered is in the 4.6.0 skip list, which now reads

## 482. What the sweeps are finding now

Nine rounds of enumerating routes, and the yield has shifted twice:

| rounds | class | code | docs | tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| XLV-XLVII | input handling | 19 | 0 | 0 |
| XLVIII-LI | contract, docs, registry copies | 0 | 12 | 0 |
| LII-LIII | formulas, call sites, the suite itself | 1 | 0 | 3 |

The middle band closed the documentation copies; this band is finding
problems in the *verification apparatus* -- a fixture that had always been
degenerate, two tests reporting a symptom instead of a cause, and one
function that returned a number where it should have raised a warning.

That progression is worth naming because it predicts where to look next.
Each band was found by the same method applied one level further out: first
the inputs the functions accept, then the claims the documentation makes,
now the assertions the tests make. The apparatus is the last thing to get
swept, and it is the thing that decides whether the earlier sweeps stay
true.

# Part LIV -- Expectations that accept anything

Part LIII swept the suite's call sites and its empty tests. The remaining
weakness in the apparatus is subtler and worse: an assertion that *looks*
specific but is not. `expect_error(f(x))` with no pattern passes on **any**
error -- including the cryptic upstream ones this loop spent Parts XLV-XLVII
replacing with messages that name the argument and the method.

## 483. Five expectations accepted any failure at all

A parse of every test file for `expect_error`/`expect_warning`/
`expect_message` calls that supply no pattern. Seven at first count, and the
first refinement matters more than the finding:

**Two of the seven were already strong.** They capture the condition and
assert on it afterwards --

```r
e <- expect_error(cpt_batch(list(good = x, short = c(1, 2), also_good = rev(x))))
expect_match(conditionMessage(e), "`short`", fixed = TRUE)
expect_match(conditionMessage(e), "2 of 3", fixed = TRUE)
```

-- which is *stronger* than a regexp, because it checks several substrings
independently. I nearly "fixed" both, which would have replaced a
two-substring assertion with a one-pattern one. The detector now recognises
capture-then-assert, and a third flag turned out to be a comment line.

Five were genuinely weak, and two of them are the reason this class matters:

| where | what it was accepting |
|---|---|
| `test-040-polish.R:1088` | `envcpt_wrapper(rnorm(10), minseglen = 400)` -- any error, so it passed equally on the engine's own "Minimum segment legnth is too large" and on the Part XLVII translation that replaced it |
| `test-new-infrastructure.R:95` | `cpt_penalty("Manual")` -- any error, including a typo in the function name |
| `test-040-polish.R:613` | any `ggplot_build()` failure, not specifically the missing `y` aesthetic |
| `test-050-inference.R:112, :116` | any warning from `cpt_test()`, not the selection-adjustment one |

All five now carry the message they mean. The envcpt one asserts
"Method `envcpt` could not segment a series of 10 observation", which is
exactly the improvement Part XLVII made and which nothing had been holding
in place.

## 484. A guard, proved by breaking it

The class is now closed by a test that scans every test file for the same
pattern, implementing the same refinement -- capture-then-assert counts as
patterned, comments are skipped -- and requiring that the scan found at
least a hundred condition expectations, so it cannot pass by matching
nothing.

It was proved to fire before being trusted. Appending

```r
test_that("TEMPORARY probe for the patternless guard", {
  expect_error(cpt_penalty("Manual"))
})
```

to a test file produced

> `weak` (`actual`) not equal to character(0).
> `actual`: "test-new-infrastructure.R:167"

naming the file and line. The probe was then removed.

## 485. Vignette pass

Bibliographies via the shipped R44, run by the gate: 63 of 63 citations
resolve, 58 of 58 `\insertRef` keys, cross-file agreement holds, nothing
dangling or unused.

The new check follows this part's theme -- an expectation that accepts
anything has a vignette analogue in a chunk that shows code but no output
while the prose implies otherwise. There are exactly three `eval = FALSE`
chunks in the whole set, and all three are the right use of it:

- `ggchangepoint.Rmd`'s `ocd` chunk, whose own comment says "Monte Carlo
  threshold calibration makes this the slowest wrapper, so it is shown but
  not run here";
- `extending.Rmd`'s reticulate example, which cannot run in a vignette
  build;
- `extending.Rmd`'s `cpt_install_engines()` example, which must not.

None has prose nearby claiming to show output ("as you can see", "the
output above", "prints", "returns"), and each explains its own silence in
place.

## 486. Verification

The gate ran clean and both check copies held all five patterns plus the new
guard.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 46 | PASS 3476`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 166 | PASS 2033`.

Statuses are the documented baselines, and `checking installed package size`
reports **OK** for the eighth round running.

`PASS` is unchanged on both runs, which is what tightening an assertion
looks like: the same expectations run, they simply accept less. `SKIP` rose
by one on each (45 to 46, 165 to 166) because the new guard is
`skip_on_cran()` -- it reads every test file from disk, which is not a
reviewer's concern.

## 487. The apparatus, three rounds in

| part | what was swept | found |
|---|---|---|
| LII | formulas against their definitions | 1 function returning a number instead of warning; 1 degenerate fixture |
| LIII | call sites, empty tests | 2 tests reporting a symptom instead of a cause |
| LIV | condition expectations | 5 accepting any failure |

Three rounds of sweeping the verification apparatus, and every finding has
the same shape: **something that reported success without having checked
what it claimed.** A power run that produced `NaN` and called it a rate. A
fixture that had never once completed a replicate. Two tests announcing
"empty test" where a reason belonged. Five expectations that would have
passed on the very errors this loop replaced.

None of these would fail a check, and none is a bug a user could hit. What
they threaten is the standing of every earlier round: the input sweeps of
Parts XLV-XLVII are only worth what the tests holding them in place are
worth. Tightening those was the natural end of the progression -- inputs,
then documentation, then the assertions themselves -- and the guards added
along the way mean the next weak assertion fails a test rather than waiting
to be noticed.

Two habits carried this part and are worth keeping. The detector was refined
*before* acting on it, which stopped me replacing two strong
capture-then-assert idioms with weaker single patterns. And the guard was
proved to fire by breaking it, which is the only way to know a test that
currently passes would ever fail.

# Part LV -- Penalty semantics, and markup in the wrong language

`cpt_penalty()`'s help carries a section, "Penalty semantics across
engines", that Part XLIX noted and never verified. It makes five precise,
checkable claims about a two-dimensional surface -- method against penalty
-- and no test touches any of them.

## 488. Four claims verified exactly

**The MBIC formula.** The help states it as
\eqn{0.5(k+1)\log n + \log{n \choose k}}, deliberately stronger than
`"BIC"`, and explicitly *not* the modified BIC of Zhang and Siegmund
(2007). Checked at every combination of \eqn{n \in \{100, 200, 1000\}} and
\eqn{k \in \{1, 2, 5\}}: **nine of nine agree to floating point**, and MBIC
exceeds BIC at every size.

**The SegNeigh exception.** The help says \pkg{changepoint} does not
implement MBIC for segment neighbourhood, so `cpt_detect(method =
"segneigh")` falls back to `"SIC"` when the default penalty is left in
place, which is why a segneigh result is not penalty-comparable with a PELT
one. Confirmed: `pelt`, `binseg` and `amoc` report `penalty$type = "MBIC"`
and `segneigh` alone reports `"SIC"`.

**Functional pruning resolves a character penalty before dispatch.** For
`fpop`, `cpop` and `decafs`, `penalty = "BIC"` arrives as
`Manual / 10.6` -- a number, as documented.

**Search-based methods ignore the penalty.** `wbs`, `not`, `mosum`,
`idetect` and `tguh` return the identical segmentation under the default,
`penalty = "AIC"` and `penalty = 999`.

## 489. `wbs2` is not reproducible, and it is not the penalty

The sixth method in that list, `wbs2`, appeared to *respond* to the
penalty: its last changepoint moved from 188 to 183 under
`penalty = "AIC"`. That reading was wrong, and the truth is worse.

Repeating one configuration ten times in a session, with `set.seed()` re-run
before each call so the input is byte-identical:

```
penalty = 999, ten identical calls:
  9,15,71,100,169,171,183   5
  9,15,71,100,169,171,188   5
```

The default and `penalty = 2` mix the same two answers. **The penalty is
irrelevant; `wbs2` returns different segmentations for identical input.**

It is not R's random number stream. Printing `.Random.seed[2:3]` before each
call gives `400, -470581440` every time, and the answers still differ --
which is also why the wrapper has no `seed` argument to fix it: there is no
stream to pin.

It is not this package. Calling
`breakfast::breakfast(x, solution.path = "wbs2", model.selection = "sdll")`
directly reproduces it exactly on \pkg{breakfast} 2.5.

And it is state carried between calls, not per-call randomness: **five
separate fresh R sessions all returned 188**, while calls 1 through 6 within
one session ran 188, 183, 183, 183, 183, 188.

`tguh`, which uses the same package, was stable over the same experiment, so
this is specific to WBS2's steepest-drop selection near a tie. The wrapper's
help now carries a Reproducibility section stating all of it -- the
measurement, that no argument can fix it, that it is upstream, and what to
do instead.

Two existing tests compare two `wbs2` calls (a scale-invariance check and a
flat-series check). Neither is failing, because neither uses a series with a
near-tie, but both are exposed; that is recorded here rather than papered
over.

**A correction to Part L.** That round's reproducibility sweep declared
`wbs2` "stable" on the strength of two runs agreeing. With a roughly even
split, two draws match half the time. The conclusion was luck, and the
method was too weak for the question -- one more instance of an assertion
that accepted too much.

## 490. Markup in the wrong language, in both directions

While regenerating the Rd for §489 I used `**not reproducible**`, and it
came out of `document()` as those exact characters. This package does not
enable roxygen markdown -- `DESCRIPTION` has no
`Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)` -- so markdown written in a roxygen block
reaches the rendered help page verbatim.

Scanning for it found **three pages already affected**, one of them written
by this loop:

| page | text |
|---|---|
| `ggchangepoint-package.Rd` | `**Detection engines.**` |
| `ggchangepoint-package.Rd` | `**What surrounds the detectors.**` |
| `network_wrapper.Rd` | `**mean edge weight**` -- added in Part XLVIII |

All three are now `\strong{}`. Two other pages the scan flagged were
backticks inside `\examples{}`, where they are ordinary characters in R
comments, so those blocks are excluded from the check.

Then the mirror image, which is the same mistake pointing the other way:
**Rd markup inside a Markdown vignette**. `supervised.Rmd` had

```
When \pkg{penaltyLearning} is installed, `cpt_learn_penalty()` delegates
```

and pandoc renders `\pkg{penaltyLearning}` as those characters. It is now
`**penaltyLearning**`, which is how the vignettes write every other package
name -- `**changepoint**`, `**fpop**`, `**stepR**` and the rest.

One guard covers both directions: no `**bold**` or `[text](link)` in an Rd
body, and no `\code{}`, `\link{}`, `\emph{}`, `\strong{}`, `\pkg{}`,
`\item{}` or `\insertRef{}` in a vignette. It also asserts that markdown
really is disabled in `DESCRIPTION`, because that is the premise the first
half rests on -- if a later round enables it, the check should be revisited
rather than silently inverted.

The pairing is the point. Each file type has a markup language, and text
written in the other one survives the build, produces no warning, and is
visible only to a reader of the rendered page. Neither direction can fail a
`R CMD check`.

## 491. Verification

The gate ran clean and both check copies held all four edits -- the `wbs2`
Reproducibility section, the two `\strong{}` conversions, the vignette's
package name, and the new guard.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 47 | PASS 3476`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 167 | PASS 2033`.

Statuses are the documented baselines, and `checking installed package size`
reports **OK** for the ninth round running. `PASS` is unchanged and `SKIP`
rose by one on each run, the new guard being `skip_on_cran()` because it
reads every Rd page and vignette from disk.

Worth noting what the checks could *not* have told me. Every finding this
round -- a wrong MBIC formula would have been silent, `wbs2`'s
non-determinism is silent, and markup in the wrong language is silent --
passes `R CMD check` without a murmur. Four of the five claims in that help
section were already true; the fifth was true for five of its six engines.
None of that is visible from a check log.

## 492. Where the loop stands

Eleven rounds of sweeping, and the shape of what turns up has changed twice
and is now changing again:

| rounds | swept | found |
|---|---|---|
| XLV-XLVII | what functions accept | 19 code defects |
| XLVIII-LI | what the documentation claims | 12 doc defects |
| LII-LIV | what the tests assert | 1 code, 3 apparatus |
| LV | what the *rendered* output says | 4 doc defects |

The newest band is the one hardest to see from inside the repository,
because the source is correct in every case: `**bold**` is valid roxygen
text, `\pkg{}` is valid Markdown text, and both survive the build. They are
only wrong on the page a reader sees. The same is true of `wbs2` -- the
wrapper is correct, the engine is not, and only a repeated experiment
distinguishes them.

That suggests the next thing worth checking is the rendered artefacts
themselves rather than their sources: the built HTML of each vignette and
the text of each help page, read as a reader would meet them.

# Part LVI -- Reading the rendered pages

Part LV closed by predicting where to look next: "the rendered artefacts
themselves rather than their sources: the built HTML of each vignette and
the text of each help page, read as a reader would meet them." This part
did that, and the prediction was wrong -- the rendered layer is clean. What
it produced instead is a set of verifications that could not have been made
any other way, and two lessons about the harness.

## 493. All 125 help pages, rendered and read

`tools::Rd2txt()` over the installed package, which is the form a user
meets with `?cpt_detect`:

- **125 of 125 render** with no error.
- **No unexpanded macro** survives into the text -- no `\code{`, `\link{`,
  `\eqn{`, `insertRef` appears as literal characters anywhere.
- **All 52 pages that use `\insertRef` render a dated reference.** This is
  the check worth having: Rdpack expands at build time through the
  `RdMacros: Rdpack` field, and a failure there would leave help pages
  quietly citation-free.
- **No `\value{}` renders empty**, and the shortest pages (`reexports`,
  `print.ggcpt`, `tidy.ggcpt`) are short because they are re-exports and
  print methods.
- **No literal markdown**, which is Part LV's fix holding.

Then a prose scan over the 125 rendered pages *and* the seven vignettes with
code chunks stripped -- doubled words (`the the`, `of of`, and fifteen other
common words), and leftover `TODO`/`FIXME`/`XXX`/`TBD`/`placeholder`
markers. **132 files, zero hits.**

## 494. Two error messages that are documentation

`inference.Rmd` and `monitoring.Rmd` each contain an `error = TRUE` chunk,
which means a package error message is printed into the vignette as
explanatory text. Those two messages are user-facing documentation, so their
wording has to match the prose introducing them, and both do:

> An engine that exposes none of these says so, and names the ones that do:

renders as

> Engine `pelt` does not expose a per-location statistic. These do: amoc,
> wbs, not, mosum, bcp, beast, nsp, pettitt, buishand, snht.

and

> it stops, and says which methods do read one series:

renders as

> Method `ocd` is high-dimensional and needs at least two coordinates, but
> `baseline` has 1. Use method = "edetector" or "cpm" for one series.

The first list is the registry's `statistic` column and the second names the
two univariate monitor methods, both of which this loop verified in earlier
parts. And both are **built from the registry at run time** --
`subset(cpt_methods(), statistic %in% TRUE)$method` -- so they cannot go
stale the way the hard-coded documentation lists of Parts XLVIII-L did. That
is the pattern those fixes were converging on, already in place here.

## 495. The one thing R CMD check structurally cannot test

`R CMD check` runs examples with every `Suggests` installed. It therefore
cannot tell whether an example would work for the user who has only the
three `Imports` engines -- and that user is the one most likely to copy a
line out of a help page.

All 117 Rd pages with examples guard theirs, via `\examplesIf`,
`\dontrun{}` or `\donttest{}`. The single apparent exception was
`mcp_wrapper.Rd`, and reading it settled the matter rather than the
detector: it uses `\dontrun{}` with a comment explaining why an
availability test would not help --

> whether this works depends on a *system* library, and no test of
> installed R packages predicts that reliably -- `rjags` can be present and
> still fail to find JAGS at run time.

-- which my pattern simply did not recognise as a guard. The check is now
shipped, recognising all four forms.

## 496. Two harness corrections

Both worth recording, because both produced a confident wrong answer before
being caught.

**`Rd2txt` needs the package's macros.** Rendering from the source tree with
`tools::loadPkgRdMacros(".")` reported that **all 52** pages using
`\insertRef` had no dated reference. That was the harness: Rdpack's macro
was not loaded, exactly as `tools::parse_Rd()` had warned earlier in the
round ("unknown macro '\insertRef'"). Rendering from an installed copy gives
52 of 52.

**`Rd2txt` underlines headings with backspaces.** A section heading comes
out as `_D_e_s_c_r_i_p_t_i_o_n:`, so `grep("^References:")` matches nothing
and every page looks as though it has no References section. The scan strips
`_\b` before matching.

Two false alarms in one round, both from believing a scan before checking
what it was scanning. The pattern is familiar enough by now to state as a
rule: **when a sweep reports that everything is broken, the sweep is
broken.**

## 497. Verification

The gate ran clean and the check copy held the new test.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 48 | PASS 3476`.
Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, **4 NOTEs**.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 168 | PASS 2033`.

`PASS` is unchanged and `SKIP` rose by one, the new guard being
`skip_on_cran()` -- it reads every Rd page from disk.

The fourth NOTE on 4.4.1 is the installed-size one, back after nine
consecutive rounds of `OK`:

```
* checking installed package size ... NOTE
  installed size is  5.2Mb
  sub-directories of 1Mb or more:
    doc   3.8Mb
```

Nothing in this round touched a figure, a vignette chunk or a dataset -- the
only source changes were one test and the ledger -- so this is the boundary
behaviour §444 measured and §469 called settled: the package sits within a
rounding error of CRAN's 5.0Mb threshold and the step reports `OK` or `NOTE`
depending on nothing that matters. Saying it was "settled" was slightly too
strong; it is *understood*, and it will keep flickering. The profile behind
it is unchanged and recorded in §444 -- 65 figures already at `dpi = 72`,
largest 96Kb, no waste to remove -- so the explanation for a CRAN reviewer
is ready either way.

## 498. A prediction that did not pay off, and why that is worth recording

§492 predicted the rendered artefacts would hold defects, on the reasoning
that Part LV's findings were invisible in the source. They do not. Every
check in this part came back clean: 125 pages render, 52 of 52 references
expand, no macro leaks, no empty `\value{}`, no doubled words, no leftover
markers, 117 of 117 example blocks guarded, and the two error messages the
vignettes display are both registry-derived and match their prose.

The prediction was reasonable and wrong, and the distinction matters for
what to do next. Part LV's defects were **markup in the wrong language** --
a class that is invisible in the source but *systematic*, so one grep found
all four instances at once and one guard closed the class permanently.
There was no residue left in the rendered layer for this round to find.

So the rendered layer is not a new seam of defects; it is a place to
*verify*, and that is what this part contributed -- three properties nothing
else could have established (Rdpack really expands, examples really are
guarded for a user without Suggests, displayed error messages really match
their prose), two of them now shipped as tests.

Eleven rounds of sweeping have reached the point where the honest report is
sometimes "this is correct, and here is how I know". The `wbs2`
non-determinism of §489 is the reminder that unswept ground still exists --
but it was found by a *repeated experiment*, not by reading anything.

# Part LVII -- How rare is the non-determinism?

Part LVI closed by noting that §489's `wbs2` finding came from a repeated
experiment rather than from reading anything, and that unswept ground
therefore still exists. This part sweeps it, and the result changes how
alarming the finding should sound.

## 499. Repeats on one series: 45 of 50 deterministic

Part L's reproducibility sweep ran **two** calls per method and pronounced
`wbs2` stable, which §489 showed was luck against a near-even coin flip. So
the sweep was rebuilt with eight identical calls per method -- same input,
`set.seed()` re-run before each so the RNG state is byte-identical on entry.

**45 of 50 methods returned exactly one distinct answer across eight
calls.** Five could not be called with the probe's input shape (`ocd` times
out on its Monte Carlo threshold, `mcp` needs JAGS, `hdreg` needs a
`response`, and two more need theirs).

Zero varied -- **including `wbs2`**.

## 500. Which is the more interesting result, because it locates the blind spot

`wbs2` reporting one distinct answer here does not contradict §489. The two
experiments used different series:

| | series | result |
|---|---|---|
| §489 | seed 7, `c(rnorm(100), rnorm(100, 4))` | flips 183/188 |
| §499 | seed 11, `c(rnorm(90), rnorm(90, 4))` | one answer, eight calls |

Both re-confirmed this round: the §489 configuration still splits 6/4 over
ten calls, and the §499 one returns `9,15,75` every time. **The
non-determinism is a property of the series, not of the seed or the
method alone** -- it needs an SDLL model selection sitting near a tie.

That is a blind spot no amount of repetition can cover: a sweep that
repeats one series many times measures only whether *that* series is
unstable. So the design was inverted -- **eight different series, three
identical calls each** -- trading repeats for diversity, which is what finds
a tie.

**Every method was stable on every series.** All 50 completed: 45 stable
across eight series with three identical calls each, five unreachable with
the probe's input shape (`ocd`, `mcp`, `hdreg` and two more), and **zero
unstable** -- `wbs2` itself stable on all eight of its series.

So across the two designs together, 45 methods were checked eight ways for
repeat-stability and 45 were checked eight series wide, and the only
instability anywhere is the single `wbs2` configuration §489 found.

## 501. The caveat, made proportionate

§489's help text said the instability "matters only where the model
selection is close to a tie", which was the right shape but unquantified --
and a bare statement that an engine is not reproducible reads as far worse
than the measurement supports. It now carries the number:

> In practice this is rare, and needs a series whose model selection sits
> near a tie. Measured over eight other series with three identical calls
> each, `wbs2` was stable on all eight; the flip above reproduces only on
> that one configuration. `tguh`, which uses the same package, was stable
> throughout, as were the other 35 methods this experiment covered.

That is the honest version: a real hazard, rare, engine-specific, with the
evidence for both halves stated.

## 502. Vignette pass

Bibliographies via the shipped R44, run by the gate.

The check this round follows §489 directly: **a vignette that displays
`wbs2` output would not be reproducible between builds.** Two do --
`ggchangepoint.Rmd` (`wbs2_wrapper(x)`) and `introduction.Rmd`
(`tidy(wbs2_wrapper(x_multi))`) -- so the exposure was bounded exactly.

Each calls `wbs2` **once**, and each vignette is knit in its own R session,
so each is a first call -- and §489 established that the first call in a
fresh session is consistent (five separate sessions agreed). Neither chunk
has prose asserting a specific changepoint, so even a flip would not
contradict surrounding text.

The same question for the help pages: `R CMD check` runs every example in
one session, so a second `wbs2` call would be exposed to the first one's
state. **Only `wbs2_wrapper.Rd` calls it**, once. The other pages that
mention `wbs2` do so in a `@family` cross-reference, not a call.

So the exposure is three call sites, each a single first-call in its own
session. Bounded, and now written down.

## 503. Verification

The gate ran clean and the check copy held the quantified caveat.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 48 | PASS 3476`.
Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, **3 NOTEs**.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 168 | PASS 2033`.

`checking installed package size` reports **OK** again this round, having
been a NOTE last round with nothing relevant changed in between -- which is
the boundary flicker of §444 and §497 doing exactly what those sections
predicted. Two consecutive rounds now show both faces of it.

Counts are unchanged on both runs, which is right: this round added no
expectation and changed no behaviour. The only source edit was the
quantification in one help page.

## 504. What a repeated experiment is for

Three rounds have now touched `wbs2`, and the sequence is the useful part:

- **Part L** ran two calls, saw them agree, and recorded "stable". Wrong,
  by luck.
- **Part LV** ran ten calls on one series, saw a 5/5 split, and recorded
  non-determinism. Right, but unquantified -- and the wording implied a
  property of the engine.
- **Part LVII** ran eight series three ways and found it stable on every
  one of them, then re-confirmed that the original configuration still
  splits. The truth is narrower than Part LV implied and wider than Part L
  did: the engine *is* non-deterministic, on series where its model
  selection sits near a tie, which is rare.

Each round's method was sound and each conclusion was as good as the
experiment behind it. What changed the answer was not more care but a
different **design**: repetition finds instability in the series you have,
diversity finds the series that are unstable. A sweep answers the question
its design encodes, and the previous two designs encoded narrower questions
than the ones I was reporting answers to.

That is worth carrying forward as the standing caution for this loop's
method, which has otherwise been "enumerate the routes": **enumerating one
dimension thoroughly can hide a defect that lives in another.** The input
sweeps of Parts XLV-XLVII enumerated argument types across every entry
point; none of them varied the *data*, and this round is the first to do so.

# Part LVIII -- The data dimension

Part LVII ended on the caution that "enumerating one dimension thoroughly
can hide a defect living in another", and named the one this loop had never
varied: **the data**. Parts XLV-XLVII swept argument types across every
entry point, and every one of those sweeps used the same shape of series --
a clean mean shift in Gaussian noise. This part varies the shape.

## 505. Fifty methods against five signal shapes

The package ships the standard test signals for exactly this purpose:
`signal_blocks()` (Donoho-Johnstone blocks), `signal_fms()`,
`signal_teeth()`, `signal_stairs()` and `signal_mix()`. They differ in
*structure* rather than in noise -- piecewise-constant plateaux, frequency
modulation, a sawtooth, a monotone staircase, a mixture -- which is a
different axis from anything varied so far.

Each of the 50 methods was run against all five at n = 400, and each result
checked against the contract: changepoints integer, sorted, de-duplicated,
finite, within `1..n-1`, and `nrow(segments) == length(cp) + 1`.

All 250 cells account for cleanly:

| outcome | cells | |
|---|---|---|
| ran, contract holds | 195 | 39 methods succeed on all five shapes |
| refused by shape | 50 | exactly the 10 multivariate-only methods x 5 |
| engine unavailable | 5 | `mcp` x 5, needing JAGS |
| **contract violated** | **0** | |

The 50 refusals are the right answer rather than a gap: `ocd`, `geomcp`,
`hdcov`, `network`, `var`, `hdreg`, `fmean`, `fcov`, `kwc` and `fabisearch`
need a matrix, and each says so by name.

Zero contract violations, and zero genuinely cryptic errors. My classifier
flagged five as cryptic; all five were `mcp`'s own "Package 'mcp' is
required, and it samples through JAGS", which the heuristic misread because
it carries no backticks. That is the harness, not the package -- the fourth
time in three rounds a scan has needed checking before its output was
believed.

## 506. Vignette pass

Bibliographies via the shipped R44, run by the gate.

`comparison.Rmd` makes a claim about these generators that nothing verified:

> Every generator attaches its true changepoints as a
> `true_changepoints` attribute, which is exactly the `truth` argument
> `cpt_metrics()` expects.

**All five do**, and all five feed `cpt_metrics()` directly -- scoring an F1
of exactly 1 against themselves, which is the sharpest way to confirm the
attribute really is in the units `truth` expects rather than merely present.

And the figure's alt text claims the blocks signal has "eleven true
changepoints". It has exactly **11**, at n = 500, 1024 and 2048 -- the
classical Donoho-Johnstone count, so the attribution to that paper is right
as well. Alt text is read aloud to screen-reader users and is the one piece
of vignette prose no sighted reader proofreads, which makes a number in it
worth checking.

Both are now shipped tests, along with the contract sweep across three of
the five shapes.

## 507. Verification

The gate ran clean and the check copy held both new tests.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 49 | PASS 3494`.
Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 4 NOTEs.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 169 | PASS 2051`.

`PASS` rose on both runs -- 3476 to 3494 and 2033 to 2051 -- which is the
contract sweep across three signal shapes plus the five generator checks.
The generator test needs no engine, so it runs on the Imports-only library
too, which is why both numbers moved by the same 18.

The installed-size NOTE is present again, this time at **5.1Mb** rather
than 5.2Mb. Three rounds have now reported `5.2Mb NOTE`, `OK`, `5.1Mb NOTE`
with nothing between them that touches a figure or a dataset, which is the
clearest demonstration yet of what §444 measured: the package sits on the
5.0Mb line and the reported figure moves by a tenth of a megabyte between
identical builds. Nothing to fix, and now three data points saying so.

## 508. Four dimensions, and the one that is left

Sweeping has now covered four axes, each found by asking what the previous
sweeps held fixed:

| axis | varied | rounds | defects |
|---|---|---|---|
| argument type | factor, character, NA, Inf, constant, too-short | XLV-XLVII | 19 |
| documentation | claims against behaviour | XLVIII-LI, LV | 16 |
| the apparatus | what the tests assert | LII-LIV | 4 |
| the data | repeats, series, and now shape | LVII-LVIII | 1 |

The data axis has yielded one defect in two rounds -- `wbs2`'s near-tie
non-determinism -- against 19 from the argument axis. That is not because
the data axis is less important but because the argument axis was swept
first and the package was young; the ordering flatters the earlier rounds.

What is still held fixed everywhere is **length**. Every sweep in every
round has used a series between 120 and 400 points, with Part XLVII's
short-series work the only exception and that one deliberately at the floor
(3 to 25). Nothing has run a method at n = 10,000 or n = 100,000 except
`vignette("benchmarks")`, whose tables are labelled indicative and were
measured once, offline, in August 2026. The `segneigh` memory figure in
that article -- 1,208 MB against 42-62 MB for `pelt` -- is the kind of claim
that would matter to a user sizing a run and has never been re-measured
here.

That is the next axis, and it is expensive rather than difficult, which is
why it has stayed unswept.

# Part LIX -- Length, the axis that was expensive rather than difficult

Part LVIII closed by naming the last dimension every sweep had held fixed:
**series length**. Nothing in fifty-eight parts had run a method at
n = 10,000 or beyond except `vignette("benchmarks")`, whose tables were
measured once, offline, in August 2026 and never re-checked here. Those are
the numbers a reader sizes a run by.

## 509. The memory claim, re-measured

The article's sharpest operational claim, and the one whose being wrong
would cost a user most:

> At n = 10,000 `segneigh` used **1,208 MB** against **42-62 MB** for
> `pelt` on the same data: segment-neighbourhood search stores a cost
> matrix, so its footprint is quadratic where `pelt`'s is linear.

Measured on the same length, reporting the heap attributable to the call
rather than the session peak -- the distinction matters, because a bare
`gc()` reading includes about 108 MB of loaded-package baseline and would
have made `pelt` look like 143 MB:

| method | attributable | elapsed | article |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pelt` | 35.6 MB | 0.08 s | 42-62 MB |
| `binseg` | 35.6 MB | 0.08 s | -- |
| `amoc` | 34.8 MB | 0.07 s | -- |
| `segneigh` | **1,158.6 MB** | 12.89 s | **1,208 MB** |

`segneigh` lands within 4% of the published figure. `pelt` comes in a
little *below* its published range -- 35.6 against 42-62 MB -- which makes
the measured ratio 33x where the article implies 23x, so the quadratic
-versus-linear point holds with room to spare. The article states its own
tolerance ("indicative, not published rates ... re-measure on your own
hardware"), and a 15% difference on one figure is inside it.

## 510. The dividing line holds exactly

> Five of those already exceed [120 seconds] at n = 10,000: `cpop`,
> `strucchange`, `bocpd`, `taylor`, `ecp`

All five do. The three the article calls fast were run as controls on the
same series:

| method | n = 10,000 |
|---|---|
| `cpop` | > 125 s |
| `strucchange` | > 125 s |
| `bocpd` | > 125 s |
| `ecp` | > 125 s |
| `taylor` | killed at 200 s |
| `pelt`, `binseg`, `fpop` | 0.1 s each, 3 changepoints |

Two orders of magnitude either side of the line, exactly as described.

## 511. `taylor` cannot be interrupted, which the article does not say

The one row that behaved differently is the finding. `cpop`,
`strucchange`, `bocpd` and `ecp` all stopped when R's elapsed-time limit
fired. **`taylor` ignored it.** A `setTimeLimit(125)` was still unhonoured
at 200 seconds, and a second run with `setTimeLimit(45)` was still running
at 170 -- both had to be killed from outside the R session.

R checks elapsed-time limits and keyboard interrupts at the same points in
evaluation, so a call that outlives one will outlive the other:
**`Ctrl-C` will not stop `taylor` either.** A user who starts it on a long
series has no way back except killing the session, which on a shared
machine or inside a knitr build is a materially different problem from
"this method is slow".

That is now in `taylor_wrapper()`'s help, with the measurement, the reason
(R cannot look while the engine works), and the knob that actually helps --
`n_bootstraps`, whose cost is roughly linear. The article's own row for
`taylor` is accurate as far as it goes; what it omits is that this is the
one slow method you cannot abandon once started.

Writing that section, I reached for `**minutes**` and `**Ctrl-C**` --
markdown, in a package that does not enable it. Part LV's guard is exactly
for this, and running it caught nothing only because I converted both to
`\strong{}` first. The habit that produced the defect is evidently still
live; the guard is why it no longer matters.

## 512. Verification

The gate ran clean and the check copy held the new help section, with no
literal markdown in it.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 49 | PASS 3494`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 169 | PASS 2051`.

Counts are unchanged from Part LVIII, which is right: this round added no
expectation. The only source change is one help page.

`checking installed package size` reports **OK**, the fourth reading in four
rounds of the sequence `5.2Mb NOTE`, `OK`, `5.1Mb NOTE`, `OK`. Nothing
between any pair of those runs touched a figure, a vignette chunk or a
dataset. §444's measurement is now beyond argument.

No test was added for this round's findings, deliberately. A test that
runs a method at n = 10,000 costs minutes -- `segneigh` 13 seconds,
`taylor` unbounded -- and the four measurements here are documentation of a
*published article's* numbers, not invariants of the package. They belong in
the article and in `taylor_wrapper()`'s help, which is where they went.

## 513. Five axes, and what the last one was worth

| axis | rounds | code | docs |
|---|---|---|---|
| argument type | XLV-XLVII | 19 | 0 |
| documentation claims | XLVIII-LI, LV | 0 | 16 |
| the test apparatus | LII-LIV | 1 | 3 |
| the data | LVII-LVIII | 1 | 0 |
| **series length** | **LIX** | **0** | **1** |

The length axis cost more compute than the previous four combined and
returned one documentation defect. That is a fair trade, and worth saying
plainly rather than dressing up: the article's four operational claims were
**all substantially correct**, measured a year earlier on different
hardware, which is a good result for the article and a dull one for the
round.

What the axis did produce is the `taylor` interruptibility finding, and its
shape is worth keeping. It was not a wrong number; it was **a true
statement whose consequence was unstated**. The article says `taylor`
exceeds 120 seconds at n = 10,000, which is accurate and sounds like
information about patience. What it means in practice is that the call
cannot be abandoned -- no time limit, no `Ctrl-C`, only killing the session.
Nothing about the source, the documentation or a shorter run would have
revealed that; only running it long enough to want to stop it.

That is the argument for the expensive axis existing at all, and also the
argument for not sweeping it again soon: it is now swept, the numbers hold,
and the one thing it found is written down.

# Part LX -- Composition: does the contract survive a round trip?

Part LIX closed the length axis and said it should not be swept again soon.
The axes so far have all been about *inputs* -- their type, their shape,
their length -- or about what the documentation says. This part asks a
different kind of question: not whether one function is right, but whether
two of them **compose**.

## 514. The round trip nothing had checked

`extending.Rmd` documents `as_ggcpt()` as the way an external result enters
the package and `tidy()` as the way one leaves. A result taken out and put
back should be the same result, and nothing anywhere checked that the two
functions compose.

Swept across every method, on a three-segment series:

| outcome | methods |
|---|---|
| round trip lossless | **39** |
| refused a univariate series | 11 |
| **broken** | **0** |

"Lossless" here is stronger than it needed to be. The changepoints, the
segment count and the data length were the properties I expected to hold.
`cp_value` and `param_estimate` also matched, for **every one of the 39**,
which is a result about the class rather than about `as_ggcpt()`:
`as_ggcpt()` recomputes segment means from the series it is handed, so
`param_estimate` matching means every engine's `$segments$param_estimate`
really is the segment mean of the data.

That confirms the separation Part XLVIII discovered from the other side.
There, `augment()` was found to *prefer* the engine's own fitted signal for
`.fitted`; the question left open was whether that signal ever leaked into
the segment summaries. It does not -- the engine's signal lives in
`$data$fitted` and `$segments$param_estimate` is always the arithmetic
segment mean, for all 39 methods. Two rounds approaching the same boundary
from opposite directions and agreeing is better evidence than either alone.

## 515. An off-by-one that would have been invisible

The vignette's `as_ggcpt()` example turns on a detail worth verifying,
because a mistake in it produces perfectly plausible output:

> `cp_convention = "right"` matters: some engines report the first index of
> the new segment and some the last index of the old one, and getting it
> wrong shifts every location by one. The conversion happens on the way in,
> so the stored result is always on this package's convention.

Both halves hold exactly. Given `c(101, 199)`:

| call | stored `cp` | `$cp_convention` |
|---|---|---|
| `cp_convention = "left"` | 101, 199 | `"left"` |
| `cp_convention = "right"` | **100, 198** | `"left"` |

The right-convention input is shifted by exactly one, and the *stored*
convention is `"left"` in both cases -- so everything downstream compares
like with like, which is the point of doing the conversion on entry rather
than carrying a flag around. The vignette's own metric line,
`cpt_metrics(tidy(fit)$cp, truth = c(100, 200), n = 300)`, returns an F1 of
exactly 1, so the example's numbers work out under the conversion it
demonstrates.

This is the kind of claim that no other test could have caught. Both
conventions yield sorted, de-duplicated, in-range changepoints; every
contract check in the package passes either way. Only comparing the two
against each other, with the documented semantics in hand, distinguishes
them.

Both properties are now shipped tests.

## 516. 179K of figures nothing pointed at

The installed-size NOTE has flickered for five rounds -- `5.2Mb`, `OK`,
`5.1Mb`, `OK` -- and this round's 4.4.1 run read **6.6Mb**, which is a jump
rather than a flicker. Chasing it found a real defect, and the chase itself
is worth recording because two plausible culprits were wrong.

**Not the ledger.** `next_release.md` has grown to 1,008K over sixty parts
and sits in the package root, which looked like an obvious answer. It is in
`.Rbuildignore` and absent from the tarball -- checked rather than assumed,
by listing the built `.tar.gz`.

**Not `man/` growing.** `du` reports `man/` as 1.8M, which looked alarming
next to a 400K content total. That is filesystem block overhead: 125 files
at ~14K of blocks each regardless of content. R's size NOTE uses the same
block accounting, which is why the number is coarse.

The breakdown told the real story: **6.6Mb = doc 3.8Mb + help 2.0Mb**, with
`doc` unchanged from every previous reading. So `help` had crossed the 1Mb
reporting line, and `help/` is only 555K of actual Rd database -- the rest
is `help/figures/`, installed from `man/figures/`, at **1.3M**.

That directory holds the README's rendered plots under knitr's default
names, `README-unnamed-chunk-NN-1.png`. Those names **renumber** whenever a
chunk is added or removed above them, so every re-knit of `README.Rmd`
leaves the old numbers behind. Of 28 files, 24 were referenced by
`README.md` and **four were orphans**: 179K shipped in every tarball,
installed for every user, pointed at by nothing in the repository -- checked
against every `.md`, `.Rmd`, `.Rd`, `.yml` and `DESCRIPTION`, with
`logo.png` as the control that came back correctly referenced.

Removed: `man/figures/` 1.3M to 1.1M, 24 files, every one referenced.

A guard now checks that every file in `man/figures/` is referenced by
something the package ships or builds from. The renumbering is the reason it
is worth having: nothing about editing `README.Rmd` tells you that a figure
somewhere else has been abandoned, and the only symptom is a package that
grows a little each time.

## 517. Verification

The gate ran clean and the check copy carried 24 figures and the new guard.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 51 | PASS 3500`.
Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, **3 NOTEs**.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 171 | PASS 2057`.

`checking installed package size` reports **OK on both runs**, where the
pre-removal run of this same round read `6.6Mb` with a NOTE.

One honest qualification. Removing 179K cannot by itself account for a swing
from `6.6Mb NOTE` to `OK`, and the installed tree still measures 6.1M
apparent. So the deletion is a real improvement -- 179K of genuinely dead
files, gone, with a guard -- but it is not the whole explanation for the
number moving, and I cannot say what the rest was. What the round
established firmly is the *composition* of the size, which no previous round
had: `doc` 3.8Mb of vignette figures, `help` 2.0Mb of which 1.3M was
`figures/` and only 555K the Rd database. That breakdown is the thing worth
having when a CRAN reviewer asks, and §444's older explanation covered only
the `doc` half.

`PASS` rose on both runs -- 3494 to 3500 and 2051 to 2057 -- the round-trip
sweep, the convention test and the figure guard.

## 518. Composition, and where the sixth axis leads

Five axes were about inputs and documentation. This round's was
**composition**: not whether a function is right but whether two of them,
run back to back, agree.

It found the strongest positive result of the loop so far. The
`tidy()` to `as_ggcpt()` round trip is lossless for all 39 applicable
methods -- not only the changepoints and segment count I expected, but
`cp_value` and `param_estimate` too. That last one is a statement about the
whole class: `as_ggcpt()` recomputes segment means from the series it is
given, so their matching proves that no engine's own fitted signal leaks
into `$segments$param_estimate`. Part XLVIII established from the other
direction that `augment()` prefers the engine signal for `.fitted`; the two
findings together fix the boundary exactly, and neither alone would have.

It also found the one off-by-one that no contract check could catch, because
both answers look valid: `cp_convention = "right"` really does shift on
entry, and really does store `"left"`.

And chasing a size NOTE found 179K of figures abandoned by knitr's chunk
renumbering -- which is a composition defect too, between `README.Rmd` and
the directory its plots are written to. Nothing in either place is wrong;
they simply stopped agreeing, silently, and only the total size ever
noticed.

# Part LXI -- More compositions, and one test that claimed too much

Part LX's composition axis -- whether two functions agree when run back to
back -- produced the loop's strongest positive result and one off-by-one no
contract check could catch. This part continues along it.

## 519. `cpt_batch()` agrees with running each series alone

The invariant a panel user relies on without thinking about it: batching
three series should give what detecting each one separately gives. For
`pelt`, `binseg` and `amoc`, on a three-series panel with different
changepoint structures, the batch result matches the individual result for
every series and every method.

## 520. The one result class `tidy()` cannot reach

Following `cpt_confint()`'s documented claim that its bootstrap is "the
`cpt_stability()` scheme" led somewhere else first: reading a stability
object turned up

> Error in UseMethod("tidy") : no applicable method for 'tidy' applied to
> an object of class "ggcpt_stability"

Eleven `ggcpt_*` result classes exist. All eleven have `print()` and
`autoplot()`. Nine have an explicit `tidy()` method. Of the two that do
not, one is reachable anyway:

| class | class vector | `tidy()` |
|---|---|---|
| `ggcpt_consensus` | `c("ggcpt_consensus", "ggcpt")` | works, via `tidy.ggcpt` |
| `ggcpt_stability` | `"ggcpt_stability"` | **errors** |

`ggcpt_stability` is the only result class that inherits nothing, so it is
the only one with no route.

**The documentation is right about this.** `cpt_stability()`'s `@return`
says, precisely, "Methods: `print()` and `autoplot()` (frequency profile
with the original detections marked)". It does not claim `tidy()`. Adding
`tidy.ggcpt_stability` would be a new method, which this loop is not for.

What was wrong is a **test name**:

> `test_that("tidy() works on every result class the package returns", ...)`

It covers ten classes and omits the eleventh -- the one where the claim is
false. That is Part LIV's class of defect exactly: an assertion, or here a
description, that promises more than it checks. A reader scanning test names
for coverage would conclude the surface is complete.

The name is now "tidy() works on every result class **that offers it**",
with the exception pinned in both directions -- `class(st)` really is
`"ggcpt_stability"` alone, `tidy()` really errors, and `autoplot()` and
`print()` really work. So if a later round adds the missing method, this
test fails and prompts updating `cpt_stability()`'s `@return` in the same
change, rather than leaving the help stale.

## 521. The bootstrap interval and the stability profile really are the same experiment

`cpt_confint()`'s help describes its bootstrap provenance as

> within-segment residual resampling (the `cpt_stability()` scheme),
> re-running the detector and taking quantiles of the re-detected location

which is a claim that two exported functions run the same experiment. The
first attempt to check it produced a misleading answer, and the reason is
worth recording.

Comparing `cpt_confint(method = "bootstrap")`'s interval against
`cpt_stability()`'s frequency profile at default settings showed only
**27.3%** of the frequency mass inside the interval -- which looks like a
contradiction. It is not. `cpt_stability()`'s `freq` is documented as "the
proportion of replicates detecting a changepoint **within `margin`** of that
index", and at the default `margin = 5` a single changepoint at 100 gives
eleven positions a proportion of 1.0 apiece. The profile is deliberately
smeared; it is not a histogram, so its mass is not the quantity an interval
should contain.

Run with `margin = 0`, the profile *is* a histogram of re-detected
locations:

| position | 98 | 99 | 100 | 101 | 102 | 103 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| proportion | 0.010 | 0.043 | **0.877** | 0.050 | 0.017 | 0.003 |

and `cpt_confint()`'s interval of `[99, 101]` contains **97.0%** of it --
exactly where the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of that distribution fall. The
documented claim holds, and the two functions agree because they are the
same resampling scheme summarised two ways.

I had written the conclusion line before seeing the numbers -- "the interval
should sit where the frequency mass is, and it does" -- and it printed
above 27.3%, which contradicted it. That is worth noting because it is the
failure mode a scan invites: the sentence was true of the right experiment
and false of the one I had run.

## 522. Verification

The gate ran clean and the check copy carried the narrowed test name and the
pinned exception.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 51 | PASS 3504`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 171 | PASS 2061`.

`checking installed package size` reports **OK on both runs**, the second
consecutive round of `OK` since the orphaned figures went. `PASS` rose by 4
on each run, which is the pinned `ggcpt_stability` exception.

Statuses are otherwise the documented baselines.

## 523. What composition has been worth

Two rounds on the composition axis, and the pattern is different from every
earlier axis. The input sweeps found things that were *wrong*. Composition
mostly finds things that are *right*, and establishes them in a way no
single-function test could:

- The `tidy()`/`as_ggcpt()` round trip is lossless for all 39 applicable
  methods, and `param_estimate` matching proves no engine's fitted signal
  leaks into the segment summaries -- pinning from the opposite side the
  boundary Part XLVIII found.
- `cpt_batch()` returns exactly what individual `cpt_detect()` calls return.
- `cpt_confint(method = "bootstrap")` and `cpt_stability()` are demonstrably
  the same experiment: at `margin = 0` the interval `[99, 101]` holds 97.0%
  of the re-detection histogram.
- `cp_convention = "right"` shifts on entry and stores `"left"` -- the one
  off-by-one in the package that no contract check could ever catch, because
  both answers look valid.

The two defects it did find were both **descriptions that outran the
thing described**: 179K of figures whose names no longer matched what
`README.md` referenced, and a test named for a coverage it did not have.
Neither is a bug a user could hit. Both are the kind of drift that
accumulates in a package nobody is checking this way, and both were found by
asking whether two things still agree rather than whether one thing works.

# Part LXII -- Descriptions that outran the thing described, looked for on purpose

Part LXI's two defects were both of one kind: a set of figure names that no
longer matched what `README.md` referenced, and a test named for coverage it
did not have. §523 named that pattern. This part goes looking for more of
it, deliberately, and mostly does not find any -- but the looking produced
one guard worth keeping.

## 524. Chunk labels, and a false positive that was better than the check

A vignette chunk labelled after a method ought to call that method; a label
that no longer matches its body is the same drift as a stale figure name.
Across all seven vignettes, exactly one chunk was flagged:
`ggchangepoint.Rmd`'s `cpop-fallback`, whose body never mentions `cpop`.

Reading it settled the matter against the check:

```r
{r cpop, eval = has_cpop}
y_slope <- cumsum(c(rep(0.4, 100), rep(-0.3, 100))) + rnorm(200)
res_cpop <- cpop_wrapper(y_slope)

{r cpop-fallback, include = FALSE, eval = !has_cpop}
# y_slope is reused by the segmented example below
```
