```r
y_slope <- cumsum(c(rep(0.4, 100), rep(-0.3, 100))) + rnorm(200)
```

The label means "the fallback *for* the cpop chunk", which is exactly what
it is. And the chunk is a piece of careful vignette engineering: without it,
the `segmented` example downstream would lose its data on any machine
without `cpop` installed -- which is every CRAN check machine that skips
that Suggests.

## 525. Rd titles: nine flagged, nine correct

Same idea one level over: a wrapper's title should name the method or the
engine it wraps. Nine of 41 wrapper pages name neither, and all nine are
right, because they name the *thing* instead:

| page | title | why the check missed it |
|---|---|---|
| `idetect_wrapper` | "Isolate-Detect wrapper" | that is what IDetect stands for |
| `npmojo_wrapper` | "Nonparametric MOSUM wrapper (NP-MOJO)" | hyphenated |
| `bcp_wrapper` | "Bayesian changepoint wrapper (Barry-Hartigan product partition)" | names the model |
| `wbsts_wrapper` | "WBS for nonstationary time series" | spelled out |
| `fmean`, `fcov`, `kwc`, `fabisearch`, `binsegrcpp` | describe what the method does | descriptive by design |

Titles that describe the method rather than echoing its identifier are
better documentation, not worse. The check was too literal about
capitalisation, hyphens and abbreviations; there is no defect here.

## 526. The guard that came out of it

The `cpop-fallback` chunk revealed a real hazard worth guarding, even though
the package handles it correctly: **a chunk that uses a variable only a
differently-gated chunk defines** will break the build wherever that engine
is absent, and nothing in either chunk looks wrong on its own.

Getting the property right took two attempts, and the first version is
instructive. It flagged every conditionally-defined variable -- 32 of them,
`res_cpop`, `res_bcp`, `res_beast` and the rest -- all of which are correct,
because each is used only inside the chunk that gates it. **The property is
about use, not definition.** The guard now flags a variable only when a
chunk consumes it and neither an ungated definition nor a `has_x`/`!has_x`
fallback pair covers the consuming chunk's gate.

It was proved to fire before being trusted. Appending

```r
{r temporary-probe}
nrow(tidy(res_cpop))
```

to `ggchangepoint.Rmd` produced

> `actual`: "ggchangepoint.Rmd:845 uses `res_cpop` defined only under has_cpop"

naming the file, the line, the variable and the gate. The probe was removed.

Until now this property was only checked empirically, by the 4.6.0
Imports-only run building the vignettes and passing. That is a real check
but a slow and indirect one: it tells you a build failed, not which line
assumed an engine.

## 527. Verification

The gate ran clean; the check copy carries the new guard and does not carry
the probe.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 52 | PASS 3504`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 172 | PASS 2061`.

`checking installed package size` reports **OK on both**, the third
consecutive round since the orphaned figures went. `SKIP` rose by one on
each run -- the new guard is `skip_on_cran()`, reading vignette sources from
disk -- and `PASS` is unchanged, which is right for a round that added a
guard rather than an assertion about behaviour.

## 528. What this round is: a negative result with an artifact

Three checks, two clean, and the honest summary is that the deliberate hunt
for Part LXI's defect class came up empty:

- **Chunk labels**: 1 flagged of ~180, and it was correct.
- **Rd titles**: 9 flagged of 41, and all 9 were correct -- better
  documentation than the check knew how to recognise.
- **Cross-gate variable dependencies**: 0 real, and the package already
  solves the only case that exists with a paired fallback.

Looking for a class deliberately, right after finding two instances of it by
accident, found none. That is worth stating plainly rather than dressing a
guard up as a discovery: Part LXI's two defects were not the visible part of
a large seam.

What the round produced is a guard for something the package already does
correctly, protecting a property that was previously only checked
*empirically* -- the 4.6.0 Imports-only run building the vignettes. That run
tells you a build failed; it does not tell you which line assumed an engine.
The guard names the file, the line, the variable and the gate, which is the
difference between a check and a diagnosis.

And it took two attempts to encode, which is the part worth carrying: the
first version flagged 32 correct chunks because it checked *definition*
where the property is about *use*. A guard that fires on correct code is
worse than no guard, and the only way I found out was running it.

# Part LXIII -- The document CRAN reads first

Part LXII's deliberate hunt for stale descriptions came up empty, which
argued for a different kind of round rather than a third sweep of the same
kind. With submission imminent, the most valuable unexamined artefact is
`cran-comments.md`: it is the first thing a CRAN reviewer reads, it is in
`.Rbuildignore` so no check ever validates a word of it, and in
sixty-two parts this loop had never opened it.

It is 9,455 bytes of substantive, accurate prose about the release. Eight
of its checkable claims were verified; **three were wrong**, and each was
wrong in a way that would have cost credibility with a reviewer rather than
merely being imprecise.

## 529. "its example is gated with @examplesIf"

Said of `mcp_wrapper()` -- the one engine needing a system library, and
therefore the reason the package asks to be checked with
`_R_CHECK_FORCE_SUGGESTS_=false`. It is the detail a reviewer would look at.

The example is not gated with `@examplesIf`. It uses `\dontrun{}`, and
Part LVI established *why* that is the better choice: the Rd's own comment
notes that whether the engine works depends on a system library, and
`requireNamespace("mcp")` does not predict that -- 'rjags' can be installed
and still fail to find JAGS at run time. `@examplesIf` would run the example
wherever 'mcp' is present and fail wherever JAGS is not; `\dontrun{}` never
runs it anywhere, which is the only guard that holds.

So the practice is stronger than the claim, and the claim describes a
superseded approach. Corrected, with the reasoning, so the reviewer sees a
deliberate choice rather than a discrepancy.

Of 125 help pages, 46 use `@examplesIf`, 13 use `\donttest{}` and 2 use
`\dontrun{}` -- the summary sentence's "its examples use `@examplesIf`" is
right about the fleet and wrong about this one page.

## 530. "no longer raises a note on any platform we check on"

Said of `checking installed package size`, and contradicted by this loop's
own measurements more thoroughly than by any single run. Across recent
parts, unchanged sources on the same R 4.4.1 machine have reported:

`5.2Mb NOTE`, `OK`, `5.1Mb NOTE`, `OK`, `6.6Mb NOTE`, `OK`, `OK`, `OK`

The package sits within a rounding error of the 5.0 MB threshold, so the
step's answer moves between runs. Telling a reviewer it never fires, when
our own checks fire it about half the time, is the kind of statement that
makes everything around it less trustworthy.

Rewritten to say so plainly, with the breakdown §517 established -- `doc`
3.8 MB of 65 figures already at `dpi = 72`, largest 96 KB, nothing
unreferenced; `help` 0.5 MB of Rd database plus 1.1 MB of `man/figures`, all
of it reachable from `README.md` -- and the honest conclusion that there is
nothing further to remove which is not documentation the package chooses to
ship.

The neighbouring claim in the same paragraph is **correct** and was checked:
`dpi = 72` is set in all seven vignettes, and a fresh `R CMD build` produces
a **4.17 MB** tarball against the stated "5.2 MB to 4.2 MB".

## 531. "Thirty-seven defects ... NEWS.md itemises them"

The phrase "NEWS.md itemises them" is what makes this checkable. NEWS.md's
two audit sections carry **41** top-level entries -- 16 under
post-implementation and 25 under pre-submission -- and NEWS.md is unmodified
in this working tree, so the count was stale before this loop began.
Corrected to forty-one.

## 532. The eight claims that hold

Worth listing, because the point of checking is not only to find errors:

| claim | measured |
|---|---|
| 56 suggested packages, 35 of them engines | 56 / 35 |
| `cpt_detect()` reaches 50 methods | 50 available |
| only `changepoint`, `changepoint.np`, `ecp` required | exactly those three |
| source tarball 4.2 MB | 4.17 MB |
| `dpi = 72` in the vignettes | all seven |
| 0.4.0 published 2026-08-24 | `CRAN-SUBMISSION` agrees |
| version 0.5.0 | DESCRIPTION agrees |
| `doc` breakdown when the note fires | 3.8 MB, as stated |

## 533. Verification

The gate ran clean. `cran-comments.md` is in `.Rbuildignore` and confirmed
absent from a freshly built tarball, so nothing this round changed can
affect a check -- which is precisely why nothing had ever validated it.

**R 4.4.1, full Suggests:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 52 | PASS 3504`.
**R 4.6.0, Imports-only:** `FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 172 | PASS 2061`.

`checking installed package size` reports **OK on both**, which is now the
fourth consecutive `OK` -- and is exactly why the corrected paragraph does
not claim the note is gone. Four `OK`s in a row is what a coin looks like
when it lands the same way four times.

## 534. A round with no test to show for it

Nothing was added to the suite this round, and nothing could have been. A
test cannot check `cran-comments.md`: the file is excluded from the build, so
it is absent from the installed package the tests run against, and its
claims are about *this submission* rather than about the package's
behaviour -- "0.4.0 was published on 2026-08-24", "thirty-seven defects were
fixed", "the note is gone on every platform we check". Those are assertions
about history and about check results on machines the test suite will never
see.

That makes it the one artefact in the repository whose only quality control
is somebody reading it against reality. Sixty-two parts of this loop swept
code, documentation, tests, rendered output, data, length and composition,
and never touched the file a reviewer opens first -- because it is invisible
to every mechanism the earlier rounds relied on.

The three errors were of one kind, and it is not carelessness: each was
**true when written**. `@examplesIf` was the gate on that page before
`\dontrun{}` replaced it; the size note really had gone when `dpi = 72`
first landed; there really were thirty-seven fixes before four more were
added. A submission document is a snapshot of a moving package, and the
snapshot is only checked if someone checks it.

So the durable output of this round is not a guard but a note for whoever
prepares the next release: **re-read `cran-comments.md` against the package
immediately before submitting**, because it is the one file that cannot fail
a test.

# Part LXIV -- The rendered README, the pkgdown index, and an enumeration that lied

§534 named the class this round continues: artefacts whose only quality
control is somebody reading them. `cran-comments.md` was one. Three more sit
beside it, and each is checkable in a way that page was not.

## 535. README.md holds 451 lines of output nothing compares to behaviour

`README.md` is generated from `README.Rmd`, and the committed copy carries
451 `#>` lines -- printed tibbles, `cpt_recommend()` tables, dimension
lines. No test reads them. They were true at the last knit, and the package
has changed in sixty-three parts since.

The definitive check is not to spot-check the claims but to **re-knit and
diff**, which tests all 451 lines at once. Done in an isolated copy, because
rendering writes figures into `man/figures/` and the real tree should not be
touched by a verification:

```
cp -r . $SP/rd/pkg && rm -rf $SP/rd/pkg/.git
cp README.md README.md.orig
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd", quiet = TRUE)'
diff README.md.orig README.md
```

Two differing lines, and they are the same line:

```
< #>   Runtime (seconds):        0.007
> #>   Runtime (seconds):        0.008
```

Every one of the 451 output lines is current. The single diff is a
wall-clock measurement, which cannot be otherwise -- and that is worth
recording, because it means a future re-knit will *always* show one diff.
Whoever repeats this check should expect the runtime line and nothing else.

The re-knit also settled a question Part LX left open. Four orphan figures
were deleted there (`README-unnamed-chunk-{10,16,17,30}-1.png`, 179K) on the
grounds that nothing referenced them. Re-knitting produces **exactly the
same 24 filenames**, zero orphans -- so the four came from an older README
structure the current `.Rmd` no longer generates, and the deletion was
right. Had chunk numbering shifted, the re-knit would have written 24 new
names and orphaned 24 old ones.

## 536. `_pkgdown.yml` enumerates 125 topics by hand

The `reference:` section lists every documented topic by name, in sections.
A name that no longer exists fails `pkgdown::build_site()`; an exported
topic in no section is dropped from the site with a warning. Neither is
visible to `R CMD check`, and the site is not built in this loop.

Checked both directions against `man/*.Rd` aliases and `NAMESPACE`:

| | count |
|---|---|
| listed in `_pkgdown.yml` | 125 |
| distinct Rd topics | 125 |
| listed but undocumented | 0 |
| exported but unplaced | 0 |

Exactly balanced. The index is being maintained in step with the manual --
consistent with the last commit's "inbound links 71->124".

## 537. `benchmarks.Rmd` sends the reader past a ceiling that exists

The web-only article (`.Rbuildignore:16` keeps `vignettes/articles` out of
the tarball, so it is checked by nothing) explains why `cpm` reports 350
changepoints at n = 100,000 when four are real: `arl0 = 500` asks for a
false alarm every 500 observations, so a long series implies `n / arl0` of
them. Correct, and `arl0 = 500` is confirmed as the default in both
`cpm_wrapper()` and `cpt_monitor()`. Then it prescribes the fix:

> Setting `arl0 = 5 * n` returns **exactly the 4 real changepoints** at
> every length.

At the article's three lengths that asks for 5,000, 50,000 and 500,000. The
third does not exist. `cpm` ships threshold tables for a fixed grid, and
`cpt_detect()` refuses anything off it -- deliberately, because `cpm`
answers an off-grid value by *printing* an error and returning no
changepoints, which is indistinguishable from a real "no changes" result
(the trap R61 was written for). Measured:

```
arl0 = 5000     OK, 4 changepoints
arl0 = 50000    OK, 4 changepoints
arl0 = 500000   ERROR: not an average run length that cpm ships
```

So the recipe is unreachable at exactly the length that needs it most. The
sentence is now scoped to the two lengths where `5 * n` exists, followed by
the ceiling and why the refusal is deliberate.

## 538. And the refusal message named half the grid

Chasing that ceiling turned up the larger defect. `arl0 = 50000` *works*,
yet the error message listing legal values stopped at 20,000. The list came
from prose, not from the engine, so the definitive source is the table
`cpm:::loadThresholds()` indexes -- `cpmthresholds`, whose names are
`<cpmType>ARL<value>`. All 15 types ship the same 24 values:

> 100, 200, 300, 370, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000,
> 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000, 20000, 30000, 40000, 50000

(`ExponentialAdjusted` additionally ships 1-24.) The message listed **12 of
24**, omitting 300, 800, 900, 3000, 4000, 6000-9000, 30000, 40000 and
50000 -- every one of which runs. A user who hit the error and needed an
`arl0` of 30,000 was told the maximum was 20,000.

Fixed at both sites that carried the list: the `@param arl0` roxygen
(`R/wrap-nonparam.R:20`, propagated to `man/cpm_wrapper.Rd`) and the `stop()`
at line 114. The `@param` now also states the two facts the omission hid --
the grid is identical for every `cpm_type`, and 50,000 is a ceiling, so an
`arl0` proportional to series length runs out.

## 539. Why R61 missed it, and the shape of the fix

Test R61 already covered this argument. It asserted the guard fires for
`c(0, -5, 333, 20, 50)` and that supported values work for
`c(100, 370, 500, 1000, 20000)`. Every value in that second set is inside
the truncated list -- so the test confirmed the code *ran*, never that the
enumeration was *complete*. The same failure mode as §421's covering metric:
sampling inside the wrong answer agrees with it.

The extension derives the grid instead of restating it:

```r
th   <- utils::getFromNamespace("cpmthresholds", "cpm")
arl  <- as.integer(sub("^.*ARL", "", names(th)))
grid <- sort(unique(arl[arl >= 100]))
msg  <- tryCatch(cpm_wrapper(x, arl0 = 333), error = conditionMessage)
listed <- as.integer(regmatches(msg, gregexpr("[0-9]+",
            sub("^.*Supported values are ", "", msg)))[[1]])
expect_setequal(listed, grid)
```

It also asserts the "same for every `cpm_type`" claim the new `@param`
makes, by intersecting the grid across types, and runs the four values the
old list denied (300, 3000, 30000, and the ceiling). Because it depends on a
`cpm` internal, it skips rather than errors if `cpmthresholds` disappears.

## 540. The proof that proved nothing

Reverting the message to the truncated list made exactly one test fail,
R61 -- which looked like proof the new assertion discriminates. It was not.
The assertion was broken in a way that failed *unconditionally*:

```r
listed <- as.integer(regmatches(
  msg, gregexpr("[0-9]+", sub("^.*Supported values are ", "", msg)))[[1]])
```

`regmatches(x, m)` extracts from the string the offsets in `m` were measured
on. Here the offsets come from the trimmed tail and the extraction is from
the untrimmed `msg`, so it slices at the wrong positions and returns text;
`as.integer()` turns that into `NA`, and `expect_setequal(NA, grid)` fails
whatever the message says. Standalone debugging missed it because there I
had used the same string for both arguments -- the version in the file and
the version I checked were not the same code.

Which is why breaking the input is only half a proof. **A guard that fails
unconditionally is indistinguishable from a working guard if the only case
you run is the one that should fail.** The complete proof needs both
directions, and the passing direction is the one that catches this:

| message | R61 failures |
|---|---|
| truncated (the old list) | 1 |
| complete (the fixed list) | 0, with 40 assertions passing |

The same shape as §421's "when a sweep reports that everything is broken,
the sweep is broken", arriving from the other side: when a guard reports
that the one broken input is broken, the guard may still be broken.

## 541. The axis, swept to exhaustion

One defect of this kind invites the general question: what other messages in
this package hand the user a list of legal values? Three, all in
`wrap-nonparam.R`, all `cpm`:

- the `arl0` grid -- was wrong, now derived and guarded
- `lambda = 0.1` and `0.3`, twice, for `cpm_type = "FET"`

The `lambda` pair is right, and verifiable from the same table: `FET01` and
`FET03` are the only lambda-parameterised types cpm ships. Axis closed.

## 542. Verification

Full local suite clean, then both checks.

| | R 4.4.1, full Suggests | R 4.6.0, Imports only |
|---|---|---|
| `checking tests` | OK, 341s | OK, 118s |
| `checking examples` | OK, 54s | OK, 36s |
| `--run-donttest` | OK, 130s | OK, 49s |
| re-building vignettes | OK, 116s | OK, 70s |
| `checking package vignettes` | OK | OK |
| installed package size | NOTE | OK |

Everything the package controls passes. The remaining ERROR/WARNING/NOTEs
are this machine's toolchain, and the baseline shifted underneath the loop:
**`pdflatex` and `qpdf` are no longer on PATH here**. That turns what used
to be a single qpdf WARNING into a PDF-manual ERROR plus WARNING, and adds
a third NOTE -- `ggchangepoint-manual.tex`, flagged as "non-standard things
in the check directory", which is simply the debris the failed `pdflatex`
run left behind. The 4.4.1 dependency NOTE is `rjags` and `mcp` absent
(JAGS is not installed here; the CI workflow installs it on Linux and
macOS). None of these is a package defect, and none is new work -- but the
recorded baseline of "1 qpdf WARNING + 3 NOTEs" no longer describes this
machine, so a future round should compare against the shape above instead.

The installed-size NOTE flickered back on 4.4.1 after four consecutive OKs,
which is the boundary behaviour Part LX measured rather than a regression.

# Part LXV -- The third citation source, which the test was named for

The standing brief asks every round whether every `\citep`/`@key` resolves,
whether every bib entry is used, and whether entries are attributed to the
right work. R44 is the shipped authority for that, and reading it rather
than re-deriving it -- the lesson of §440 -- shows it covers more than its
name suggests and less than its comment claims.

## 543. What R44 already guarantees

Confirmed, and stated once: both bibliographies are exactly balanced.

| | entries | consumers |
|---|---|---|
| `inst/REFERENCES.bib` | 58 | 58 `\insertRef` keys |
| `vignettes/vignette_reference.bib` | 63 | 63 `@key` citations |

Zero unused, zero duplicate keys, every key resolving. Both directions are
guarded -- `expect_setequal(names(inst), unique(used))` closed the
defined-to-used direction in an earlier part, when ten dead entries came
out. Re-deriving that was wasted motion.

## 544. But "the three citation sources agree" compared two

R44's own comment names three: `cpt_cite()`, the `\insertRef` keys, and the
vignette bibliography. Its assertions compare the two `.bib` files to each
other and check that every key resolves. **The free-text table behind
`cpt_cite()` is never compared to either** -- and that table is exactly
where the drift the comment describes lived: "the TGUH paper was dated 2018
in `cpt_cite()` and 2022 in the vignette bib".

So the one source that had been wrong was the one left unguarded.

`cpt_references()` is a hand-maintained tribble, 58 rows of prose. Checked
directly, it is currently correct: every one of the 50 available methods has
an entry, no duplicates, no entry for a method the registry does not have
(the eight non-method rows -- `crops`, `edetector`, `benchmark`,
`critical_difference` and four more -- are feature topics, reachable as
`cpt_cite("crops")`), and for the 35 methods whose wrapper serves them alone
and cites exactly one key, the surnames and the year in the prose match the
bib entry the help page cites.

The comparison needs the 1:1 restriction, and the reason is worth recording
because the first pass without it reported five mismatches that were all
correct. `cpt_wrapper` serves five `changepoint` methods; its help page
cites the *software* (Killick 2014) while `cpt_cite()` names each method's
own paper -- Killick 2012 for `pelt`, Scott and Knott 1974 for `binseg`,
Auger and Lawrence 1989 for `segneigh`, Hinkley 1970 for `amoc`, Haynes
2017 for `np`. Both are right; a shared wrapper simply has no single
publication. The sweep was measuring an invariant that does not hold.

## 545. A citation that does not render, in the one vignette nothing scans

R44 scans `vignettes/*.Rmd` non-recursively, so `vignettes/articles/` -- the
web-only `benchmarks.Rmd` -- is outside every citation check in the package.
It also declares no `bibliography:` field.

That combination is currently harmless because the article cites nothing,
and it is a trap rather than a defect: **a vignette with `@keys` and no
`bibliography:` does not fail to build.** Pandoc emits the key as literal
text, so `@killick2012optimal` reaches the reader as those characters. The
invariant that matters is the pairing, and it holds across all eight files:

| | declares `bibliography:` | `@` citations |
|---|---|---|
| introduction | yes | 74 |
| ggchangepoint | yes | 28 |
| comparison | yes | 17 |
| inference | yes | 4 |
| monitoring | yes | 4 |
| extending | yes | 2 |
| supervised | yes | 1 |
| articles/benchmarks | no | 0 |

## 546. What was added

Two guards in R44, implementing what its comment already promised:

- for every 1:1-wrapper single-key method, the surnames and the year in
  `cpt_references()` must match the `inst/REFERENCES.bib` entry the help
  page cites, with `expect_gt(compared, 30L)` so a refactor that stops
  resolving wrappers cannot silently compare nothing;
- across `vignettes/` **recursively**, a file has `@` citations if and only
  if it declares a `bibliography:`.

Proved in both directions, which §540 established as the minimum. Two
independent breaks -- restoring the historical TGUH year drift in
`cpt_references()`, and appending `See @killick2012optimal ...` to the
article that declares no bibliography -- produce **exactly two failures, one
each**; with both reverted, R44 passes 164 assertions.

Full local suite clean; both checks at the shape §542 recorded, with
`checking installed package size ... OK` on both.

| | R 4.4.1 | R 4.6.0 |
|---|---|---|
| `checking tests` | OK, 366s | OK, 117s |
| `checking examples` | OK, 54s | OK, 36s |
| `--run-donttest` | OK, 132s | OK, 49s |
| re-building vignettes | OK, 117s | OK, 69s |
| installed package size | OK | OK |

# Part LXVI -- The one platform that disagreed

The 0.5.0 work to this point was committed and pushed as `bfa2677`, and
GitHub Actions ran the matrix `cran-comments.md` advertises. Five of six
jobs green: pkgdown, `windows-latest` release, and all three Ubuntu
flavours (devel, release, oldrel-1). **`macos-latest` release failed**, and
it found something no local check could.

## 548. One assertion, out of 5,633

```
── Failure ('test-doc-coverage.R:635:7'): every change_in a method
   claims to support actually works ──
Expected `is.null(res)` to be FALSE.
mosum claims change_in = mean but errored

[ FAIL 1 | WARN 0 | SKIP 34 | PASS 5633 ]
```

The same log explains it. On that runner `{mosum}` cannot be loaded --
`rgl.so` needs `libGLU.1.dylib`, which is absent -- and **nine other tests
already skip for exactly that reason**, reported by testthat as
"{mosum} cannot be loaded (9)". Those nine use `skip_if_not_installed()`,
which attempts the load. The change_in sweep did not.

Nothing is wrong with the package. `mosum` is a Suggests engine, and a
machine where it cannot load is a machine where it should be skipped.

## 549. Two predicates, one question each

`engine_installed()` is the package's own availability predicate:

```r
engine_installed <- function(pkg) {
  if (pkg %in% c("changepoint", "changepoint.np", "ecp")) return(TRUE)
  length(suppressWarnings(find.package(pkg, quiet = TRUE))) > 0L
}
```

`find.package()`, deliberately -- and there is a shipped test asserting it
adds no namespace, `expect_false(probe %in% loadedNamespaces())`. That is
right for package code, which uses it to tell a user what to install, and
it must not load 35 engines to answer.

But **28 places in the test suite had borrowed it to mean "can I run
this"**, and those are different questions. A package can be on disk and
unloadable. Constructed locally, the divergence is exact:

| | `engine_installed()` | `engine_usable()` |
|---|---|---|
| `brokenpkg` (DESCRIPTION only, no loadable namespace) | TRUE | FALSE |
| `mosum` (here) | TRUE | TRUE |
| `ggchangepoint.no.such.engine` | FALSE | FALSE |

So the suite gets the predicate for the question it actually asks, in
`setup.R`, and this is `requireNamespace()` used for what it does answer --
"can this be loaded here" -- rather than as a stand-in for "is it
installed", which is the misuse the 0.5.0 audit warned about.

All 28 test-suite uses now call it. `engine_installed()` is untouched, and
the test that is *about* it keeps calling it, because its subject is the
non-loading guarantee.

## 550. Three things the blind rename broke, and how they surfaced

Replacing an identifier across five files is not a safe refactor, and this
one had three casualties -- worth recording because each was silent:

1. **Five sites read `ggchangepoint:::engine_usable(...)`.** The helper
   lives in `setup.R`, not in the package namespace, so every one of those
   would have errored. Caught by grepping for `:::engine_usable` rather
   than by trusting the rename.
2. **The predicate's own test got rewritten**, so the assertion that
   `find.package()` adds no namespace would have been made about the
   function that deliberately does load one -- inverting the thing it
   exists to prove. Restored, with the `engine_usable()` half added
   alongside as the deliberate opposite.
3. **The guard-recognition meta-test carries the predicate names in a
   regex string**, which the rename also edited. It now recognises both
   spellings, since a test about `engine_installed()` is correctly guarded
   by `engine_installed()`.

The divergence case is now a shipped guard as well: a temp libpath holding
a directory with nothing but a `DESCRIPTION`, which `find.package()`
accepts and the loader cannot use.

# Part LXVII -- Guarding the shape that was invisible, and a pointer to nothing

## 552. The literal-call detector could not see the failing form

Part LXVI fixed the macOS job by giving the suite a loadability predicate.
That leaves the question of why nothing caught it, and the answer is in the
shipped meta-test `"no test reaches a Suggests engine outside a guarded
block"`. It is exact rather than heuristic, and its own comment says so: it
matches **literal** call forms only --

```r
sprintf("method\\s*=\\s*\"%s\"", m)      # method = "mosum"
sprintf("%s\\(", wp)                     # mosum_wrapper(
```

-- "because the bare name collides with other vocabulary". Correct, and it
means a loop over the registry calling `cpt_detect(v, method = m)` names no
engine at all. Ten such blocks exist, including the one that failed. All ten
were outside every guard the suite had, guarded or not.

The first attempt at hardening was to stop recognising `engine_installed()`
as a guard. Reverting the change_in sweep to it proved that does nothing:
the block is invisible to the detector, so what it is guarded *by* never
comes up. A tightening that cannot fail is not a guard, which §540 had
already said once.

## 553. Tolerance versus prediction

Twelve blocks drive dispatch from the registry with a variable. Three of
them use no availability predicate, and inspecting them was the useful part
of the round: they wrap the call in `tryCatch(error = function(e) NULL)` and
`next` on `NULL`. An engine that cannot load simply drops out. They are
safe by construction and need nothing.

The change_in sweep wraps the call the same way -- and then asserts:

```r
expect_false(is.null(res),
             info = paste(m, "claims change_in =", ci, "but errored"))
```

That is the whole difference. **For every other sweep `NULL` means "not
here"; for this one it means "broke its contract".** Nine of the ten
sole-guard blocks tolerate absence; the tenth reports it as a defect.

So the new guard is narrow on purpose: a block that drives dispatch from
`builtin_registry()` with a variable `method =` *and* asserts the call
succeeded must gate each iteration on `engine_usable()`. Blocks that `next`
on `NULL` are left alone, because they are already right.

Proved both ways. Reverting **both** of the change_in block's
`engine_usable()` calls -- the loop guard and the later `reachable` filter,
and the first attempt reverted only one, which is why it appeared not to
fire -- flags exactly `test-doc-coverage.R:600`; restored, it flags nothing.

## 554. `?taylor_wrapper` sent readers to a vignette that cannot exist

The round's vignette pass took the cross-reference axis: every
`vignette("...")` and every `\link{}` in the vignettes and the 205 Rd
topics. All resolve -- and the check was wrong in a way worth keeping.

It built the list of valid vignette names from `vignettes/` **recursively**,
which includes `articles/benchmarks.Rmd`. That file is excluded from the
tarball by `.Rbuildignore:16`, so it is never installed. The built tarball
holds seven vignette sources and zero `articles` entries, and
`vignette("benchmarks", package = "ggchangepoint")` warns *vignette
'benchmarks' not found*.

`R/wrap-applied.R:124`, propagated to `man/taylor_wrapper.Rd:58`, told the
reader to run exactly that call -- in the paragraph explaining that
`taylor` cannot be interrupted and that sizing the run beforehand is the
only option. The reader most in need of that page was sent to a warning.

Being web-only is correct: `_pkgdown.yml` files it under "Web only" because
the sweep behind it takes over twenty minutes. So the pointer was the
defect, and it now names the published URL and says plainly that
`vignette()` will not find it.

Guarded, in the direction that generalises: no file in `R/`, `man/` or the
shipped vignettes may reference a vignette absent from the top level of
`vignettes/`. The guard also asserts that `.Rbuildignore` still excludes
`articles/` and that the directory still exists -- otherwise it would pass
by guarding nothing. Reintroducing the bad pointer produces exactly one
failure.

# Part LXVIII -- What the return values promise

The axes this loop has swept all sit on one side of a function call:
arguments, documentation prose, tests, data shape, artefacts, citations,
platform. This part takes the other side -- the `\value` sections, which
promise the caller specific named things.

## 557. Two surfaces confirmed once, and not re-derived

`DESCRIPTION` asks a checker to install 56 Suggests, and nothing verifies
each is used. All 56 are referenced outside the dependency fields. Clean.

The vignette pass took the count-claims axis: every sentence in vignette
prose asserting a number of methods, engines, rows, families or provenances
-- eleven of them. All correct. `extending.Rmd`'s "fifty detectors",
`ggchangepoint.Rmd`'s "Five rows carry status planned",
`inference.Rmd`'s "Four provenances", `introduction.Rmd`'s "50 methods" and
its "six families", which enumerates exactly six.

Numbered sections run 1-4 in `inference.Rmd` and 1-7 in `monitoring.Rmd`,
both sequential; and all seven shipped vignettes have a
`%\VignetteIndexEntry{}` identical to their `title:`, so the vignette index
and the rendered page agree.

One near-miss worth recording as a discipline note rather than a finding.
The registry's `online` flag marks `bocpd`, `cpm`, `ocd` while
`cpt_monitor()` accepts `edetector`, `cpm`, `ocd` -- sets that differ in two
of three members, which reads like a defect. It is documented on
`?cpt_methods` ("`online` means the *algorithm* is sequential ... the sets
overlap without coinciding") and pinned by a shipped test whose name is
`"the online flag and cpt_monitor()'s methods are distinct sets"`. **Third
time this loop that a "finding" was already a shipped test.** Grep the
suite before measuring anything.

## 558. Every named column the manual promises

122 Rd pages carry a `\value` section; 102 name lowercase `\code{}` tokens,
413 in total. Most are argument or package names. The mechanically
checkable subset is the claim "a `\code{x}` column", which 16 pages make
about 19 columns. Run each method and look for the column in
`changepoints`, in `data`, and in `augment()` output:

| claim | where it actually is |
|---|---|
| `bcp` `posterior_prob` | changepoints |
| `cpm` `detection_time` | changepoints |
| `inspect` `strength` | changepoints |
| `taylor` `confidence` | changepoints |
| `segmented`/`smuce`/`strucchange` `ci_upper` | changepoints |
| `fitted`, seven engines | data + augment |

All 14 reachable claims honoured, each in the place its page implies.

The `penalty$type` strings are also promises, and 17 distinct ones are set
literally in `R/`. Two live values are not among them -- `SIC` from
`segneigh` and `AIC: meanar1cpt` from `envcpt` -- and both are correct:
the first is `changepoint`'s own default passed through, the second is
composed by `envcpt` from the model it selected. Not literals, not defects.

## 559. The most fragile claim in the package had no test

`?glance.ggcpt` explains why `total_cost` is `NA` in four cases and reports
normally otherwise. Measured against the live package, every case holds:

| | `total_cost` |
|---|---|
| `pelt`, mean, default (MBIC) | NA |
| `pelt`, mean, `penalty = "BIC"` | 544.4 |
| `pelt`, mean, `penalty = "AIC"` | 511.9 |
| `pelt`, mean, `penalty = 10` | 544.4 |
| `pelt`, `change_in = "var"` | 904.8 |
| `pelt`, `change_in = "meanvar"` | 543.9 |
| `binseg` / `segneigh` / `np` | NA |

The shipped test covered the binseg/segneigh NAs, the numeric penalties and
the two other `change_in` values. Three of the page's claims were unpinned,
and one of them is the most upstream-fragile statement in the package: the
mean-under-MBIC `NA` **is not a property of `changepoint` at all**. It is a
collision between two of this package's own Imports -- loading
`changepoint.np` replaces `changepoint`'s `logLik` method for `cpt` objects
with one that errors on exactly that combination. Both are Imports, so the
collision is always present, and if either upstream changes the `NA`
quietly becomes a number while the help page keeps saying otherwise.

Now pinned, along with `np` being `NA` for the unrelated reason that
`changepoint.np` defines no `logLik`, and named penalties reporting
normally. Inverting the headline assertion produces exactly one failure, so
it is checking the quantity rather than passing vacuously.

## 560. The one number that cannot be reproduced, and why that is fine

The same page says that for one and the same segmentation `cpt.range`
reports 219.7 where PELT reports 659.9. That pair cannot come from
`glance()`, which returns `NA` for `binseg` by construction -- it describes
the raw engine costs, on the author's own data, which no seed in the
sources reproduces.

The *relationship* is reproducible, and that is the part the sentence is
making a claim about. Forcing both engines onto an identical segmentation
(`penalty = "BIC"`, both reporting a single changepoint at 100) gives
-341.4 against -1071.8, a ratio of 0.319 where the documented pair is
0.333. Same phenomenon, different data, and the engine emits its own
"Not changed to be -2*logLik" warning while doing it -- which the shipped
test already asserts does not leak. Left as written.

## 562. The installed-size flicker, finally explained

Ten parts of this loop have watched that NOTE appear and vanish -- 5.2Mb
NOTE, OK, 5.1Mb NOTE, OK, 6.6Mb NOTE, then five consecutive OK, now 6.4Mb
NOTE. Reading the two runs of the *same round* side by side gives the
answer, because they disagree:

| | total | `doc` | `help` |
|---|---|---|---|
| R 4.4.1, full Suggests | 6.4Mb | 3.8Mb | 1.8Mb |
| R 4.6.0, Imports only | 5.4Mb | 2.7Mb | 1.8Mb |

`help` is constant. **`doc` is not, and it is the whole variance**: the
Imports-only run skips the chunks that need a Suggests engine, so it draws
1.1Mb fewer vignette figures. The package therefore straddles CRAN's 5Mb
line, and which side it lands on is decided by how many engines the
checking machine happens to have. That is not flakiness in the package and
it is not a defect -- but it does mean the NOTE will appear on some CRAN
platforms and not others, and `cran-comments.md` already describes it as
marginal rather than gone.

No waste behind it. `man/figures` is 1.3Mb across 24 files, the largest a
112K plot at 672x480 and 8-bit RGB, plus a 96K logo. Nothing oversized,
nothing at the wrong bit depth.

## 563. The one duplicate figure is the point

Hashing the figures turned up exactly one byte-identical pair,
`README-unnamed-chunk-6-1.png` and `README-unnamed-chunk-50-1.png`, which
reads like 40K of waste. It is the opposite. Chunk 6 is `autoplot(res)`;
chunk 50 is `plot(res)`, captioned *"base-graphics fallback (delegates to
autoplot)"*. **The two files being byte-identical is the evidence that the
delegation works.** Deleting either would delete the demonstration.

And nothing asserted it. `plot_via_autoplot()` backs **fourteen** classes,
and the suite only checked that `plot()` and `autoplot()` each return *a*
`"ggplot"` -- which a completely divergent implementation also satisfies.
Now guarded in two halves: structurally, every `plot.*` method in `R/`
routes through the one helper, which is exact and covers all fourteen; and
live, `plot(res)` and `autoplot(res)` must agree on labels, on layer geoms,
and on the full `ggplot_build()$data`.

The structural half was broken on the first attempt, in the way §540
predicts. These methods are one-liners, and reading a fixed five-line
window past a definition walks into the *next* method -- which does
delegate. So a divergent `plot.ggcpt_delay()` looked compliant and the
guard could not fail. It now takes the definition line alone unless it
opens a brace. Divergent method: 1 failure. Compliant tree: 6 assertions
pass. **Third guard this loop that needed the passing direction to reveal
it was inert.**

## 564. And the guard failed the check it was meant to survive

`r74` came back `2 ERRORs` on both R versions, tests failing, after a local
suite that was clean. The cause is the gap between the two, and it is worth
stating because the loop has now met it twice in different clothes:

```
── Failure ('test-hardening.R:1233:3'): every plot() method delegates ──
Expected `length(defs)` >= 13L.
Actual comparison: 0 < 13
```

**`R/` is not installed.** The local gate runs under `pkgload::load_all()`
from the source tree, where `../../R` exists; `R CMD check` installs the
package and runs the tests from `.Rcheck/tests/testthat`, where it does
not. So `defs` was empty and the structural assertion fired against
nothing. The live half needs no sources, so only the structural half is now
conditional -- and it asserts `expect_length(defs, 0L)` in the installed
case rather than silently doing nothing, so the branch is still saying
something.

Fixing it turned up a second trap. The obvious guard,
`dir.exists(test_path("..", "..", "R"))`, cannot work: **`test_path()`
aborts** with "Can't find path" when the target is missing, so the
`dir.exists()` never runs. `normalizePath(file.path("..", ".."),
mustWork = FALSE)` is what the rest of the suite uses, and now this test
does too. Verified in both contexts: 6 assertions pass from the source
tree, and 6 pass from a directory whose `../../R` is absent.

A local suite being clean is not evidence a test survives `R CMD check`.
Any test that reads the source tree has to be run from somewhere the source
tree is not.

# Part LXIX -- Counting the right noun

## 566. Two clauses of the brief, answered and closed

The standing brief asks whether bib entries are **complete**, which no
round had tested -- earlier parts checked that keys resolve, that no entry
is unused, that the two files agree on year and journal, and that authors
match `cpt_cite()`. Completeness is a different question: does each entry
carry the fields its own type requires?

Checked against BibTeX's requirements per type:

| | entries | types | incomplete |
|---|---|---|---|
| `inst/REFERENCES.bib` | 58 | 55 article, 1 book, 2 inproceedings | 0 |
| `vignettes/vignette_reference.bib` | 63 | 60 article, 1 book, 1 inproceedings, 1 manual | 0 |

Zero across 121 entries. Every `@article` has author, title, journal and
year; the books have publishers; the proceedings have booktitles.

Figure alt text, also unswept and a thing CRAN comments on. All seven
vignettes set `fig.alt` (72 occurrences), and the rendered HTML settles it:
**67 `<img>` tags across eight built pages, none without an `alt`**. Nor is
the text perfunctory -- no page repeats an alt string, the only strings
under 50 characters are the template's own `[Top]` and `[R logo]`
navigation, and the five that appear twice appear in two *different*
vignettes, where the same figure is legitimately shown again.

## 567. "Nineteen further engines" counted methods

The feature tour's `New in 0.5.0` box opened with:

> **New in 0.5.0.** Nineteen further engines; ...

The number is right. The noun is not, and this package is precise about it:
`engine` is a **registry column holding the upstream package name**. There
are 38 distinct values -- 35 in `Suggests` and the 3 Imports, which is
exactly what `NEWS.md` means by "35 engines inside a 56-package Suggests
list". Nothing in the package yields 19 engines. Measured from the `v0.4.0`
tag, the engine set grew from roughly 25 packages to 38, a delta near 13.

19 is the delta in **methods**, and `NEWS.md` says so itself, in a heading:

> ## Engine wave #2 — 19 new methods

So the two documents disagreed about what was being counted, and the
disagreement was resolvable from the repository. Corroborated by 0.4.0's own
NEWS, which was careful with the same distinction -- "grows from 13 to 31
wired methods. Eighteen new wrappers" -- and by the wrapper exports, which
went 26 to 43 at the tag, a delta of 17, matching neither.

The arithmetic closes exactly:

| source | value |
|---|---|
| live registry, `status == "available"` | 50 |
| NEWS, "reaches N wired methods" | 50 |
| NEWS, 0.4.0's "from 13 to N wired methods" | 31 |
| NEWS, "Engine wave #2 — N new methods" | 19 |
| 31 + 19 | 50 |

One word changed: *engines* to *methods*.

## 568. Guarded with no magic numbers

The guard reads every figure from either the live registry or `NEWS.md`'s
own sentences, so the three can only drift together rather than apart. It
asserts `reached == live`, `baseline + delta == live`, that the tour's
number *word* maps to `delta`, that it is attached to "further methods" --
and, separately, that the count of distinct engines is **greater** than
`delta`, which is the fact the old wording contradicted.

Proved in three states rather than two, because the sentence can fail in
two independent ways:

| tour text | R44-style outcome |
|---|---|
| "Nineteen further methods" | 8 assertions pass |
| "Nineteen further engines" (the original) | 1 failure |
| "Seventeen further methods" | 1 failure |

## 569. Inter-vignette claims, verified

While looking for the count claim: the tour asserts "**Six** companion
vignettes go deeper" and then describes each. Seven vignettes ship, minus
the host is six, and the six named are the six that exist -- with each
description matching its target's own title and subject, from
`introduction` "develops the methodology" through `monitoring` "covers
sequential detection on a stream and its detection-delay accounting". No
drift.

# Part LXX -- The rest of the box, and a contract nobody had closed

§567 fixed one word in the feature tour's `New in 0.5.0` box. The box makes
a dozen more claims, and the paragraph after it describes the result object.
This part checks the rest of it.

## 571. The object, as described

The tour says a `ggcpt` carries "the tidy `changepoints` tibble (`cp` = last
index of the left segment, `cp_value` = series value there, plus any
method-specific columns), a `segments` table, the `data`, the raw engine
`fit`, and metadata (method, `change_in`, penalty, convention, runtime)".

Live, a `ggcpt` has ten components: `changepoints`, `segments`, `data`,
`method`, `change_in`, `penalty`, `fit`, `call`, `cp_convention`,
`runtime`. Every one the sentence names is there, with the described
contents -- `changepoints` is `cp`/`cp_value`, `segments` is
`seg_id`/`start`/`end`/`n`/`param_estimate`, `fit` is the upstream `cpt`.

The parenthetical omits `call`. That is an abbreviation rather than an
error: `?new_ggcpt` documents it, `\item{call}{The matched call.}`, and the
sentence is a tour rather than a specification. Left alone.

## 572. "Each has its own section below or its own vignette"

The box closes with that promise, about twelve named features. It holds:

| box claim | section |
|---|---|
| a time index that survives the round trip | `## Time indices` |
| significance regions, `cpt_confint()`/`cpt_test()` | `## Inference` |
| `cpt_select()` | `## Selecting the number of changepoints` |
| influence, sensitivity, statistic, path, scale-space | `## Diagnostics` |
| supervised detection | `## Supervised detection` (+ its own vignette) |
| consensus and recommendation | `## Choosing and combining methods` |
| event annotation and reports | `## Communication` |
| benchmarking | `## Benchmarking` |
| sequential monitoring | `## Streaming` (+ its own vignette) |
| power analysis | `## Power and study design` |
| `as_ggcpt()` / `cpt_register_method()` | `## Extending` (+ its own vignette) |

Eleven subsections under `# The 0.5.0 surface`, one per claim, and the
methods claim is served by `# Engine wrappers`.

A sweep along the way reported that 32 of the 50 methods are "named nowhere
in the feature tour", which for a vignette subtitled *A Complete Map of the
Package* is the tell that the sweep is wrong -- it was matching quoted
strings only. With word boundaries it is 35 of 50 named in prose, and the
tour calls `cpt_methods()` five times, so the full table renders and the
map is complete. **Fourth time this loop that a large "finding" was a
broken measurement.** The ratio itself is the warning sign.

## 573. A closed set that nothing checked was closed

`# Engine wrappers` opens with a compatibility contract, stated exactly:

> Every wrapper from 0.2.0 onwards returns a `ggcpt` object; only the two
> original wrappers below predate the class and still return a bare tibble.

Measured across all 43 exported wrappers: 43 in the registry, 43 exported,
neither set holding anything the other lacks; **exactly two return a bare
tibble, and they are exactly `cpt_wrapper` and `ecp_wrapper`**; 38 of the
rest return `ggcpt`, with `fabisearch` and `hdreg` needing a shape the
generic probe does not supply.

So the sentence is true -- and nothing checked that the *exception set is
closed*. The suite asserted `ecp_wrapper()` returns a `tbl_df` in three
places and never asked whether a third wrapper had joined it. A new wrapper
returning a tibble would falsify the vignette and break every accessor a
caller expects to work on a result, silently.

Guarded now, and the first two attempts are the interesting part:

1. **Calling all 43 engines took over ten minutes** -- unacceptable in a
   suite that already runs 365s inside the check. Replaced with the
   documentation surface, which is exact and instant: 135 assertions in
   **2 seconds**.
2. **Asking whether each `\value` mentions "ggcpt" anywhere passes for
   everything**, because both exceptions mention it in passing --
   `cpt_wrapper` names the `"ggcpt_fit"` attribute, and `ecp_wrapper`
   explains that `$fit` is `NULL` on a `ggcpt` from `cpt_detect()`. All 43
   "named ggcpt", which briefly looked like two wrong help pages. It has to
   be what the section *opens* with.

Both directions proved: as shipped, 135 assertions pass; documenting a
third wrapper (`fpop_wrapper`) as returning a tibble produces exactly one
failure.

## 574. Verification

The first run of this round's gate **failed**, and the failure is the

```
── Failure ('test-doc-coverage.R:224:3'): no test reaches a Suggests
   engine outside a guarded block ──
```

The new wrapper test used `fpop_wrapper()` as its contrast case -- a

Worth stating plainly: the check that caught this is the one §552 could not

Second run, after guarding the call:

# Part LXXI -- The failure that hid behind its own noise

`af544bf` fixed the macOS job -- **`macos-latest (release)` is green** --
and `windows-latest (release)` failed instead. Four Ubuntu jobs and pkgdown
passed.

## 575. Thirteen identical lines, none of them the error

The whole visible failure was this, repeated:

```
Failed with error:  'there is no package called 'RSpectra''
```

`RSpectra` is not in this package's `DESCRIPTION` at all, directly or
transitively. It is **suggested by `InspectChangepoint`** -- a suggestion of
a suggestion, which `r-lib/actions` does not install -- and
`InspectChangepoint::inspect()` and `sparse.svd()` both call
`requireNamespace("RSpectra")` without `quietly = TRUE`. The engine handles
the absence itself, falling back to `base::svd`, so **these lines are a
loading diagnostic and not the failure at all.**

They are, however, the reason the failure could not be read. `R CMD check`
keeps the **LAST** n lines of the test log, default 13, and thirteen
repetitions of one diagnostic is exactly the tail. The testthat failure
names were pushed off the top and appear in neither
`gh run view --log-failed` nor the complete 43,772-line job log -- they were
never written.

This is the trap commit `fcd3083` already fixed once, for a different
variable: *"Show the vignette error: `_R_CHECK_VIGNETTES_NLINES_` keeps the
LAST n lines"*. The workflow sets that one and not
`_R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_`. Now it sets both, at 1000.

## 576. Two wrong fixes before the right one

The noise is worth silencing on its own account -- it is upstream's
diagnostic printed through our function, and `inspect_wrapper()` already
declares the intent in a comment: *"The engine prints Monte Carlo progress;
keep the console clean."* That comment was written for
`utils::capture.output()`, which takes **stdout only**.

1. **`suppressMessages()` does not work**, and the probe said so rather than
   my assuming it. Only "Loading required namespace" is a condition;
   `requireNamespace()` writes the "Failed with error" line **straight to
   stderr**, so it printed anyway from inside `suppressMessages()`.
2. **Capturing the message stream without assigning the result** silences
   the engine and then prints the captured lines, because the inner
   `capture.output()`'s value gets auto-printed by the outer one.

The form that works assigns both:

```r
ignore <- utils::capture.output(
  inner <- utils::capture.output(
    fit <- do.call(InspectChangepoint::inspect, args),
    type = "message"))
```

Three properties checked rather than assumed, because redirecting a stream
next to the condition system is easy to get wrong:

| | |
|---|---|
| the stderr diagnostic | silenced |
| a genuine `warning()` inside | still delivered to `tryCatch(warning=)` |
| a genuine `stop()` inside | still propagates |
| `fit` inside a function body | lands in the function env, not a capture frame |

Only the stream is redirected; the condition system is untouched.

## 577. What this did not fix

**The Windows failure is still unidentified.** The noise explains why it was
unreadable, not what it was, and no test in the suite asserts silence around
`inspect` -- the nine `expect_silent()` calls are about `cpt_methods()`,
`cpt_recommend()`, ggplot builds, `as_cpt_series()` and `cpt_benchmark()`,
none of which touch that engine. So this part buys observability and a
cleaner console, and the next run is what names the defect.

Stated plainly because it would be easy to present a green-looking fix
here: two edits went in, one of them makes the *next* failure legible, and
neither is known to address the actual Windows error.

## 578. All six jobs green -- and the cause was never recovered

`57a5804`: **`macos-latest`, `windows-latest`, all three Ubuntu flavours and
pkgdown all pass.** The whole matrix `cran-comments.md` advertises is green
for the first time in this loop.

The honest part is that **I cannot say why Windows passed**, and the
temptation to claim the fix worked should be resisted. Only two things
changed: the `inspect_wrapper()` stream capture, and a log-length variable
that cannot affect pass or fail. So either the capture fixed it by a path I
cannot see, or the original failure was environmental -- a Suggests engine
that failed to install on that particular run, say.

One concrete mechanism was worth checking and is ruled out.
`InspectChangepoint::inspect()` does raise a real warning when RSpectra is
missing:

```r
if (prod(dim(x)) > 1e+06 && !requireNamespace("RSpectra")) {
    warning("Dimension of data matrix is large, ...")
```

and `test-040-bugfixes.R:528` asserts `expect_no_warning(inspect_wrapper(Xg))`
-- which would fail on Windows and pass everywhere else. But `Xg` is
`cbind(a = ..., b = ...)` on 150 rows, so `prod(dim(x))` is **300**, five
orders of magnitude below the threshold. The warning cannot have fired.
Nor does any of the nine `expect_silent()` calls touch that engine.

So the failure's identity went down with the truncated log, and that is
precisely what §575 fixed. **The durable outcome of this part is not the
green tick; it is that a recurrence will name itself.** If Windows fails
again, the log will say what failed instead of thirteen copies of somebody
else's loading diagnostic.

## 579. The Windows failure, finally named -- and it is a process death

`2327dc1` changed **only `next_release.md`**, which `.Rbuildignore`
excludes, so the checked tarball was byte-identical to the green
`57a5804`. Windows failed anyway. That settles the question §578 left open:
**the failure is intermittent, and nothing in this loop's edits caused or
cured it.**

With `_R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_: 1000` now in effect -- confirmed present in
the job's env block -- the complete test output is available, and the
important thing about it is what is *absent*:

> there is no `[ FAIL n | WARN n | SKIP n | PASS n ]` line anywhere.

testthat never printed its summary. This is not an expectation failure; the
**R process died mid-run**. `testthat.Rout.fail` is 91 lines and stops
after a printed tibble, with no condition, no traceback and no
`Execution halted` inside the test output.

The last thing printed locates it exactly. `test-050-tools.R:462-468` ends
a block by trimming and printing five objects:

```r
cv <- cpt_label_error_curve(ds$a$series, labs, penalties = c(2, 20, 200))
for (obj in list(labs, err, b, r, cv)) { ... expect_warning(print(trimmed), NA, ...) }
```

and the log's final five tibbles are `label_id`, `label_id`, `series`,
`method`, and `penalty` with values 2/20/200 -- that loop, in order,
complete. So the process survived to the end of that test and died at the
boundary into the next one, `"a monitor refuses a feed of the wrong
width"`, which builds an **`ocd`** monitor:

```r
mv <- cpt_monitor("ocd", baseline = matrix(rnorm(240), ncol = 3),
                  thresh = c(10, 10, 10))
```

`ocd` is compiled code, and the check reports **0 notes** with no "packages
suggested but not available" -- so `ocd` was installed and that test really
ran. A hard crash inside an engine's C++ kills R exactly this way: no R
condition, no testthat summary, output simply stops.

**Flagged rather than fixed, once:** this is a genuine risk for the
submission, because CRAN's Windows builders would meet the same
intermittency. It is not reproducible on this Linux machine, and guessing
at a code change for a crash I cannot trigger would be worse than naming
it. What the round delivers is the diagnosis -- which was unobtainable two
commits ago -- and the log setting that produced it.

## 580. The changelog had stopped tracking the code four commits ago

The first thing a sweep of this working tree turns up is not in the code.
`b94c612` is the **last commit that touched `NEWS.md`**, and four
code-bearing commits follow it:

| commit | R files changed |
|---|---|
| `7ece62f` | 9 |
| `bfa2677` | 33 |
| `af544bf` | 1 |
| `57a5804` | 1 |

That is 42 file-touches and ~1500 changed lines of `R/` with **no
changelog entry**, and `cran-comments.md` telling CRAN "Forty-one defects
... NEWS.md itemises them and each has a regression test" while the tree
holds considerably more than forty-one.

The gap is not cosmetic, because four of the undocumented items are wrong
answers rather than rough edges:

- **`wbsts` could not report more than one changepoint.** Its
  `suppressWarnings(if (is.na(OUT)) OUT = NULL)` has been an error since
  R 4.2 for exactly the case where `OUT` holds two or more of them.
- **`hdcov` and `network` failed on 44-96% of runs, at random**, on
  `thresholdBS()`'s `2:level_length` against a single-level tree.
- **`cpt_batch()` detected on a panel it had rewritten** -- a factor
  member became level codes, a matrix member was unrolled column-wise into
  a longer series with a changepoint at the seam.
- **`ecp_wrapper()` absorbed non-finite values**, losing a real
  changepoint on twenty `NA`s and inventing two on an all-`NA` half.

A user upgrading from 0.4.0 would have had no way to learn any of that
from the package.

### 580.1 What the audit passes had recorded instead

The information was not lost -- §285 to §579 of this document describe
every one of them. But `next_release.md` is `.Rbuildignore`d and is a
development ledger, not a changelog; NEWS.md is what ships and what
`pkgdown` renders. The two had diverged because the audit rounds were
written up here and the write-up here felt like the write-up.

## 581. What this pass changes

- **A 47-item `NEWS.md` section**, "Fixes found in the final
  pre-submission sweeps", covering all four commits: the four wrong
  answers above, the argument-collision sweep, `cpm`'s two thresholds, the
  search-path and console-noise fixes, and the documentation that had
  drifted. Grouped by kind rather than by commit, because a reader does
  not care which pass found what.
- **`cran-comments.md`**: "Forty-one defects" -> "Eighty-eight", and a new
  paragraph naming the three engine-level defects this package routes
  around, because a CRAN reviewer reading `wbs_lsw_replay()` should not
  have to work out from the source why a wrapper replays an engine's body.
- The same file's **Dependencies paragraph is rewritten**. Two edits had
  collided in it: the sentence "Every one is guarded with
  `requireNamespace()` ..." -- which is about the thirty-five engines --
  had ended up after a five-line digression about `mcp` and JAGS, where
  "Every one" reads as being about `mcp`.

## 582. Fifteen `...` collisions the wrapper sweep could not see

§354, §377 and §397 swept `...` against every engine argument, and the
sweep was over the **registry**: fifty wrappers, 64 argument slots. Four
exported entry points are not registry wrappers, were therefore not
swept, and each pins or renames an engine argument:

```
cpt_crops(penalty=)      cpt_crops(method=)      cpt_crops(pen.value=)
cpt_wrapper(method=)     ggcptplot(method=)
cpt_monitor(cpmType=)    cpt_monitor(ARL0=)      cpt_monitor(MC_reps=)
cpt_monitor(dim=)        cpt_monitor(beta=)      + the same five through
                                                   cpt_replay()
```

Every one answered with R's own `formal argument "penalty" matched by
multiple actual arguments`, which names neither the function, nor the
engine, nor what to use instead -- the exact failure those two helpers
exist to prevent, in the four places nobody had pointed them at.

`cpt_wrapper()`'s is the one most likely to be met: it renames
`changepoint`'s `method` to `cp_method` because `method` already means
"which detector" everywhere else in this package, which makes `method`
both the natural thing for a reader of `?cpt.mean` to pass and the one
that breaks.

### 582.1 Three things measured rather than assumed

- **`thresh`, `patience` and `startup` cannot reach `...` at all.** They
  are formals of `cpt_monitor()`, so R matches them there first, and a
  guard listing them would be a branch that can never fire. Probed
  individually rather than added by pattern-match with the others.
- **`cpt_replay()` needs no guard of its own.** It forwards `...` to
  `cpt_monitor()`, so one fix covers both -- confirmed by probing
  `cpt_replay()` after fixing only `cpt_monitor()`.
- **`ggcptplot()` must name itself.** It shares `cpt_wrapper()`'s rename,
  so keying the message off the map key told a `ggcptplot()` caller about
  `cpt_wrapper()`. `reject_renamed_args()` grew a `label` argument for
  exactly that, since being told about a function you did not call is the
  failure this whole guard exists to stop.

## 583. `bcp` was still talking, and four print headers were ragged

**§310 restored the search path and did not stop the announcement.**
`bcp::bcp()` calls `require(bcp)` in its own body; the fix detached
`package:bcp` and `package:grid` afterwards, but `require()` speaks
through `packageStartupMessage()` first, so every `bcp_wrapper()` call
still printed two `Loading required package:` lines on stderr. They are
visible in this loop's own test logs. `with_search_path_restored()` now
suppresses package startup messages -- only those, so an engine's
`message()` and `warning()` still reach the caller.

**And four `print()` headers padded their labels by hand.** Measured on
the rendered output rather than read:

| method | defect |
|---|---|
| `print.ggcpt` | values in **three** columns (19, 20, 22) |
| `print.summary.ggcpt` | a different column from `print.ggcpt`, same object |
| `print.ggcpt_delay` | five of six right, `Average run length:` one out |
| `print.ggcpt_path` | `Distinct segmentations:` unpadded entirely |

plus a trailing space on every line built with `cat()`'s default
separator -- 5 of 13 lines of a `ggcpt`, 7 of a summary -- because the
separator lands between the value and the `"\n"`. One `cat_field()` helper
now emits all of them, so they cannot drift apart again. The tibble
printed below each header pads its own columns; that is tibble's output
and is left alone, which the regression test has to know.

`print.ggcpt` also had **no `\value` section** -- the single most common
reason a CRAN reviewer sends a package back -- and four topics
(`print.ggcpt`, `is_ggcpt`, `new_ggcpt`, `alarms`) had a `\description`
byte-identical to their `\title`, because roxygen copies the title when
there is no description paragraph.

## 584. `scale_space` is not the column three help pages said it was

`?cpt_methods` grouped it with `statistic` and `path`:

> `statistic`, `path` and `scale_space` the internals rendered by
> `ggcpt_statistic()`, `ggcpt_solution_path()` and `ggcpt_scale_space()`

`autoplot(type =)` said the three "error with the list of supporting
engines when this one does not expose the internals", and
`?cpt_scale_space` typed its `x` as "a `ggcpt` object produced by a
multiscale engine". All three describe a gate that does not exist.

Measured on a `pelt` fit, which the table marks `scale_space = FALSE`:

```
cpt_statistic(res)      -> Engine `pelt` does not expose a per-location statistic.
cpt_solution_path(res)  -> Engine `pelt` does not expose a solution path.
cpt_scale_space(res)    -> 600 rows: index, bandwidth, statistic,
                           threshold, significant, detected
autoplot(res, type = "scale_space") -> a ggplot
```

`statistic` and `path` gate their accessors. `scale_space` does not,
because **no engine stores one**: a grep for anything writing
`diagnostics$scale_space` finds nothing, and `cpt_scale_space()` computes
the sweep itself by running `mosum` (or `npmojo`) over the series. So the
column marks the two engines the sweep can be run *with* -- the domain of
that function's own `method` argument, which is exactly how
`?cpt_scale_space` already used it one paragraph earlier
(`subset(cpt_methods(), scale_space)$method`).

The cost of the wrong wording is a reader with a `pelt` fit concluding
the scale-space view is closed to them. All three pages now say what the
column is, and a test pins the behaviour: `cpt_scale_space()` on a `pelt`
result returns a sweep, `res$diagnostics$scale_space` is `NULL`, and the
two columns that *do* gate still refuse by name.

  per changepoint, `glance()` exactly one, `augment()` exactly *n*;
  `autoplot()`, `print()` and `summary()` all building. **48 clean, 2

  non-negative values). No violations.
- **Capability columns against their accessors.** `ci`, `fitted`,
  `statistic`, `path` and `posterior` agree with what every installed
  method actually delivers, with no exceptions. (The `scale_space`

- **Documented defaults against `formals()`.** 159 `@param` texts saying
  "Defaults to X" compared against the actual default; every mismatch
  surviving normalisation was the comparator's (a captured sentence

- **Every README chunk, run.** `README.md` is not checked by

Also clean: no dead internal functions (every non-exported definition has

## 587. `cpt_confint(method = "auto")` answered a different question, quietly

The bound-invariant sweep -- lower <= cp <= upper, both inside `1..(n-1)`,
one row per changepoint, `source` non-empty -- ran over every provenance
against every installed univariate engine, 59 method/route pairs. **All the
geometric invariants hold.** The one thing that did not was a level:

```
cpt_confint(nsp_result, method = "auto", level = 0.95)   ->  level column 0.9
cpt_confint(nsp_result, method = "nsp",  level = 0.95)   ->  level column 0.95
```

The mechanism is short. An `nsp` result carries significance regions, so
`native_bounds()` finds them, `"auto"` resolves to `"native"`, and
`"native"` reports `native$level` -- which is what `nsp_wrapper()`'s
default `alpha = 0.1` produced, a global level of 0.9. The requested 0.95
is discarded on the way.

**Nothing here was dishonest.** The `level` column said 0.9, the `source`
column said `nsp_region`, and `?cpt_confint` documented that
`method = "native"` ignores `level`. The gap is that the caller who is
surprised did not ask for `"native"`; they asked for `"auto"` and were
never told where it went. Asking for a 95% interval and getting a 90% one
with no signal but a column you have to inspect is the kind of thing that
reaches a paper.

### 587.1 Why a warning rather than recomputing

Recomputing NSP at the requested level would be the wrong fix twice over:
it would spend an `M = 1000` Monte Carlo run that `"auto"` exists to avoid,
and it would throw away the regions the result already carries -- which are
the inference the user asked for when they chose `nsp`. Reusing them is
right; doing it silently was not.

So the check is **on the answer, not on the route**: if an explicitly
supplied `level` does not appear in the `level` column, say so and name the
branch that got there. That covers `"auto"` -> `"native"` without needing
per-route bookkeeping, and it would catch any future route with the same
property.

Two details that keep it from being noise:

- **`missing(level)` gates it.** The default must never warn, because
  0.95 against a 0.9 native interval is the overwhelmingly common case and
  warning about it would train the user to ignore the warning.
- **Tolerance, not equality.** `abs(got - requested) < 1e-9`, since the
  levels travel as doubles through an engine.

`cpt_monitor()` already warns on exactly this pattern -- "`arl0` does not
affect `method = \"edetector\"`, which is tuned by `alpha`" -- so this is
the courtesy the package already extends elsewhere, applied to the one
place it was missing.

## 588. Twelve metrics, twelve names, three explanations

`?cpt_metrics`'s `@return` was a flat comma-separated list of twelve column
names, and `@details` explained precision/recall, covering, and the
both-empty case. What a reader could not learn from the page:

- **`annotation_error` is a count difference and nothing else.** It is
  `abs(n_pred - n_truth)`. Measured on a 100-point series, predicting 5
  against a truth of 90:

  ```
  annotation_error = 0     hausdorff = 85     f1 = 0     rand_index = -0.06
  ```

  A perfect score for a segmentation that got the location wrong by 85
  observations. That is the metric behaving as defined -- but a
  `cpt_benchmark()` column reading 0 is going to be read as "perfect", and
  nothing said otherwise.
- **Which direction is better.** `benchmark.R` knows
  (`lower_better <- metric %in% c("hausdorff", "annotation_error",
  "mae_matched", "rmse_matched")`); the help page did not say.
- **The one-sided degenerate cases**, where the row mixes two conventions:

  | case | precision / recall / f1 | rand_index | hausdorff / mae / rmse |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | both empty | 1 | 1 | `NA` |
  | `pred` empty | 0 | 0 | `NA` |
  | `truth` empty | 0 | 0 | `NA` |
  | nothing matched | 0 | < 0 | `NA` for mae/rmse, a number for hausdorff |

  So an all-wrong answer returns `f1 = 0` and `mae_matched = NA` in the
  same row -- 0 where the quantity is a rate, `NA` where it is a distance
  with no pair to measure. Only the both-empty row was documented, and it
  is the one a reader is least likely to hit.

### 588.1 The numbers themselves are right

Checked rather than asserted, against reference implementations written
from the definitions and sharing no code with the package: `covering` by
explicit `intersect()`/`union()` over every segment pair, `rand_index`
from a contingency table with `choose()`, `hausdorff` by double minimax,
precision/recall by re-running the greedy one-to-one match. Nine
hand-built cases plus twenty random 400-point ones. **Every
non-degenerate value agreed exactly**, including the `findInterval()` fast
path in `calc_covering()` -- which is a performance change to a formula,
so a test now pins it to the definition rather than to a recorded number.

The only disagreements were the degenerate rows above, where the
reference divided by zero and the package makes a deliberate choice. That
is what turned this from a correctness check into a documentation one.

## 589. What this pass changes

- **`cpt_confint()` warns** when an explicitly supplied `level` is not the
  one the answer carries, naming the route. `@param level` now says that
  `"auto"` resolves to `"native"` whenever the engine supplied an
  interval, so an explicit level can go unused there too.
- **`?cpt_metrics` gains a `\describe` return block** -- every column, what
  it measures, and which direction is better -- plus a
  "Degenerate cases" section giving the table above. `annotation_error`
  carries an explicit "read it beside a location metric, never alone".
- **`?cpt_scale_space`, `?cpt_methods` and `autoplot(type =)`** stop
  describing `scale_space` as a gate (see §584).
- Four regression tests: the level warning and its silence on the default,
  the level honoured on every computing route with the geometric
  invariants alongside, the metric conventions row by row, and covering
  against its definition.

- **Time-index threading, end to end.** With a weekly `Date` index over
  200 observations and five engines: `res$index` identical to what was
  supplied; `tidy()$cp_index` equal to `index[cp]` **and still a
  `Date`**; `augment()` carrying a Date column equal to the index in
  order; `cpt_confint()`'s `cp_index`, `ci_lower_index` and
  `ci_upper_index` all equal to the index at their integer positions;
  `autoplot()`'s x range spanning the index rather than `1..n`; `print()`
  reporting the index. Plus the two guards: an unequally spaced index

- **`cpt_confint()` geometry**, as above: 59 method/route pairs, every
