## 591. The check that names the wrong line

Adding §589's tests made the suite fail, and the failure was informative
about the checker rather than about the tests:

```
test-hardening.R:1585 uses nsp_wrapper without skip_if_not_installed()
```

Line 1585 is `test_that("the covering metric matches an explicit set
computation", ...)`, which computes Jaccard overlaps on integer vectors and
does not touch `nsp` in any form. The only mention of `nsp_wrapper()` in
the file was in a **section comment introducing the next test** -- the
guarded one that legitimately uses it.

The cause is one line of the checker:

```r
starts <- grep("^test_that\\(", src)
ends <- c(starts[-1] - 1L, length(src))
```

A block therefore runs to the line before the next `test_that(`, so
everything between two blocks -- blank lines, and the header comment
belonging to the block below -- is attributed to the block above.

**A checker that names the wrong line is worse than no checker**, because
the failure is confusing instead of informative: the obvious response is to
add a guard to a test that does not need one, which weakens the coverage
this check exists to protect (the design note above it is explicit that a
call inside `expect_error()` must stay unguarded, for exactly that reason).

### 591.1 srcrefs, not brace counting

The fix is to take each block's extent from R's own parser:
`parse(f, keep.source = TRUE)` and the `srcref` attribute give the first
and last line of each expression, and comments *between* expressions belong
to no expression at all.

Brace counting was the other candidate and would have been wrong here:
several blocks in this suite contain a brace inside a string --
`skip("{mcp} is not installed")` is one -- so a balance counter would
mis-close them. The parser handles it because it is a parser.

### 591.2 Measured both ways

The synthetic file the new test builds has all five shapes, and the two
rules disagree exactly where they should:

| block | old rule | srcrefs |
|---|---|---|
| A: unguarded, touches nothing | **flagged** | -- |
| B: guarded, header above belongs to it | -- | -- |
| C: genuinely unguarded call | flagged | **flagged** |
| D: brace inside a string | -- | -- |
| E: call inside `expect_error()` | -- | -- |

So the change removes a false positive and keeps the true one, which is
what the test asserts -- both directions, so a future simplification back
to the line-based rule fails rather than passing quietly.

## 592. Verification

Full suite via `testthat::test_local()`: the only failure was the one in
§591, and it is now fixed; the two standing skips (`mcp` needs JAGS, the
TCPD download is not exercised) and the two `envcpt` upstream warnings are
unchanged.

## 593. §180 was the highest-severity item in this document and was never done

The audit that wrote §180 called it "the highest severity-to-effort ratio
in the document". §214.3 listed it as an action. §232 corrected its scope
from 19 sites to 35. And then:

```
$ grep -rn "with_local_seed\|with_seed" R/
$ grep -rc "if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)" R/*.R | ...
35
```

**No helper, thirty-five bare sites.** The diagnosis was written three
times and the fix zero. Re-measured against the current tree before
touching anything, because a stale finding is worth less than no finding:

| entry point | distinct datasets in a 6-iteration loop |
|---|---|
| `cpt_detect(method = "wbs")` -- no seed | 6 of 6 |
| `cpt_detect(method = "wbs", seed = 1)` | **2 of 6** |
| `cpt_detect(method = "nsp", seed = 1)` | **2 of 6** |
| `cpt_stability(B = 5, seed = 7)` | **2 of 6** |
| `cpt_simulate(seed = 3)` | **2 of 6** |
| `cpt_select(criterion = "cv", seed = 5)` | **2 of 6** |

and directly, with the data pre-generated so generation cannot be mistaken
for the effect: after `cpt_detect(x, method = "wbs", seed = 42)` the
caller's next `rnorm()` draw is not the one they would have got. Still
live, exactly as described.

### 593.1 Why the fix is a statement and not an expression wrapper

§180.2 proposed `with_local_seed(seed, expr)`. That form is cleaner in
isolation and would have meant restructuring thirty-six function bodies to
wrap everything after the seeding inside a call -- a large diff across
twenty-one files, in wrappers whose bodies are the part of the package
most worth not disturbing before a submission.

The equivalent that is a **one-line substitution** is to register the
restore in the *caller's* frame:

```r
local_seed <- function(seed, envir = parent.frame()) {
  if (is.null(seed)) return(invisible(FALSE))
  ...
  do.call(base::on.exit,
          list(substitute(f(), list(f = as.name(nm))), add = TRUE),
          envir = envir)
  set.seed(seed)
}
```

A helper's own `on.exit()` would fire the moment the helper returned, which
is why the handler goes in `envir`. `add = TRUE` because two wrappers
already register a search-path restore -- checked, and both of those use
`add = TRUE` too, so nothing is clobbered in either direction. Every one of
the thirty-six sites became `local_seed(seed)`, and `grep` confirms no bare
`set.seed()` is left in the package's code.

### 593.2 Two details that are easy to get wrong

- **A fresh session has no `.Random.seed`.** It is created by the first
  draw, so a naive save-and-restore would *leave one behind* on a session
  that had none -- itself a change to the caller's state. The helper
  records whether it existed and `rm()`s it if it did not. A test asserts
  that.
- **`cpt_power()` and `cpt_stability()` seed once and then draw many
  times.** Scoping must not truncate that: the restore fires when the
  *outer* function exits, so the replicate loop inside still walks the
  seeded stream and stays reproducible. Verified rather than assumed --
  same seed twice gives identical output.

### 593.3 Measured after

| property | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| distinct datasets, 6-iteration loop, seeded | 2 of 6 | **6 of 6** |
| caller's `.Random.seed` after a seeded call | reset | **identical** |
| same seed twice, 1000 draws between | identical | **identical** |
| same seed after an unseeded call moved the stream | identical | **identical** |
| fresh session left without `.Random.seed` | n/a | **yes** |

The two reproducibility rows are the point of the exercise: the fix removes
a side effect without costing anything the argument was for.

## 594. What this pass changes

- **`local_seed()`**, and all thirty-six `if (!is.null(seed))
  set.seed(seed)` sites replaced with it -- twenty-one files, mechanical,
  `grep`-verifiable.
- **All thirty-six `@param seed` blocks** say the seed is scoped to the
  call. §180.2's item 4 called the old wording a documentation bug and it
  was: "for reproducibility" is what a reader would take as a promise that
  the loop around the call is unaffected.
- **Three metamorphic test blocks**: the six-iteration loop for five entry
  points (with the no-seed case as the reference, so the test cannot pass
  vacuously), `.Random.seed` identity across five seeded calls plus the
  fresh-session case, and reproducibility across intervening draws and
  across an unseeded call.

## 595. And a clean sweep of the extension mechanism

`?cpt_register_method` promises that a registered detector "then works with
everything built on the `ggcpt` contract" and names ten things. All ten
were run against a registered detector (a CUSUM argmax in six lines):
`autoplot()`, `geom_changepoint()`, `geom_cpt_segment()`,
`geom_cpt_label()`, `tidy()`, `glance()`, `augment()`, `cpt_metrics()`,
`ggcpt_compare()`, `cpt_stability()`, `cpt_consensus()`,
`cpt_benchmark()`, `cpt_report()`. **All pass**, with the row counts the
`ggcpt` contract requires (one tidy row per changepoint, one glance row,
one augment row per observation).

The visibility promises hold too: `cpt_methods()` gives the method
`status = "registered"` and `installed = NA`, `print()` marks the result
`[user-registered]`, `cpt_cite()` returns the citation the registration
supplied, and a registration with no citation says so plainly --

> No citation was supplied when `nocite` was registered with
> cpt_register_method(). This method is user-supplied: ggchangepoint
> validated the shape of its output, not its statistics.

Nothing to fix. Recorded because this is the headline feature of the
release and the claim is unusually specific, so it is worth having been
checked item by item rather than in spirit.

## 596. The seed fix broke four snapshots, and that was the second finding

Scoping the seed turned the full suite red in `test-050-visual.R`:

```
Snapshot of 050-visual/cpt-monitor-timeline.svg  has changed
Snapshot of 050-visual/ggcpt-statistic.svg       has changed
Snapshot of 050-visual/ggcpt-scale-space.svg     has changed
Snapshot of 050-visual/ggcpt-solution-path.svg   has changed
```

The temptation here is to read this as the fix being wrong. It is the
opposite: **those four snapshots were relying on the leak.**

The file seeds once at the top and draws the two series every block shares:

```r
set.seed(2026)
x_step  <- c(rnorm(60), rnorm(60, 4))
x_multi <- c(rnorm(50), rnorm(50, 4), rnorm(50, 1))
```

but three blocks generate their own data with a bare `rnorm()` inside the
block, taking whatever stream state the blocks above them happen to leave.
And the block immediately above them ends with:

```r
pw <- cpt_power(n = 150, jump = c(0.5, 2), n_sim = 10, seed = 1, ...)
```

which used to pin the stream to seed 1. Remove the pin and the following
`rnorm(150)` draws a different series -- so the snapshot changes, because it
was a snapshot of *test execution order* as much as of the plot.

### 596.1 Confirming it was data and not a broken figure

Before accepting a snapshot, the question is whether the picture is still
the right *kind* of picture. Two checks, neither of which is "it looks
fine":

Structure, from the SVGs:

| snapshot | polyline | rect | text | bytes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cpt-monitor-timeline | 10 -> 10 | 6 -> 6 | 13 -> 13 | 8081 -> 8229 |
| ggcpt-statistic | 15 -> 16 | 13 -> 13 | 17 -> 18 | 18902 -> 19180 |
| ggcpt-scale-space | 13 -> 15 | 7 -> 7 | 15 -> 16 | 12705 -> 12941 |
| ggcpt-solution-path | 13 -> 13 | 13 -> 13 | 24 -> 24 | 12168 -> 12166 |

Same panels, same furniture, one or two more marks where the new series has
one more changepoint or one more axis label. Layers, from the objects:

```
monitor      alarms = 2    GeomLine, GeomVline
mosum        cp = 200      GeomLine, GeomLine, GeomVline, GeomHline
scale_space                GeomRaster, GeomPoint
wbs          cp = 199      GeomSegment, GeomPoint
```

`mosum` finds the true changepoint at 200 and `wbs` at 199, and the layer
compositions are unchanged. So the figures are correct and of a different
series, which is the only reading under which accepting is right.

### 596.2 The fix is to seed the block, not to re-record the order

Re-recording alone would have left the snapshots order-dependent -- passing
today and failing the next time anything above them changed how much
randomness it consumes. Each of the three blocks now calls `set.seed()`
before generating its data, which makes the snapshot a function of the
block.

Verified by running the file from three deliberately different starting
states -- `set.seed(1)`, `set.seed(12345)`, and 777 discarded draws --
**0 failures each**. Before, the same experiment is what produced the four
failures in the first place.

This is the §180 story in miniature: a leaked seed made something look
reproducible that was not, and the leak had to go before anyone could tell.

## 597. §180.2's item 5, measured -- and it was wrong in two ways

The roadmap's last unaddressed seed item read:

> **While there: `parallel = TRUE` is the default** on `cpt_power()` and
> `cpt_stability()`. Under `future`, `future.seed` governs worker streams
> and the local `set.seed()` does not reach them, so the sequential and
> parallel paths may not agree even with a seed fixed. [...] this is the
> specific pair to test.

Measured, and both halves of the guess need correcting.

**`cpt_stability()` has no parallel path at all.** `grep` for
`future_lapply` finds `cpt_batch()`, `cpt_benchmark()`, `cpt_consensus()`,
`cpt_influence()`, `cpt_sensitivity()`, `ggcpt_compare()` and
`cpt_power()`; `stability.R` contains none. So the "pair" was one function
and a mistake, and the real surface is seven.

**Only one of the seven diverges.** Each was run twice under a sequential
plan and twice under a real two-worker `multisession` plan, with a
*stochastic* engine (`wbs`) where the function takes a method, so the
worker stream had every chance to show:

| function | twice, sequential | twice, 2 workers | sequential vs parallel |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cpt_influence` | identical | identical | identical |
| `cpt_sensitivity` | identical | identical | identical |
| `cpt_consensus` | identical | identical | identical |
| `cpt_batch` | identical | identical | identical |
| `cpt_benchmark` | identical | identical | identical |
| **`cpt_power`** | identical | identical | **different** |

The reason is not the plumbing but what the tasks *do*: six of the seven
farm out work that is deterministic given its input -- refit with this
perturbation, score against that dataset -- so no random number enters the
answer and the worker stream is irrelevant. `cpt_power()` farms out
*simulation replicates*, which is exactly the case `future.seed` exists
for. One and the same `seed = 11` on two scenarios at `n_sim = 8`:

```
sequential   power = 0,     1
2 workers    power = 0.125, 0.875
```

### 597.1 Why this is documented rather than "fixed"

Both answers are correct estimates of the same quantity and both are
deterministic; they differ because the numbers come from different
(equally valid) streams. Making them agree would mean either abandoning
parallel-safe streams -- which is what `future.seed` is for and would be a
genuine correctness regression across workers -- or generating every
replicate's data in the parent and farming out only the detection, which
changes the numbers for the default path, is a real behaviour change, and
still would not close the gap for a stochastic detector.

So `?cpt_power` gains a **Reproducibility under a parallel plan** section
stating the guarantee that does hold -- *same seed and same plan, same
answer* -- how to pin a figure that has to be reproducible by someone else
(`parallel = FALSE`, or state the plan with the seed), and that the gap is
Monte Carlo error, which `mc_se` already quantifies. It also records that
the other six are plan-independent, because "is this affected?" is the
first question a reader of that section will have.

Two tests pin it: all four testable entry points reproduce within a plan
under *both* plans, and the three deterministic ones give identical
answers across plans while `cpt_power()` is only required to stay a valid
rate. The parallel plan is restored with `withr::defer()` so a failure
cannot leave one set for the rest of the suite.

## 598. Eleven vignette chunks drew data nobody had seeded

The same defect as §596, in the vignettes. `vignettes/ggchangepoint.Rmd`
seeds at line 90 and line 345 and then has four chunks that generate fresh
data with a bare `rnorm()`; `monitoring.Rmd` has six and `supervised.Rmd`
one. Their rendered output is therefore a function of how much randomness
every chunk above them consumed.

**And several of those upstream chunks are conditional.** `ggchangepoint.Rmd`
gates them on engine availability (`eval = has_cpop`, `eval = has_idetect`,
...), so on a machine without `cpop` the chunk at line 258 does not run,
and every unseeded chunk after it draws different data. The vignette's
numbers and figures already differed between machines with different
optional packages -- before this loop touched anything.

Each of the eleven now seeds itself. No prose claim depended on the old
values, checked chunk by chunk, so this changes the rendered output and
nothing that is said about it.

## 599. Verification

`R CMD check --as-cran` on the tarball built after the 36-site seed change:
`checking examples ... [54s] OK`, `--run-donttest ... [123s] OK`. The seed
scoping reaches every example and every `\donttest` block, so those two
lines are the ones worth quoting.

## 600. `as_ggcpt()` was losing changepoints quietly, and the docs said it should

`?as_ggcpt`'s `@param cp` read:

> Out-of-range, duplicated and missing values are dropped, and the result is
> sorted -- the same contract every built-in wrapper is held to.

So the dropping was a decision, not an oversight. Measured on a 200-point
series:

```
as_ggcpt(c(50, 500), x)  ->  1 changepoint at 50
as_ggcpt(c(0, 50), x)    ->  1 changepoint at 50
as_ggcpt(c(50, 200), x)  ->  1 changepoint at 50
as_ggcpt(50.5, x)        ->  1 changepoint at 50    (truncated, not rounded)
as_ggcpt(c(50, 50), x)   ->  1 changepoint at 50    (deduplicated)
as_ggcpt(c(50, NA), x)   ->  1 changepoint at 50
```

**The `x` side, by contrast, is validated exactly as `cpt_detect()` is** --
a factor, a character vector, an `NA`, an `Inf`, a two-point series and a
`NULL` are all refused with the same messages, verified side by side. It is
only `cp` that was unguarded.

The justification in the docs is sound *for a wrapper*: the indices come
from an engine, some of which legitimately emit a boundary value (`ecp`
reports `n`), and normalising a machine's output is what a wrapper is for.
But `as_ggcpt()`'s documented use cases are "a published paper's reported
breaks, an analyst's annotations, another package's output" -- human
transcription, where one mistyped index vanishing without a word leaves a
result that looks complete and is short a changepoint.

### 600.1 Warn, not refuse -- and why that is the right scope

Refusing was implemented first and then backed out. It is the better
behaviour in the abstract and it is the wrong change here: the dropping is
documented, so refusing would break code that works today, and the brief
for this pass is polish rather than behaviour change. What is not defensible
under any reading is the *silence*.

So the return value is byte-identical to before, and each of the five
now warns -- with the values, the range they had to fall in, and the
sentence that makes the range make sense:

```
`cp`: 1 outside 1..199 (200). 2 location(s) supplied. A "left" changepoint
is the last index of the segment before it, so 200 would leave no segment
after it.
```

Sorting stays silent, because reordering loses nothing. An integer-valued
double (`150.0`) is not a truncation and does not warn. Both convention
boundaries -- `cp = 1` under `"left"`, `cp = n` under `"right"` -- are
valid and stay silent, and their opposites warn with the right range
(`2..200` for `"right"`). Twelve legitimate calls, including `ci`,
`fitted`, `index`, multivariate and empty input, were checked to still be
silent.

## 601. Two claims the release letter makes, checked and holding

- **`cpt_test()` never lets an unadjusted p-value pass for an adjusted
  one.** 68 method/type pairs across every installed univariate engine:
  `p_value` inside \eqn{[0, 1]} everywhere, `selection_adjusted` a clean
  logical with no `NA`, and the warning firing on **exactly** the rows
  that are unadjusted -- never on a fully adjusted result, always on a
  partly unadjusted one. Two of the 68 pairs are adjusted (the engines
  with their own test), 66 are not and say so. All three `p.adjust`
  corrections (`holm`, `BH`, `bonferroni`) were checked to be
  non-decreasing, bounded by 1, and order-preserving. Zero violations.
- **No engine fabricates changepoints on no-change data at a usable series
  length.** NEWS records a 0.4.0 fix for "an `ecp` wrapper that fabricated
  changepoints on no-change data", so the property is worth re-checking
  rather than assuming. Twelve pure-noise draws at \eqn{n = 200},
  \eqn{p = 5}, per multivariate engine:

  | engine | draws reporting >=1 changepoint |
  |---|---|
  | npmojo, inspect, geomcp, fastcpd, esac, pilliat, fmean | 0 of 12 |
  | kcp, var | 1 of 12 |
  | ecp, hdcov | 2 of 12 |
  | kwc | 3 of 12 |
  | fcov | 4 of 12 |

  Ordinary Type-I error at nominal levels for the first eleven, and no
  fabrication anywhere near the `ecp` failure 0.4.0 fixed. **The two
  functional methods are the loose ones and the measurement is not
  conclusive about them:** `fcov` and `kwc` read the columns as a grid over
  a curve, so \eqn{p = 5} is a coarse grid rather than their design case,
  and `?fcov_wrapper` already records that two columns fail outright while
  three or more return a fit. Re-running at \eqn{p = 15} and \eqn{p = 30}
  to separate "wrong regime" from "loose threshold" was started and
  abandoned -- it had not finished either method at \eqn{p = 5} after forty
  minutes under load, and it is a refinement of a negative result rather
  than a blocker. **Left open, and stated as open**, rather than reported
  as either clean or broken.

## 602. §181.2's transposed-matrix finding no longer holds

The roadmap recorded:

> **7 of 9 multivariate engines accept a transposed matrix; 5 fabricate
> changepoints**

Re-measured on a 200 x 3 series against its 3 x 200 transpose, over the
eleven multivariate engines that take a plain matrix:

| behaviour | count | engines |
|---|---|---|
| refused, with a message naming the shape | 5 | kcp, npmojo, ocd, geomcp, var |
| warned (the degenerate-segmentation guard) | 3 | fastcpd, esac, pilliat |
| returned no changepoints | 3 | ecp, hdcov, fmean |
| returned a changepoint, silently | 1 | inspect |

So the intervening rounds moved this from "5 fabricate" to one engine that
returns a changepoint without comment, and the reason it is not guarded is
worth stating rather than fixing:

**a 3 x 200 input is not obviously wrong for a high-dimensional method.**
`inspect`, `esac` and `pilliat` exist for \eqn{p \gg n}; refusing more
coordinates than time points would refuse their design case. And the
existing degenerate-segmentation guard fires on `k == n - 1`, which at
\eqn{n = 3} with one changepoint is correctly not triggered. Any threshold
on \eqn{n} alone would be arbitrary, and the false-positive measurement in
§601 shows the engines are well behaved wherever a series is long enough to
be one. **Recorded as measured and deliberately not guarded**, which is a
different answer from §181.2's and the one the numbers support.

## 603. The warning reached a caller it was not written for

`test-050-registry.R` went green with four new warnings, and two of them
were the fix over-reaching. `cpt_detect()` routes a **registered method's**
bare-vector return through `as_ggcpt()`:

```r
res <- as_ggcpt(out, x, method = entry$method, ...)
```

so a user's registered detector that emits a boundary index -- or `80.4`,
or a repeat -- now warned on every call, with a message telling them to
"check the values against the series rather than relying on this
normalisation". That is advice about code they did not write. Here the
indices come from a detector, not from a person transcribing published
breaks, which is precisely the wrapper case §600 argued the dropping is
*right* for.

The report is therefore a **classed condition**:

```r
warning(structure(
  class = c("ggchangepoint_cp_dropped", "warning", "condition"),
  list(message = msg, call = NULL)))
```

and `run_registered_method()` muffles that class and nothing else, so any
other warning `as_ggcpt()` raises still reaches the caller. Text-matching
would have worked today and broken the first time the message was reworded.

**Measured after:** a registered detector returning `c(0L, 80L, 500L)`,
`80.4` or `c(80L, 80L)` is silent and still normalised to `cp = 80` with
`registered = TRUE`; the same three values through `as_ggcpt()` directly
all warn. Both directions are tested, and the test also asserts the
condition's class, so a future rewrite to a plain `warning()` fails rather
than silently un-muffling.

### 603.1 The other two were the tests, and they are better for it

`test-050-registry.R` already had a block named "as_ggcpt() drops what it
documents and refuses what it cannot read" -- so the dropping was a
deliberate, tested decision, which is the strongest argument that
warn-rather-than-refuse was the right scope call. Six assertions there and
three more in two other blocks now use `expect_warning()` with the message,
and the three that lose nothing (reordering, empty input, a numeric string)
use `expect_silent()`. The file went from four warnings to none, and the
assertions went from "the value is right" to "the value is right and the
package said what it did".

## 604. Verification

Full suite via `testthat::test_local()`: no failures; the standing two
skips (`mcp` needs JAGS, TCPD is not downloaded) and the two upstream
`envcpt` warnings are unchanged, and the four `as_ggcpt` warnings this pass
introduced into the report are gone -- asserted rather than emitted.

## 605. `cpt_simulate()` is right about everything it builds, and silent in one direction

`cpt_power()`, `cpt_benchmark()` and `cpt_datasets()` are all scored
against what `cpt_simulate()` says it generated, so its arithmetic is
load-bearing for every number the package reports about accuracy. Measured
against the definitions rather than against a recorded value:

| property | asked | realised |
|---|---|---|
| mean jump | 0.5 / 2 / 5 | error +0.0025 (se 0.017) at all three |
| sd ratio | 2 / 4 | 2.039 (se 0.021) / 4.079 (se 0.041) |
| `seg_id` breaks | 1, 2 and 4 changepoints | exactly at the requested indices |
| AR(1) `rho` | 0.3 / 0.7 | 0.301 (se 0.010) / 0.697 (se 0.008) |
| t(3) tail | heavier | kurtosis 20.2 against Gaussian 2.9 |

The sd-ratio numbers sit slightly high because `sd()` on 200 points is
biased that way, not because the generator is. **Nothing wrong with any of
it.**

### 605.1 The finding was in the direction nothing checked

`k` changepoints make `k + 1` segments, and the two mismatch directions
were treated differently:

```r
cpt_simulate(400, changepoints = 200, params = c(0))        # warns
cpt_simulate(400, changepoints = 200, params = c(0, 3, 9))  # silent
```

Too few already warned, and the comment above it says why -- the last value
is recycled, so the trailing changepoints would be recorded as ground truth
with no change behind them. Too many used the first two and dropped the
`9`: an ordinary two-segment series handed back to a caller who had plainly
meant two changepoints, whose power or benchmark numbers are then scored
against a truth they did not intend.

Now warns both ways, naming the changepoint count, the segment count and
how many entries went unused, for every `change_in` rather than only
`"mean"` -- checked on `var` and `meanvar` as well. Silent when the counts
agree, when `params` is left at its default, and when there are no
changepoints at all.

**The same shape as §600**, one file over: a documented normalisation that
is audible in one direction and silent in the other, where the silent one
is the one a miscount lands in.

## 606. Why round 6 could not finish the `fcov` measurement

§601 left the functional methods' false-positive rate open because the
finer-grid run had to be abandoned. The reason turns out to be worth more
than the answer. Timed one call at a time, against `fmean_wrapper()` on
identical input so the comparison is the same package and the same data:

| input | `fmean` | `fcov` |
|---|---|---|
| \eqn{n = 60}, \eqn{p = 5} | 4.5 s | **316 s** |
| \eqn{n = 120}, \eqn{p = 5} | 2.9 s | **598 s** |
| \eqn{n = 120}, \eqn{p = 15} | 4.5 s | not measured |

**`fcov` is five to ten minutes on a hundred-point series** and roughly
linear in \eqn{n} -- a factor of seventy to two hundred over `fmean`. So
round 6's twelve-draw sweep at \eqn{p = 5} was an hour of work before it
reached \eqn{p = 15}, and round 7's smaller retry (8 draws, \eqn{n = 120})
was still unfinished at 43 minutes. That is not a defect in the sweep; it
is the engine.

It *is* a documentation gap. Two wrappers already carry a cost section --
`?taylor_wrapper`'s "Series length, and why you cannot interrupt it" and
`?ocd_wrapper`'s "How long this takes" -- and `fcov` is the third and by
far the most extreme. Someone who picks it out of `cpt_methods()` and calls
it on their data will conclude the session has hung. `?fcov_wrapper` now
says so, with the numbers, the linearity in \eqn{n}, the fact that the cost
is in the engine's covariance-operator estimation rather than in anything
this wrapper could tune, and the explicit advice not to put it in a loop
(a twelve-replicate study at \eqn{n = 120} is two hours).

**Interruptibility was deliberately not claimed.** Both runs were killed
from outside the session, which is not the same as testing whether
`setTimeLimit()` is honoured -- the experiment `?taylor_wrapper` did do.
Recorded as untested rather than asserted either way.

### 606.1 And the false-positive question stays open, now with a reason

`fcov` reported a changepoint on 4 of 12 pure-noise draws at \eqn{p = 5}
and `kwc` on 3 of 12 (§601). Whether that is a coarse grid outside the
methods' design case or a loose threshold is still unresolved, and at
roughly ten minutes a call the study that would settle it costs hours.
Left open, with the cost documented so the next attempt can be budgeted
rather than abandoned.

## 607. The three closed-form criteria are right, and one of three was reproducible

`cpt_select()`'s `value` column is what a user compares rungs by, so the
first question is whether it is the number it claims. Checked against
reference implementations written from the definitions, sharing no code
with the package:

```
cost   = n log(RSS/n)
bic    = cost + (2K + 1) log n
aic    = cost + 2(2K + 1)
mbic   = cost + 3K log n + sum_i log(l_i / n)      (Zhang & Siegmund 2007)
```

Every rung of a seven-rung ladder, for all three criteria, at that rung's
own changepoint locations: **exact agreement, 21 comparisons, no
violations.** The `cost` column is the Gaussian profile cost at those
locations, exactly one row is marked `chosen`, and it is the argmin of
`value`.

The behaviour is a bonus check on the docs. On a 300-point series with
changes at 100 and 200:

| criterion | chose |
|---|---|
| `bic` | K = 2 |
| `mbic` | K = 2 |
| `aic` | K = 6, the largest rung offered |

which is precisely what `?cpt_select` warns about -- "its \eqn{2k} penalty
does not grow with \eqn{n}, so it over-selects changepoints, often taking
every rung offered". The prose was right and is now a test.

### 607.1 The gap was which formulas got written down

Inside one `\describe` block, `"mbic"` was given in full and the other two
were not:

> \item{`"bic"`}{Gaussian BIC over the ladder.}
> \item{`"aic"`}{Gaussian AIC over the ladder. ...}

"Gaussian BIC" does not identify a number. Both the cost convention
(\eqn{n\log(\mathrm{RSS}/n)} against \eqn{-2\log L} with its constants,
against the raw RSS) and the changepoint parameter count (\eqn{2K + 1},
\eqn{2K + 2}, \eqn{K + 1}) vary between authors, and the reader who wants
to know why rung 3 beats rung 2 cannot get there from the page. Both
formulas are now stated, with the parameter count spelled out as \eqn{K}
locations plus \eqn{K + 1} segment means, and a pointer that the first term
is the `cost` column they can already see.

Same shape as §588: a returned number whose definition was not on the page.
The test pins the formulas rather than recorded values, so a change to what
a criterion *means* fails instead of passing with a new number.

`signal_mix()`, `signal_stairs()`, `signal_teeth()`, `rcpt()`,

Confirmed independently by the check below: `checking examples ... OK` and
`re-building of vignette outputs ... OK` with no new warnings, so the three

## 610. Three quantities that are right, and the one argument that is not

Round 9 measured four computed surfaces against their definitions. Three
came back clean, which is worth recording so they are not re-swept.

**`cpt_delay()`** -- seven hand-built alarm tables where the answer is known
before the call, plus the matching rules and every summary:

| case | expected | got |
|---|---|---|
| alarm 5 after the change | delay 5, detected | correct |
| alarm *before* the change | miss + 1 false alarm | correct |
| alarm exactly at the change | delay 0 | correct |
| two alarms after one change | first wins, second is a false alarm | correct |
| `max_delay = 10`, alarm at +20 | miss + false alarm | correct |
| `max_delay = 10`, alarm at +8 | delay 8 | correct |
| no alarms at all | miss, 0 false alarms | correct |

and: one alarm cannot be claimed by two changes; an alarm past the *next*
true change is not credited to the earlier one; alarms partition exactly
into detections plus false alarms; `mean_delay`, `median_delay`,
`n_detected` and `arl = n_obs / n_false_alarms` all equal their
definitions; `arl` is `Inf` rather than `NaN` when nothing fired falsely.
**No violations.**

**`cpt_label_error()`** -- Hocking's definition, region by region. All nine
combinations of the three label types against 0, 1 and several
changepoints inside; both window boundaries inclusive as documented; per
region counting; and both guards refusing by name (an unknown `change`
level, and `end < start`). **No violations.** This matters more than most:
it is the objective `cpt_learn_penalty()` minimises, so an error here
would propagate the way a wrong `cpt_simulate()` would.

**`cpt_report()`** -- both text formats write a file and return the lines;
markdown fences balance and headings exist; `session = FALSE` drops the
section (78 to 40 lines) and `confint` behaves exactly as documented --
skipped for an engine with no native intervals whether `TRUE` or `FALSE`,
and a nine-line "Location intervals" section for `smuce`, which is the
"uses the engine's own intervals when it has them and skips the section
otherwise" the help page promises. A no-changepoint result still produces
75 lines, and a path in a nonexistent directory is refused before the
report is built.

## 611. `min_votes` had an unreachable setting and a boundary in the worst place

`cpt_consensus()`'s clustering is also correct -- eight hand cases,
including that the tolerance boundary is inclusive (100 and 105 merge at
`tolerance = 5`, 100 and 106 do not), that clustering is by **leader**
rather than transitive (100, 105, 110 gives two clusters, not one), that a
single method contributing two nearby locations is still one vote, and that
`cp` is the cluster median with `spread` its range.

The argument on top of it is where the two findings are.

### 611.1 A threshold nothing can reach

```r
cpt_consensus(x, methods = c("pelt", "binseg"), min_votes = 3)
```

resolves to a threshold of 3 against two methods, keeps nothing, and
returns an ordinary empty consensus. **An empty consensus is a finding** --
it means the methods agreed on nothing -- so returning one for an
arithmetic impossibility spends the reader's trust on the wrong thing. Now
warns, and names the number of methods that *ran* rather than the number
requested, because a method that errors is already excluded from the vote
and that is exactly how someone lands here without having typed a silly
number.

Same reasoning as round 1's `cpt_benchmark(methods = character(0))` guard.

### 611.2 The boundary is at "unanimous"

The rule is: strictly between 0 and 1 is a proportion, anything else is a
count. Measured with three methods:

| `min_votes` | threshold | means |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 2 | half |
| 0.99 | 3 | all three |
| **1** | **1** | **any one method** |
| 2 | 2 | two |
| 3 | 3 | all three |

So the two neighbouring values 0.99 and 1 mean *opposite* things -- the
strictest setting available and the loosest -- and 1 is precisely what a
reader thinking in proportions writes for unanimity. Nothing was wrong with
the arithmetic; what was missing is that the page said only "pass a
fraction in \eqn{(0, 1)} for a proportion", which is true and does not warn
anybody. `@param min_votes` now gives the table's content in prose, names
the trap, and says to pass the method count or a fraction just below 1 for
unanimity. The new warning repeats it, since an over-large count is the
likeliest way to discover the boundary the hard way.

Deliberately **not** changed: `min_votes = 1` still means a count of one. A
count of one is a legitimate request ("any method that saw it"), and
reinterpreting it would break code that works.

## 612. The Demsar diagram cited nobody

`autoplot(plot_type = "critical_difference")` is documented as

> the Demsar diagram: mean ranks with the Nemenyi critical distance, the
> standard way this literature says "method A beats method B"

which names a method, a diagram and a literature. `grep` for the citation:

```
$ grep -n "demsar" inst/REFERENCES.bib
$ grep -rn "insertRef" R/benchmark.R
54:  \insertRef{vandenburg2020evaluation}{ggchangepoint}
472:  \insertRef{vandenburg2020evaluation}{ggchangepoint}
```

**Nothing.** The metrics on the same page cite van den Burg and Williams;
the statistical procedure the plot is built on cited no one. The package's
own standard is stricter than that -- a test asserts that every
`\insertRef` key in `R/` resolves in `inst/REFERENCES.bib`, and another
that every available method has a `cpt_cite()` entry -- so the omission is
against the house rule rather than merely thin.

### 612.1 The arithmetic was right, which is why this is the finding

`nemenyi_cd()` is three lines and correct:

```r
q <- stats::qtukey(1 - alpha, nmeans = k, df = Inf) / sqrt(2)
q * sqrt(k * (k + 1) / (6 * N))
```

Checked against **Demsar (2006) Table 5** rather than against a
re-derivation, for \eqn{k = 2, \ldots, 10}:

| k | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| published | 1.960 | 2.343 | 2.569 | 2.728 | 2.850 | 2.949 | 3.031 | 3.102 | 3.164 |
| computed | 1.9600 | 2.3437 | 2.5690 | 2.7278 | 2.8497 | 2.9483 | 3.0309 | 3.1017 | 3.1637 |

Worst deviation \eqn{7 \times 10^{-4}}, which is the table's own rounding.
The `sqrt(2)` -- the constant most often dropped in reimplementations of
this diagram -- is there.

`benchmark_ranks()` is right too: rank 1 to the largest value for a
higher-is-better metric and to the smallest for a lower-is-better one, `NA`
taking the **worst** rank in both directions rather than being dropped,
ties sharing the average, `mean_rank` averaging over datasets (hand-checked
at 1.25 and 1.75 on a two-dataset grid with one tie), and an all-`NA`
metric returning `NULL` instead of a table of ties.

### 612.2 What the section adds

A correct number that no one can interpret is not much use, and this one
invites a conclusion. `?cpt_benchmark` gains "Reading the
critical-difference diagram", covering the three things the picture cannot
say:

- **what rank 1 means, and which way each metric is ranked** -- the
  `lower_better` set lives in the source and was nowhere on the page;
- **that `NA` takes the worst rank**, so a method that failed on a dataset
  is penalised for it rather than quietly scoring on a smaller sample;
- **the formula for the bar**, since round 8 established that a plotted or
  returned number should be reproducible from the page.

And the caveat the diagram structurally cannot show: **Nemenyi is a
post-hoc test.** The convention is to run it only after a Friedman test
rejects the null of equal ranks, and `autoplot()` does not run that omnibus
test -- it draws what it is asked for. With the handful of datasets
`cpt_datasets()` supplies, \eqn{N} is small and \eqn{CD} correspondingly
wide, so the page says to read such a diagram descriptively. Left as a
caveat rather than made into a gate: refusing to draw the diagram without
a Friedman test would remove a feature, and running one silently would
change what the function does.

## 613. `cpt_stability()`, and a fixed bug that stayed fixed

`freq = hits / B` where `hits` counts, per index, the replicates whose
\eqn{\pm} `margin` window covered it. The code carries a note about an
earlier defect -- incrementing once per changepoint double-counted a
replicate wherever two detections' windows overlapped, and the old
`pmin(hits / B, 1)` clipped the excess out of sight, reporting 1.00
("re-detected every time") for indices only half the replicates covered.

The invariant that catches a regression is not the range but the
granularity: if `hits` is a count of replicates then **every frequency is
an exact multiple of \eqn{1/B}**, and double-counting breaks that before it
breaks \eqn{[0, 1]}. Measured at \eqn{B = 40}: every one of 240 frequencies
is a multiple of 0.025, 1.00 at the true change and 0.00 in the quiet
stretches. Now a test, phrased as the multiple rather than the bound.

## 614. Three surfaces measured, three correct -- and the finding was in reading one

Round 11 took the remaining computed quantities. Recorded because after ten
passes the informative result is increasingly *which* surfaces are clean.

**`cpt_penalty()`** -- 96 comparisons against the documented formulas,
across four series lengths and four changepoint counts:

```
BIC = SIC = k log n            AIC = 2k
MBIC = 0.5(k+1) log n + log C(n, k)
Hannan-Quinn = 2k log log n    sSIC = k (log n)^alpha
```

Exact at every point, `None` is 0, each penalty increases in \eqn{k}, and
the orderings the page asserts hold at all nine \eqn{(n, k)} pairs tried:
sSIC > BIC, MBIC > BIC, BIC > AIC. All six guards refuse by name --
`alpha <= 1` for sSIC (the definition needs \eqn{\alpha > 1}), `k`
outside \eqn{[0, n]} for MBIC (where `lchoose` would return `-Inf` and
silently invert the penalty), \eqn{n < 3} for the \eqn{\log n} penalties,
and an unknown type -- including the documented exemption that AIC is fine
at \eqn{n = 2} because \eqn{2k} does not involve \eqn{n}.

**`cpt_min_detectable()`** -- the bisection holds its invariant. The trace
opens on both range endpoints, adds at most `max_iter` midpoints, and every
midpoint lies strictly inside the interval the earlier evaluations left
(measured: final bracket \eqn{[0.866, 1.019]} around a reported 1.019 at
achieved power 0.833). Both degenerate brackets are *reported* rather than
returned as a number the search never found: an unreachable target gives
`jump = NA` with "Even the largest change tried (0.05 sd) reached only 0
power", and a target already met at the bottom gives `jump = range[1]` with
"the answer is at or below it".

**`cpt_annotate_events()`** -- the matching is right in every direction
tried. The tolerance boundary is inclusive on the position scale (offset 5
matches at `tolerance = 5`, offset 6 does not, offset 1 does not at
`tolerance = 0`), and a `Date` column is read on the index scale rather
than as a position: an event on the first date lands at position 1, not at
the changepoint 100 positions away.

### 614.1 The finding: I misread the table while holding the source open

`tidy()` on a `ggcpt_events` flattens the object's three slots into **one**
table with a `status` column:

```
                   status  cp event position distance
1 unexplained_changepoint 100  <NA>      100       NA
2        undetected_event  NA     e      106       NA
```

so the row count is the number of changepoints *plus* the number of events,
and -- the part that matters -- **an `unexplained_changepoint` row carries
a non-missing `cp`.** The sweep for this round inferred "matched" from
`!is.na(cp)` and reported seven false violations before the table was
printed. That is the natural reading, and in a user's hands
`subset(tidy(x), !is.na(cp))` returns the matched pairs *and* the
changepoints no event explains -- silently overstating how much the events
account for, which is the whole question `cpt_annotate_events()` exists to
answer.

`@return` documents the object's three slots (`matched`, `unexplained`,
`undetected`) thoroughly and never said what `tidy()` does with them, nor
that the three `status` values exist. They appeared nowhere but two
`tibble::tibble(status = ...)` calls in `communicate.R`. Now on the page,
with which column is `NA` in each row shape and an explicit "filter on
`status`, not on `is.na(cp)`".

Same class as §588 and §607: a returned table whose values were not
documented. The distinguishing feature of this one is that the evidence it
was worth writing down is that it caught me.

### 614.2 What this round ships

No behaviour change. One documentation fix, and **three previously
untested contracts pinned**: `cpt_penalty()`'s formulas, orderings and
guards; `cpt_min_detectable()`'s bracketing and both degenerate reports;
and the events table's three statuses, tolerance boundary and index-scale
handling. §232.4's conclusion was to pair every documentation fix with the
assertion that keeps it true, and the measured record is that checked
surfaces stay complete while unchecked ones decay -- so on a round that
found the code right, the tests are the deliverable.

## 615. The penalty learner is right, and its coefficients do not mean what they look like

Round 9 verified `cpt_label_error()` -- the objective. Round 12 takes the
two pieces built on it, neither of which had a test.

**`target_interval()`** implements Hocking's construction: the longest run
of penalties achieving the minimum label error, open at whichever end of
the grid the run touches. All seven grid shapes:

| grid errors | target |
|---|---|
| `2 0 0 1 3` | \eqn{[\log 2, \log 4]} |
| `0 0 1 2` | \eqn{(-\infty, \log 2]} |
| `2 1 0 0` | \eqn{[\log 4, \infty)} |
| `0 0 0` | \eqn{(-\infty, \infty)} |
| `2 0 1 3` (single optimum) | \eqn{[\log 2, \log 2]} |
| `0 1 0 0 0 1` (two runs) | \eqn{[\log 4, \log 16]}, the longer |
| `NA NA NA` | \eqn{(-\infty, \infty)} |

**`interval_regression()`** is the squared-hinge fit. Its reported loss
equals the objective recomputed at the weights it returns, the search
improves on the constant it starts from (2.500 to 0.501), a prediction
comfortably inside every interval costs exactly zero, and an infinite bound
contributes nothing on its side rather than `Inf`.

**End to end**, five labelled series: every learned penalty lands inside
that series' own target interval. And the model is genuinely a function of
the series -- four series of very different length and noise give four
distinct predictions from eight non-zero feature weights, so the earlier
observation that five near-identical series all got 63.036 was the right
answer rather than a degenerate learner.

### 615.1 What the numbers looked like, and why that is a doc fix

```
       intercept            log_n        log_log_n           log_sd
         4.46931         -0.03716         -0.01238         -0.00985
```

Every non-intercept coefficient negative, so the predicted penalty
*decreases* with \eqn{n}:

```
  short_loud   n=80   64.88
  long_loud    n=800  59.35
```

A reader who knows BIC grows like \eqn{\log n} will read that as the model
having learned the opposite, and it has learned nothing of the kind. **The
labels did not pin the slope.** Every one of those four target intervals is
open above -- \eqn{[\log 8, \infty)} -- because the largest penalty on the
grid still keeps the single changepoint the labels ask for. When every
interval is open above, any sufficiently large prediction is optimal, the
problem is under-determined in the slopes, and the \eqn{L_2} term settles
them near zero with whatever sign BFGS happened to reach. The predictions
are all inside their targets, which is the only property the fit is for.

That is the common case, not a contrived one: a one-change label plus a
generous penalty grid produces an open-above target nearly every time.

So `?cpt_learn_penalty` gains two things. The `@return` now states that
**`coef()` is on the log-penalty scale and `predict()` on the natural
one** -- previously it said only that both methods exist, which leaves a
coefficient of \eqn{-0.04} looking additive when it is multiplicative. And
a "Reading the coefficients" section says the signs are usually not
interpretable, why (the open-above targets), and what to do if they need to
be: widen `penalties` until the largest over-segments, so the intervals
close above, with `cpt_label_error_curve()` to show whether they did.

A test pins the scale relation by rebuilding a prediction from
`coef()` and `cpt_features()` by hand, so the two scales cannot drift
apart silently.

## 615.2 The test asserted a property of the data, and the suite said so

The block written for §615 ended with

```r
expect_gt(length(unique(round(preds, 6))), 1L)
```

-- four series of very different length and noise must get four different
penalties. It passed on the seed used while measuring and **failed in the
full suite**, where a different seed produced four series whose targets are
all open above. Then the fit is a constant, all four predictions are equal,
and the assertion is false.

Which is the finding, stated more sharply than §615.1 had it: with
open-above targets the model does not merely have uninterpretable slopes,
it **reduces to a constant** -- `predict()` returns the same penalty for
every series. Both measured outcomes (slightly negative slopes on one
draw, all-zero weights on another) put every prediction inside its target,
which is the only property the fit is for.

The test now asserts the implication rather than the antecedent: *if* any
feature weight is non-zero the predictions must differ, and if none is they
must all be equal. That is a property of the model form, true whichever way
the labels fall. `?cpt_learn_penalty` gained the constant case explicitly,
because a user who asked for a *learned* penalty and got one number back
would otherwise reasonably think something had gone wrong.

Worth recording as my own instance of the mistake this loop keeps finding
in the package: an assertion about what the data happened to do, in place
of one about what the code guarantees.
